title: Tozero announces first delivery of recycled lithium carbonate to customers - electrive.com
content:
The German lithium-ion battery recycling startup Tozero has delivered its first recycled lithium carbonate to an industrial customer, Botz GmbH. The material was produced at Tozero's new demonstration plant in the Gendorf Chemical Park near Munich.
Image: Tozero
Tozero specialises in recovering lithium carbonate
The recyclate is produced in a
demonstration plant opened in March
at the Gendorf chemical park in Upper Bavaria. The site is located just a few kilometres from the German-Austrian border and is expected to process around 500 tonnes of battery waste per year.
Processing black mass, the chemical mix after batteries are collected and crushed, is currently dominated by China, where more than 85% of global refining capacity is concentrated. The remaining capacity is highly concentrated elsewhere in Asia.
Daniel Schulze Zur Verth, Managing Director of Botz GmbH, states: “Receiving recycled lithium carbonate from tozero marks an important milestone in our collaboration and reflects our shared ambition to build more sustainable, resilient and regionally anchored supply chains. Increasing the use of recycled raw materials will be an important part of reducing reliance on primary resources and lowering the environmental footprint of industrial production.”
Tozero was founded in 2022 and has developed an efficient process to recover high-purity lithium and graphite from used batteries. The startup aims to recover over 80 per cent of the lithium from old batteries. Tozero focuses on processing the black mass containing valuable battery active materials, while battery dismantling is outsourced to specialised partners.
Dr Ksenija Neumann, founder and Co-CEO of Tozero, said, “Delivering a product that meets the requirements of an industrial customer is an important moment for any deep-tech company. It reflects years of dedication, problem-solving and determination by our team. From the beginning, we believed that innovation needs to have a clear industrial purpose and that every euro invested should move us closer to creating real value for our customers.”
Although Tozero already delivered its first batches of recycled material to European customers in 2024, this lithium was still produced on a small scale from the pilot plants in Munich. With the demonstration plant in Gendorf, near Munich, the plant’s output is expected to increase to scale. The company is also expanding its network and, according to its own statements, now works with partners in ten European countries. The recycled lithium carbonate is currently being sold primarily to customers in the construction, ceramics, and lubricants sectors. Further raw materials and industries are to follow, says Tozero. The German company says it is also targeting the battery industry, with the long-term goal of returning recycled lithium from end-of-life batteries directly to battery cell production. The first prerequisite is the recovery of battery-grade lithium.

title: Cadillac Vistiq Sport Review Tested
content:
Charging
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
We spent a week testing Cadillac's electric SUV on Tesla chargers and busy highways, with mixed results.
November 11, 2026
4 Min Read
Cadillac Vistiq EV.
General Motors Co.
At a Glance
NACS port lets Vistiq charge at Tesla stations, but cable length creates parking challenges
Supercruise handles open highways well, but hesitates in dense, aggressive traffic
Stiff suspension and big wheels mean the Vistiq rides rougher than classic Cadillac luxury
A week in the $83,256 (as tested, including destination) 2027
Cadillac
Vistiq Sport provided more time with General Motors’ Supercruise driver assistance system and our first use of Tesla Supercharger charging stations with the Vistiq’s new
North American Charging System (NACS)
charging port.
The car’s dual-motor all-wheel-drive system is rated at 615 horsepower and 650 lb.-ft. of torque, which is obviously more than sufficient for a mid-sized three-row family SUV.
NACS Charging
The EPA estimates the Vistiq’s 102-kilowatt-hour NCMA lithium-ion battery pack provides 300 miles of driving range on a charge, but in recent mild fall weather, our test vehicle’s computer predicted 311 miles. The EPA turned out to be right, as a 233-mile trip consumed 240 miles of the forecast range.
Angling the Vistiq into the Supercharger station so the short charging cable will reach the car's side-mounted charge port. DAN CARNEY
For the 2027 model year, the Vistiq gains a NACS charging port, and it provided our first chance to visit a Tesla Supercharger station. On arrival at the row of 8 charging stations, there were two Tesla Model Ss on hand. Fortunately, they were on one end of the row, because I quickly realized that the stubby little charge cable on the Tesla chargers is too short to reach the Vistiq’s charge port on the driver’s side front fender.
This is a convenient location for home charging, and it works fine at other public charging stations, but the shorter Tesla cables are designed to reach only the rear-mounted charge ports on the company’s own cars, when they are backed into the space in front of the charger. To charge the Vistiq, I had to parallel park across several spaces in front of the chargers to get the port close enough.
The 67 kWh of juice cost $41.65, and charging from a 20% state of charge to 75% took 31 minutes even though the battery was preconditioned before starting. The car promised to charge to 80% in 30 minutes, but it began tapering the charge rate early in the process, so the initial 166 kW rate slowed to only 80 kW by a 70% SoC. Then the car predicted that it would take 40 minutes to reach 80%, but the prospect of additional slowing caused me to pull the plug at 75%.
Supercruise
The Vistiq’s Supercruise system works as advertised on the highway, though it continues to struggle with the multilane mayhem of roads like Interstate 95. In terms of providing adaptive cruise control and managing stop-and-go traffic while automatically following the road, the system works well.
But in terms of interacting with other cars, Supercruise has the awkward timing and lack of foresight of driver’s ed student. The system can change lanes automatically on its own or when the driver prompts it by activating the turn signal. In either case, it is far too timid and slow in initiating the lane change.
This is surely meant as a conservative, safe-driving approach, but it has the effect of more frequently cutting off fast-approaching drivers in the lane being entered. That’s because Supercruise waits too long to realize that it wants to overtake slower traffic in its current lane. By the time it decides to make the change, it often has to slow to match the speed of that slow-moving car.
Now, when it moves into the next lane, where the traffic is moving faster, it is going more slowly than it would have been going if it had made the merge before catching up to the car that was in the way. This is exacerbated by Supercruise being slow to actually then make the merge into the other lane.
Nature abhors a vacuum, and a traffic opening is the same, attracting drivers to fill open space. These delays invite others to move into that space, at which point Supercruise stumbles belatedly toward the rapidly closing spot, cutting off the other car.
The system is also bad at recognizing when other drivers are behaving aggressively. In the belated merge situation, there are drivers who won’t yield. Supercruise seems pretty willing to collide with them, or come closer to doing so that I’m comfortable with, so I found myself overriding lane changes and/or braking to avoid collisions caused by its inept decision-making. This is supposed to make driving more relaxing, remember?
Supercruise seems very useful on lightly traveled highways, but at this point, using it on congested roads filled with aggressive drivers seems more trouble than it is worth.
Road Manners
The Vistiq rolls on 21-inch wheels, which are not absurdly huge by contemporary standards. But the low-profile tires they use, combined with the stiff spring rate needed to support the car’s heavy battery pack combine to transmit harsh road impacts directly to the cabin.
Rolling on a rural highway that seemingly suffered heat-related asphalt buckling made it clear that the Vistiq does not ride like a Cadillac. The heat buckles had been shaved off, leaving behind stripes of asphalt patches across the lane at regular intervals, sort of the tarmac equivalent of concrete expansion joints. These hammered the Vistiq’s occupants relentlessly, leaving us to fantasize about the Cadillac road yachts of yore, which would have absorbed these road imperfections imperceptibly.

title: IEA: Batteries Move to Center of Renewable Energy Growth
content:
Battery Applications
Stationary Batteries
Market Analysis
Industry Trends
IEA says batteries are central to renewable growth, with storage reshaping solar economics, grid flexibility, and energy resilience worldwide today.
November 10, 2026
4 Min Read
Battery energy storage system for residential use with solar panel on roof.
2229678200/iStock / Getty Images Plus
Battery storage was often framed as a complementary technology to renewable energy rather than central to it. Solar and wind attracted most of the attention, but the balance is now shifting. The International Energy Agency’s
Renewables 2026
report suggests batteries, especially behind-the-meter systems installed at homes and businesses, are becoming increasingly important to how renewable electricity is used, valued, and integrated into power systems.
Recent coverage in
Battery Technology
also reflects this shift. The article “
7 Residential Battery Storage Systems Worth Buying in 2026
” shows that home batteries are increasingly positioned as part of an integrated energy system, with newer models combining storage, controls, and EV charging. The piece “
Understanding Base Power’s role in energy storage solutions
” similarly highlights how distributed batteries are linked to grid reliability and cost savings. Together, the articles suggest that batteries are viewed less as stand-alone products and more as a bridge between the home and the wider power system.
Related:
Why Solid-State Batteries Matter for Space
Rapid growth changes the scale of the story
The IEA’s projections indicate that behind-the-meter battery storage is moving beyond a niche market. The report says installed capacity is set to “expand more than fivefold, exceeding 670 GWh by 2031,” while power capacity reaches roughly 290 GW. Over 2026-2031, more than 550 GWh of energy storage capacity is expected to be added.
Those figures suggest storage is no longer peripheral to renewable deployment. It is becoming part of the infrastructure that supports the next phase of market growth. As renewable electricity takes a larger share of total generation, systems need more flexibility to absorb and shift that power. Batteries are increasingly providing part of that flexibility.
Global installed behind-the-meter energy storage capacity (left) and power storage capacity (right) by segment, 2020-2031. Courtesy of IEA.
According to the report, declining battery costs are improving the case for households and businesses to install storage alongside solar. In many markets, batteries now offer a clearer route to self-consumption, cost savings, and reduced exposure to high retail electricity prices.
Behind-the-meter storage gains strategic importance
Behind-the-meter batteries differ from utility-scale storage because they are installed on the customer side of the meter. The IEA notes that behind-the-meter systems allow households and businesses to “increase self-consumption, lower electricity costs and reduce peak demand.” That combination is important at both the consumer and system level. For the user, storage can improve the value of solar generation and reduce reliance on expensive electricity purchased during peak periods. For the grid, widespread battery adoption can ease pressure on networks and reduce demand spikes.
Related:
Robot Dogs & Mobile Chargers Power Up Detroit's Smart Parking Test Bed
Commercial demand broadens the market
Another sign that batteries are becoming central to renewable growth is the changing customer mix. Residential batteries still account for the majority of behind-the-meter storage capacity today, but the IEA expects commercial deployment to accelerate sharply over the next several years.
According to the report, “growth is increasingly balanced across customer segments,” with commercial storage expected to account for almost half of global additions during 2026-2031. That marks a meaningful shift from the previous period, when residential systems dominated more clearly.
Global net additions of behind-the-meter energy storage capacity (left) by segment, 2020-2031 and (right) by country and segment, 2026-2031. Courtesy of IEA.
This matters because broader commercial adoption suggests the market is maturing. Storage is no longer limited mainly to early adopters in the residential sector. Businesses are increasingly seeing value in batteries for peak shaving, load shifting, and energy cost management. In some markets, batteries are also becoming part of virtual power plant models and demand-response participation.
Solar-plus-storage becomes more common
The growing connection between batteries and distributed solar is another reason storage is moving closer to the center of the renewable story. The IEA projects that annual residential battery additions will rise from the equivalent of 13% of rooftop solar PV additions in 2025 to more than 35% by 2031.
Related:
Public-Private Collaboration Advances Nuclear Power for Space Exploration
That trend shows batteries are being deployed faster than rooftop solar itself in many markets. The report states that in mature rooftop solar markets, battery adoption is “becoming the norm rather than the exception.” Germany illustrates this change clearly: around 80% of new residential solar PV systems installed in 2025 included battery storage.
The implication is straightforward. Renewable generation alone is no longer the full measure of progress. Increasingly, the ability to store and shift that electricity is part of the value proposition.
Annual residential storage additions and residential electricity prices in selected markets, 2021-2025. Courtesy of IEA.
Batteries are increasingly influencing how efficiently renewable electricity can be consumed, monetized, and integrated into the system. As costs fall and deployment expands across residential and commercial markets, battery storage is becoming more central. It is helping renewable power become more flexible, reliable, and practical for everyday use. That shift is making storage a bigger part of how energy systems are built and managed.

Maria Guerra
Senior Editor-Battery Technology, Informa Markets

Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. In addition to her engineering roles, Guerra worked as a freelance technical editor, refining complex technical content for clarity and accuracy. She later became a Power/Analog Editor at

Battery Technology

She is passionate about uncovering the stories that shape the future of electrification, from cutting-edge battery innovations to policy shifts driving sustainable energy.
Guerra is also a member of

title: Hyundai's Boston Dynamics Launches Stretch Gen 2 robot
content:
Hyundai's Boston Dynamics Launches Stretch Gen 2 robot
Prioritise Us
on Google
Boston Dynamics has released an updated version of its Stretch robot, Stretch Gen 2. Credit: Boston Dynamics
Boston Dynamics VP & GM of Logistics Robotics Brian Donnelly has launched an updated model of its Stretch autonomous mobile robot
Inbound logistics remains one of the most labour-intensive and physically demanding nodes within global supply chain networks. Mobile robotics pioneer Boston Dynamics - a wholly-owned subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Group - has unveiled Stretch Gen 2, a next-generation autonomous mobile robot (AMR) specifically designed for warehouse activities, including trailer unloading.
Built upon
operational
data harvested from more than 100,000 industrial operating hours and tens of millions of handled cases, this second-generation platform introduces hardware, electrical, and structural upgrades designed to maximise unit availability, and improve dock-door throughput.
Hardened Hardware for High-Velocity Material Handling
The operational reality of trailer unloading involves navigating unstructured environments, uneven dock floors, and shifting cargo loads. To withstand these harsh physical conditions, Boston Dynamics has re-engineered Stretch’s core electrical and mechanical architectures. The robot now features heavy-duty, automotive-grade connectors specifically rated to withstand the continuous, high-torque vibrations of rapid box grasping.
"With Gen 2, we focused on the things that actually took robots offline in the real world. We made it tougher, we made it simpler to service, and we made sure it keeps getting better long after it's deployed," says Brian Donnelly, Vice President & General Manager of Logistics Robotics at Boston Dynamics.
The upgraded Stretch model has improved robustness and battery life, which will help to improve availability. Credit: Hyundai
Redefining On-Site Maintainability and Fleet Diagnostics
In modern fulfilment centers, every minute of robotic downtime creates a backlog at the receiving dock. Stretch Gen 2 addresses this by utilising a highly modular design that simplifies routine maintenance. By standardising high-strength fasteners and simplifying mechanical sub-assemblies, facility operators can perform rapid component swaps without relying on specialised external robotics field technicians.
This simplified maintenance framework is supported by an upgraded onboard computing platform running advanced, real-time diagnostics. The computing system enables over-the-air software updates that continuously improve case detection, spatial modelling, and motion planning across an entire warehouse fleet.
To safely handle unpredictable case configurations, Stretch Gen 2 features an upgraded vacuum-based gripper head integrated with sensitive pressure valves and advanced spatial array sensors. These sensors detect case shifts in real time, adjusting the robot's approach angle and vacuum seal to prevent drops or carton punctures.
Boston Dynamics showcased the capabilities of its first-generation Stretch robot in 2025. Credit: Hyundai
Key facts about Stretch Gen 2
1,000 cases per hour throughput: Processing mixed-SKU container freight and variable-weight cartons autonomously under real-world dock conditions.
81% internal cabling reduction: Eliminating a half-mile of internal wiring to remove common electrical failure points and reduce maintenance overhead.
1-hour swerve drive replacement: Reducing a critical drive-unit maintenance procedure from 24 hours down to less than 60 minutes.
Dual-shift battery endurance: Operating continuously across two consecutive warehouse shifts on a single charge, supported by a 75-minute fast-charging cycle to 90% capacity.
Zero-programming vision deployment: Utilising a pre-trained machine-learning model that instantly recognises, segments, and picks diverse packaging types from day one.
Hyundai investment in robotics hub
Hyundai acquired full ownership over Boston Dynamics in August 2026, purchasing SoftBank’s remaining shareholding. The acquisition is in line with Hyundai’s strategic focus on robotics.
announced
plans at CES 2026 in Las Vegas earlier this year that production of Boston Dynamics’ Atlas robot, an enterprise grade humanoid robot that can perform a wide array of industrial tasks, from material handling to order fulfilment, was beginning at its Boston manufacturing hub. Hyundai’s Robotics Metaplant Application Center (RMAC) and Google DeepMind were the initial customers for Boston Dynamics’ Atlas model.
In April 2025, Hyundai announced that it was allocating a proportion of a US$26bn investment to build a Robotics Innovation Hub in Georgia. The leading edge robotics facility will have an annual capacity of 30,000 units, and will act as a US hub for design, manufacturing, testing, and deployment.
Strategic Technology & Integration Partners
DHL Supply Chain (3PL Deployment Partner)
is a global leader in third-party logistics, managing contract logistics and supply chain solutions across 220 countries. As an early adopter of Boston Dynamics' automation technology, DHL integrates autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) into its regional distribution networks to streamline retail fulfilment, mitigate labour shortages, and improve workplace safety for its warehouse associates.
Microsoft (Technology Partner)
Microsoft Corporation is a technology leader providing advanced cloud computing infrastructure, database software, and enterprise solutions. In October, Microsoft announced that it would integrate its Copilot AI system directly into Boston Dynamics’ fleet, helping warehouse operators to issue commands in natural language to improve obstacle navigation and spatial reasoning for units in warehouse environments.
Zebra Technologies (Industrial RFID & Scanning Partner)
Zebra Technologies specialises in enterprise asset intelligence, providing barcode printing, mobile computing, data capture, and indoor location solutions. Serving 100 countries, Zebra’s robust warehouse technologies integrate seamlessly with robotic systems, allowing automated guided vehicles (AGVs) and AMRs to instantaneously scan, track, and verify shipping labels during high-speed unloading operations.

title: Unilever & Iron Mountain Establish UAE Logistics Partnership
content:
Unilever & Iron Mountain Establish UAE Logistics Partnership
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leaders gathered for the opening ceremony of the Iron Mountain facility in the UAE. Credit: Iron Mountain
Ahmed Kadous, Customer Operations Head, Unilever GCC, explains the partnership is accelerating flexibility and sustainability in supply chain operations
Unilever and Iron Mountain are taking part in a milestone partnership as they expand their collaboration into the physical supply chain space.
In order to meet demands in the region, Iron Mountain is opening its first warehousing and logistics facility in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), in collaboration with Unilever.
This warehouse represents the first physical one in their partnership which will encourage the organisations to
work together to increase efficiency
in logistics.
Developing global logistics
Iron Mountain is opening its first warehousing and logistics facility in the UAE. The facility will be a 37,000 square foot operation, located in the EZDubai Logistics Hub at Dubai South.
Through the partnership, Iron Mountain is bringing its logistics services to Unilever’s divisions. It will have the capacity to bring bonded and non-bonded warehousing under one roof, demonstrating its capabilities in handling multiple challenges and priorities.
“This partnership marks Iron Mountain's first strategic warehousing and logistics collaboration with Unilever in the UAE and lays the foundation for a more integrated, long-term relationship,” Ako Djaf, Managing Director, Warehousing & Logistics – MENAT / APAC at Iron Mountain, tells Supply Chain Digital.
Ako Djaf, Managing Director, Warehousing & Logistics – MENAT / APAC at Iron Mountain
“By bringing together bonded and non-bonded warehousing, fulfilment, co-packing, product-set assembly and value-added services in a single operation, we're creating a more connected and efficient supply chain.”
As the availability of technology in supply chain and logistics advances, the partnership is looking to integrate drones and automated robotics into its
inventory management operations
. This will help to improve the visibility of inventory and operations, ultimately leading to better and more efficient services.
“Given Unilever's extensive global footprint and Iron Mountain's strong international presence and logistics capabilities, we see significant potential to build on this collaboration beyond the UAE,” Ako continues.
The companies are enhancing logistics efficiency and introducing new technologies in order to drive success in the industry. As the wider aim is to “maximise operational synergies”, Ako anticipates the partnership could be replicated in other markets around the world.
At a glance
Iron Mountain partners with more than 240,000 customers across 61 countries
Its partner base includes approximately 95% of the Fortune 1000
Iron Mountain and Unilever are introducing a 37,000 square-metre facility in the UAE
More than 3.7 billion people use Unilever products every day
Unilever Arabia has 18 brands in operation
Ribbon cutting ceremony for the new facility. Credit: Iron Mountain
A long standing partnership
As modern supply chains become more complex, the need for resilience and control increases. Iron Mountain’s solutions are built to adapt and grow, helping businesses maintain performance throughout disruption.
The partnership between Unilever and Iron Mountain spans two decades, with Unilever having chosen Iron Mountain Digital's Connected Backup/PC solution to secure and
automate data recovery
for its employees in 2016. Now, the partnership is being moved into the physical supply chain space, with the aim of enhancing inventory visibility and logistics coordination.
Through this facility, Iron Mountain is physically establishing itself in the region, demonstrating a commitment to the UAE as a strategic base.
Unilever has more than 70 years of business in the region, with 18 brands and more than 1,000 employees in factories and offices across its Unilever Arabia branch.
“At Unilever, our customers and consumers are at the heart of how we operate, and we are continually looking for ways to become more responsive, agile, resilient and reliable in serving them,” explains Ahmed Kadous, Customer Operations Head at Unilever GCC, Turkey, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
Ahmed Kadous, Customer Operations Head at Unilever GCC, Turkey, Pakistan and Bangladesh
“Our partnership with Iron Mountain brings together local market and export operations with value-added capabilities under one roof, giving us greater flexibility to tailor solutions to evolving customer needs.”
Through the launching of the new facility, the two companies are working to meet customer demand more efficiently, with increased value-added services and technology-enabled inventory management.
We're creating a more connected and efficient supply chain.
Ako Djaf, Managing Director, Warehousing & Logistics – MENAT / APAC at Iron Mountain
The opening ceremony for the warehouse as part of the Unilever x Iron Mountain partnership. Credit: Iron Mountain
Key Partners
Unilever
Unilever is a British-Dutch multinational consumer goods company headquartered in London. It produces food, beverages, cleaning agents, and personal care products. The company owns over 400 brands including Dove, Axe, Lipton, Hellmann's, Knorr and Ben & Jerry's. With operations in approximately 190 countries, Unilever serves 3.4 billion people daily, making it one of the world's largest consumer goods companies by revenue.
Iron Mountain
Iron Mountain is a global leader in information management services, specialising in records storage, data protection, and management of physical and digital assets. Founded in 1951, the company operates in over 50 countries, serving 225,000 organisations worldwide. Services include secure storage facilities, data backup and recovery, document management and secure shredding, helping companies protect critical information and comply with regulatory requirements.
Sanofi is a French multinational pharmaceutical company headquartered in Paris, specialising in prescription medicines, vaccines, and over-the-counter products. As one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, Sanofi focuses on immunology, oncology, rare diseases, diabetes and cardiovascular treatments. Operating in approximately 100 countries with over 100,000 employees, Sanofi invests heavily in research and development to deliver innovative healthcare solutions worldwide.
Boeing is a US multinational aerospace manufacturer and defense corporation, headquartered in Chicago. Founded in 1916, it's one of the world's largest aerospace companies, producing commercial airplanes, military aircraft, satellites, missiles and space vehicles. Major products include the 737, 777, and 787 commercial jetliners, and defense systems. Boeing serves customers in over 150 countries, employing approximately 170,000 people globally.

title: Toyota and Subaru hit the 'sweet spot' with affordable electric SUVs
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 11 2026 - 7:41 am PT
and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
Toyota and Subaru EVs catch on at affordable prices
The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to
Kelley Blue Book
estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.
Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.
Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.
2027 Toyota bZ (Source: Toyota)
While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.
After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the
fourth best-selling EV in the US
, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.
Toyota bZ interior (Source: Toyota)
Starting at $35,000, the
Toyota bZ
is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.
Toyota and Subaru now each sell
three electric SUVs
, which share the same platform and technology.
With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at
Cox Automotive
, said (via
Bloomberg
) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.
Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.
2027 Subaru Uncharted EV (Source: Subaru)
Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).
Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told
Bloomberg
that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”
While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.
Subaru Trailseeker (Source: Subaru)
The Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.
According to the latest
Kelley Blue Book
figures, the average price for a new vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.
Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.
Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

title: Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla's 'flying' Roadster stunt show
content:
Tesla Roadster
Fred Lambert
| Nov 11 2026 - 6:34 am PT
Tesla Roadster image: Tesla. Porsche Mission S image: Porsche
Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,”
according to Bloomberg
Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.
Thrusters vs. a supercar concept
finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster
last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.
It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once.
We reported in June that it had been pushed to August
to make room for SpaceX thruster work.
There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”
Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.
Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.
Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna
rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10”
last month.
Electrek’s Take
Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.
I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he
called the upcoming demo “unforgettable”
and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”
That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then
refilling it takes six to seven hours
So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.
That’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.
It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

title: Genesis reveals GV90 prices start at $100K+ in Korea, but it will cost more for coach doors
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 11 2026 - 6:22 am PT
opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.
Genesis GV90 prices and driving range in Korea
Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.
After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (
which we had the pleasure to see firsthand
), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.
It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.
In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.
Genesis GV90 Neolun (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).
Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis said the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).
Genesis GV90 Trim
Starting Price

Genesis GV90 price by trim in South Korea
A luxury private lounge on wheels
The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.
When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”
The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.
The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.
Together, they create what Genesis calls a new realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.
Genesis GV90 Neolun infotainment display (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.
Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.
A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.
In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.
The GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.
Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.
Genesis GV90 debut (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
Dimensions, battery size, other specs
As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.
That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).
To power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.
The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.
It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.
When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.
Genesis GV90 Neolun (left) GV90 Neolun First Edition (middle) and GV90 (right) Source: Hyundai
“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”
Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.
Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.
What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

title: QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm
content:
Solid-state batteries
batteries
QuantumScape
Fred Lambert
| Nov 11 2026 - 6:00 am PT
QuantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the company says the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.
That’s a big deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement shows these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with important conditions.
QSE cells use a liquid catholyte; Osprey replaces it with a solid sulfide catholyte (Image: QuantumScape)
QuantumScape’s current cells aren’t all-solid-state
Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.
The new white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its
Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose
, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”
The solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.
Osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.
Sulfides as separators: QS still says no
The interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.
The company lists four issues: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.
QuantumScape’s illustration of what 20 atm of stack pressure means on a single cell (Image: QuantumScape)
The pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.
And 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.
So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.
What the Osprey data shows
QuantumScape published four main data sets:
Cycle life: the real result
This is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.
Osprey cycle life: 1C/1C at 30°C and 1 atm in a 2-layer cell (Image: QuantumScape)
QuantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.
But this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.
Fast charging: at 80°C
The press release says “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper shows that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at
(176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”
The 5-minute charge test was run at 80°C (Image: QuantumScape)
Batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.
Cold weather: a tiny cell
“Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.
Capacity retention from -20°C to 45°C in a single-layer test cell (Image: QuantumScape)
That’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.
Energy density: projected
The “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS says high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.
For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.
QuantumScape’s projected energy density and charge-time targets vs. current EVs. Osprey’s position is a QS projection (Image: QuantumScape)
An “open platform” for everyone else’s sulfide cathodes
The business model is the bigger story.
QuantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS says it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.
In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.
That fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and announced a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.
There’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper says the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.
Where this fits in the solid-state race
Everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027.
BYD plans small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027
, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026.
Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform
is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.
CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, said in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.
None of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.
Electrek’s Take
This is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.
The cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.
But you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have said so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.
So QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.
The question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production plans lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

title: It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 11 2026 - 3:40 am PT
Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.
The formula is already sitting right there.
The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created,
with well over 100 million produced
since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.
And a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.
In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.
The beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.
An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.
And Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.
Even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its
Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system
used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.
The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.
The Honda EV Cub concept
unveiled 10 years ago
and subsequently abandoned
There are millions of people riding electric bicycles today
who will eventually want something faster
, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.
It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that
companies specialize in retrofit kits
to convert classic Cubs into EVs.
The Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.
And perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.
Honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a
Cub-like e-scooter in China
. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.
So here I am once again, Honda.
You’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.
Just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

政策第5级: 投资补助/资本支出补贴
政策分类依据: 奥地利EAG光伏与储能补贴，覆盖投资成本30%的补助机制
content:
Markets & Policy
Austria’s third and final funding round for solar and storage in 2026 attracted more than 41,000 applications, but only 7,007 received approval. Funding for the smallest PV systems was exhausted within 29 seconds of the application window opening.
Cornelia Lichner
11 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Highlights
Residential
Only applications for subsidies for photovoltaic systems with a capacity of up to 10 kW submitted between 5:00 p.m. and 5:00:29 p.m. on Oct. 8 were successful in the latest funding round.
The third and final funding round for solar and energy storage systems in Austria for 2026 has concluded. The Renewable Energy Expansion Act (EAG) funding agency announced on Wednesday that it had approved 7,007 applications out of 41,322 submissions, representing approximately €192 million ($212.8 million) in requested subsidies.
The rebates cover up to 30% of eligible investment costs, subject to fixed subsidy rates per kW of installed solar capacity and per kWh of battery storage.
Under the EAG, applications for smaller PV systems are approved on a first-come, first-served basis. In Category A, covering systems up to 10 kW, the available budget of €30.5 million was sufficient only for applications submitted within the first 29 seconds of the funding window opening at 5 p.m. on Oct. 8, according to the agency.
Funding for Category B, covering systems between 10 kW and 20 kW, was exhausted even faster, after just 18 seconds. Systems in Categories A and B are eligible for investment subsidies of €150/kW and €140/kW, respectively, as well as €150/kWh for battery storage.
In Categories C and D, applications are ranked according to the amount of funding requested. In Category C, projects requesting up to €97/kW were approved, while the threshold for Category D was €94/kW.
Annual installation target likely to be missed
Industry association PV&B Austria reiterated its criticism of the Ministry of Energy following the announcement.
“Whether it’s 33 seconds or 29 – if the federal government truly intends to secure Austria’s independent energy supply, we need clear facts and a modern legal framework for the subsidy system from 2027 onwards,” said Vera Immitzer, managing director of PV&B Austria. “The declining figures for new photovoltaic installations are clear proof that an entire industry is left in limbo, despite high demand.”
The effects of the current subsidy system are becoming apparent in Austria’s solar market. Following 1.6 GW of new installations in 2025, PV&B Austria expects approximately 1 GW of additional PV capacity in 2026, a year-on-year decline of about 38%.
This would mark the first time Austria has missed the annual installation target of at least 1.1 GW set out in the EAG. However, the large number of subsidy applications suggests that demand for solar and battery storage remains strong.
Draft EAG amendment expected next week
Austria’s State Secretary for Energy, Elisabeth Zehetner, has announced plans for a fundamental overhaul of the existing subsidy system.
“If a matter of just a few seconds determines whether a small-scale system receives funding, then we must change the rules of the game,” Zehetner said. “We are therefore developing a new model designed to provide greater planning certainty and place a focus on intelligent storage solutions. We are currently preparing the legislative implementation.”
The planned EAG amendment would replace traditional investment subsidies for PV modules with a storage bonus. The new incentive would support both battery storage installed alongside new PV systems and storage retrofits for existing installations.
Zehetner outlined the main elements of the proposed reform shortly after the October funding round. According to the Ministry of Economy, Energy and Tourism, the government intends to replace individual funding calls with fixed application deadlines with a continuous application process, allowing project owners to apply for subsidies after completing their installations.
The proposed system would also place greater emphasis on European manufacturing. New battery storage systems installed alongside PV systems would be required to use European-made inverters. For storage retrofits to existing PV installations, an additional bonus for European-made equipment would remain available. The current funding round allocated €7.6 million for this purpose.
Zehetner also said applicants who missed out on funding in the latest round would have another opportunity to apply.
“Under current planning, projects featuring intelligent storage systems that are commissioned on or after November 1, 2026, will be eligible for submission under the new 2027 framework, provided they meet the updated funding requirements,” she said.
PV&B Austria remains critical of the proposed changes. Although the EAG amendment is expected to be introduced in parliament next week, the association warned that the industry could still face weeks of uncertainty before receiving the details needed for investment planning.
“Crucial details regarding the planned funding reform from 2027 – as well as the interim solution announced for all projects completed from November 1 onwards – are still missing,” the association said.
PV&B Austria called for the swift adoption of the EAG amendment, including appropriate transitional provisions.

title: German utility plans 30 MWh zinc-bromine BESS - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Stadtwerke Gaggenau and Capac AG are planning a €15.2 million ($16.8 million) project featuring US manufacturer Eos’ stackable zinc-bromine battery technology, with construction due to begin in 2027 and commissioning scheduled for 2028.
Patrick Jowett
11 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
Visualization of the project
Stadtwerke Gaggenau, the municipal utility of southwest German town Gaggenau, and German energy infrastructure company Capac AG are planning a stackable, large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) based on zinc-bromide technology.
Construction of the 7.5 MW/30 MWh system, which will be built on the former site of the utility’s liquefied gas plant, is set to begin next year. Capac is acting as general contractor, handling the technical planning, procurement, system integration and construction up to commissioning, which is planned for 2028.
Benjamin Henecka, CEO of Capac Energy, told
ESS News
the main benefit of zinc-bromine technology is the combination of a non-flammable, water-based electrolyte, a long expected operating life and low projected capacity degradation.
“The zinc-bromine battery technology is designed for a 25-year operating life with capacity degradation of around 3.6% over that period,” Henecka explained. “These characteristics make it an attractive option for utilities taking a long-term infrastructure investment approach. The safety case is also critical as there is no thermal runaway and the water-based electrolyte is non-flammable.”
Long-term infrastructure cost focus
Stadtwerke Gaggenau and investment company JP Holding, parent company of Capac, are jointly investing €15.2 million ($16.8 million) in the project. Henecka said that from the companies’ perspective, the economic question is not simply which battery has the lowest purchase price but also which system delivers the required storage service most economically over the full investment period.
“A higher initial investment can be justified by low capacity degradation and a reduced need for subsequent capacity additions or replacements,” he explained. “That comparison must also account for auxiliary consumption, maintenance and financing costs under the same operating profile. Our argument is about lifecycle value, not a claim that zinc-bromine wins on every individual metric.”
Henecka added that the project is structured as a long-term infrastructure investment. Its planned revenue sources include arbitrage trading in the day-ahead and intraday markets, alongside additional ancillary services.
The zinc-bromine BESS will be built using battery systems supplied by US manufacturer Eos. Eos’ Intensity architecture uses modular battery units installed within an engineered steel support structure that allows units to be arranged both horizontally and vertically. Its zinc-based batteries, manufactured in Pennsylvania, use materials including zinc bromide, conductive plastic and graphite felt.
“The non-flammable aqueous chemistry is an important enabler of this compact layout,” Henecka added. “Together with the system’s protective controls and physical design, it provides a different fire-risk profile from conventional lithium-ion systems.”
Henecka told
ESS News
the partnership offers a practical way to reduce exposure to Chinese-dominated lithium-ion supply chains.
“It is not about replacing one dependency with another or claiming complete supply-chain independence. It is about giving European utilities a broader choice of technologies and suppliers, reducing concentration risk and strengthening their ability to respond to changing market conditions,” he explained. “We combine that alternative technology with local engineering, system integration and long-term operational support.”
In June, Capac and Eos unveiled
plans for a 5 MW/22 MWh zinc-bromine battery project
in the German city of Bruchsal. At the time, they also announced a deal covering 2 GWh of storage capacity across Germany, Austria and Switzerland through 2031.

title: Advansor installs 1.2 MW of CO₂ heat pumps at Swedish retailer - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Danish manufacturer Advansor said two of its plug-and-play ValueBox heat pumps, each with a heating capacity of 600 kW, will provide heating for an entire retail building. The outdoor units feature factory-assembled components and can reportedly deliver water temperatures of up to 95 C.
Emiliano Bellini
11 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Heat pumps
The plug-and-play design allows the heat pumps to be delivered as fully assembled units.
Denmark-based heat pump manufacturer
Advansor
has installed two ValueBox air-to-water heat pumps at a large retail building operated by an unnamed Swedish retailer. Each unit has a heating capacity of 600 kW, providing a combined capacity of 1.2 MW to meet the building’s heating requirements.
Advansor has not disclosed the location of the installation, its commissioning date or project-specific efficiency figures.
The heat pumps are installed outdoors next to the building and use CO₂ (R744) as a refrigerant. Advansor said the plug-and-play design simplifies transportation, installation and commissioning, as the units are delivered fully assembled and factory-tested.
Each ValueBox is supplied as a single frame-mounted unit incorporating multiple evaporators, an outdoor enclosure, a water pump and integrated control equipment. The systems are designed to fit on a truck for transportation, while the frame facilitates lifting and positioning on site.
According to Advansor, installation primarily requires connections to the building’s water and electricity infrastructure. The units are pre-charged with CO₂ and oil, pre-programmed and tested at the factory to reduce on-site commissioning work.
The heat pumps also feature integrated defrost control, a touchscreen for monitoring and operation, and protective mesh around the evaporator fins, eliminating the need for additional fencing around the equipment.
Advansor
introduced its ValueBox range in January 2025
, targeting commercial and industrial heating applications. At the time, the company said the systems could provide between 200 kW and 700 kW of heating capacity per unit, with multiple units operating in parallel to achieve capacities of 5 MW or more.
The initial product range comprised four versions, with maximum heating capacities ranging from 311 kW to 654 kW and maximum cooling capacities between 308 kW and 365 kW.
According to specifications published at the launch, the heat pumps achieve a heating coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 2.68 to 2.69, depending on the configuration, and a combined heating and cooling COP of up to 5.56. The systems can reportedly deliver water temperatures of up to 95 C.
Advansor said the units can maintain heating output during defrost cycles, making them suitable for commercial space heating, domestic hot water and industrial applications.
The manufacturer has positioned the factory-assembled design as a way to reduce installation complexity and address shortages of skilled installation personnel. At the product launch, Advansor said installation could be completed within one or two days under suitable site conditions.

title: CASC completes maiden flight of solar-powered UAV in China - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
China Aerospace Science and Technology Corp. (CASC) has completed the maiden flight of its Light Cavalry solar-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The aircraft has an 8-meter wingspan and is designed to fly continuously for up to 30 hours, targeting applications including infrastructure inspection, environmental monitoring and emergency response.
Vincent Shaw
11 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Cells & modules
China Aerospace Science and Technology Corp.’s (CASC) 11th Research Institute completed the maiden flight of its Light Cavalry solar-powered UAV on Nov. 11 at an undisclosed airfield in northwestern China. The flight marks a milestone in the institute’s efforts to develop a commercially deployable solar-powered aircraft.
The UAV has an 8-meter wingspan, a maximum takeoff weight of 45 kg and a payload capacity of more than 5 kg. According to the institute, the aircraft is designed to operate continuously for up to 30 hours at altitudes of up to 7,000 meters. It can be launched from a vehicle without a runway and requires approximately 20 minutes of ground preparation.
The specifications represent design targets rather than independently verified performance figures. The maiden flight demonstrated basic flight capability and system integration, but the institute did not report endurance testing.
The aircraft is powered entirely by solar cells integrated into its wings. During daylight hours, the photovoltaic modules supply electricity to the propulsion system while charging onboard batteries. The batteries provide power after sunset, enabling the UAV to continue operating overnight without consuming fuel.
The 11th Research Institute, which also develops the Rainbow series of military and civilian UAVs, said it developed the aircraft’s key subsystems in-house, including flight controls, avionics and energy management systems.
The institute is targeting commercial applications such as inspections of power transmission lines, pipelines and railway corridors. Its proposed 30-hour endurance could enable extended inspection missions covering several hundred kilometers, depending on operating conditions.
Other potential applications include environmental monitoring, emergency response and communications relay services. The aircraft’s vehicle-based launch capability is intended to support operations in remote locations without dedicated aviation infrastructure.
The development comes as China promotes its low-altitude economy, encouraging the use of civilian UAVs in sectors including logistics, agriculture and infrastructure inspection.
Solar-powered, long-endurance UAVs could occupy a niche between battery-powered multirotor aircraft, which typically have shorter flight times, and conventional fuel-powered UAVs. Solar propulsion offers the potential to reduce fuel consumption and operating emissions, although commercial viability will depend on acquisition costs, payload capabilities, operating conditions and demonstrated endurance.
CASC has not disclosed a timeline for commercial certification, production plans or pricing.
The maiden flight represents an initial development milestone. Further flight testing, regulatory approvals and customer qualification will be needed before the aircraft can enter routine commercial service.

title: The PPA market has a flexibility problem, hybrid PPAs are part of the answer - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
With hybrid PPAs such as solar-plus-BESS models commanding premiums, the case is obvious. But risk remains part of a complex problem for further growth in the market, writes Paolo Grossi.
Paolo Grossi
11 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Paolo Grossi, CCO of Galileo
The European PPA market is changing. The simple 10-year, pay-as-produced solar PPA still has its place. Many buyers continue to sign these agreements, often as financial PPAs, because they want a long-term price reference and a credible renewable claim, and are comfortable managing the shape themselves. But for a growing share of the market, that product alone is no longer enough.
As solar penetration has increased, so has cannibalisation. Renewable generation is increasingly concentrated in the same hours, while many buyers need power regardless of when the sun shines. For these customers, a solar-only contract covers only part of their real exposure and leaves them buying the rest on the spot market, including when prices peak.
Hybrid PPAs, combining solar with wind or storage, can help meet that need. They deliver a profile closer to actual consumption and a more predictable cost, which makes the business case easier to build internally. For developers, they open the door to buyers who would never sign a pure solar deal, while preserving more of the value of each megawatt-hour produced. Together, pay-as-produced and hybrid structures let us serve a much wider range of customers.
Europe contracted more than 700 MW of hybrid PPAs in 2025, with much of that activity coming in the second half of the year. In the first half of 2026 alone, around 1.1 GW of hybrid deals were announced, across solar-plus-storage and other multi-technology combinations. These figures cover more than just solar and batteries, but show growing demand for a better generation profile.
A battery can shift solar production away from low or negative price hours into periods when electricity is more valuable. It can also allow a developer to offer an offtaker something closer to the profile it actually needs.
We see solar-plus-BESS PPAs commanding premiums of around €10–15 ($11.12 to $16.69)/MWh in some markets and structures, equivalent to roughly 18–25% depending on the underlying PPA price. In Germany, specialist market analysis suggests that adding storage to a solar project can increase its capture factor from around 50 per cent to over 80 per cent of the average wholesale electricity price, depending on battery sizing, market conditions and operational constraints.
But the premium also pays for a transfer of risk. Under a hybrid PPA, the seller or optimiser can take on responsibility for shaping the generation profile, alongside the risks associated with battery degradation, efficiency, operational management and replacement capacity.
That complexity is currently one of the biggest challenges to further growth. There is no established rulebook for pricing hybrid PPAs. Every project can have a different combination of solar resource, storage duration, grid constraints, optimisation strategy, market prices and offtaker requirements. Buyers are also being asked to understand contracts that are considerably more sophisticated than traditional pay-as-produced arrangements.
The next PPAs will be more flexible
The market needs structures that capture the value of flexibility, but are simple enough for an offtaker to understand and commit to over 10 or 15 years. Developing these will take time, particularly while there is still limited historical experience of how these contracts perform through different market conditions.
Grid infrastructure is another constraint. A battery needs sufficient import and export capacity to operate as modelled. A shared connection can accelerate project development, but may limit the battery’s ability to operate independently. These limits directly affect the economics of the hybrid.
I expect utilities and traders to become increasingly important. They can aggregate solar, wind and storage across portfolios and use diversification to manage profiling and balancing risks that individual corporate buyers may be unwilling to take. The rise of hybrid PPAs could therefore accelerate a broader shift away from purely bilateral developer-to-corporate contracts.
The standalone PPA will not disappear. But for buyers seeking a closer match to their consumption, one renewable asset under a fixed-price, a pay-as-produced contract may not provide an adequate long-term hedge.
Solar and storage will increasingly be contracted together. Wind and solar will be combined, and utilities and traders will become more important partners for developers, as buyers seek to manage the complexity of these structures.
In a renewables-heavy electricity system, when power is produced can be almost as important as how much is produced.
