title: Agrivoltaics can increase profitability of indoor farming agrotunnels - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at Canada’s Western University have found that PV-powered indoor farming agrotunnels could achieve returns on investment of up to 499%, with payback periods of less than three years. Their analysis covered six North American locations and identified basil prices and cultivation strategies as key factors affecting profitability.
Emiliano Bellini
11 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
Agrotunnel supposed to be powered by agrivoltaic arrays installed in Corn and Soybean farms in Ilderton, United States.
Researchers at Canada’s
Western University
have demonstrated that agrivoltaic installations can improve the profitability of indoor farming (IF) agrotunnels by reducing electricity costs.
These facilities are enclosed, tunnel-shaped structures that combine conventional agricultural polytunnels with indoor farming technologies. They provide controlled or semi-controlled growing environments, protecting crops from adverse weather, pests and diseases while potentially improving yields.
“We have known for a long time that there are a lot of environmental benefits of indoor farming. Sadly, many indoor farms go bankrupt because of high energy costs,” corresponding author Joshua Pearce told
pv magazine
. “This is where solar comes in, as it can provide known low-cost power that makes the economics of indoor farming much more attractive.”
The researchers conducted experiments in Ilderton, Ontario, focusing on Genovese basil grown at different planting densities and under different lighting conditions. They subsequently scaled the experimental findings to a commercial agrotunnel featuring 12,816 growing ports integrated into vertical cultivation walls. Their energy analysis accounted for electricity consumption by LED lighting, heat pumps, ventilation fans, dehumidifiers and irrigation pumps.
The team optimized a grid-connected, battery-free PV system to minimize electricity costs. It also assessed different lighting schedules and PV configurations using computational optimization techniques to identify the most cost-effective operating strategies.
The researchers developed a comprehensive economic model covering capital investment, operating and maintenance expenses, electricity costs and crop revenues. They evaluated the system across six North American locations – London, Montreal and Edmonton in Canada, and Boston, Santa Fe and San Francisco in the United States – to account for differences in solar resources, climate and operating costs.
The analysis assumed a 25-year system lifespan and compared cultivation strategies involving one to three basil plants per pot, with lighting periods of either 18 or 24 hours per day.
The scientists found that the most profitable configuration involved three basil plants per pot under continuous 24-hour lighting, resulting in an annual yield of 3,573 kg. Integrating grid-connected PV systems substantially reduced electricity costs and enabled near-zero net electricity consumption in most of the locations analyzed.
Total capital investments ranged from approximately $567,000 to $745,000, while annual operating expenses varied between $60,000 and $119,000. Basil production costs ranged from $12.10/kg to $22.70/kg.
The researchers calculated returns on investment of approximately 317% to 499%, with discounted payback periods ranging from 1.6 to 2.2 years. The Canadian locations generally achieved higher net present values than their US counterparts, although profitability depended on local market conditions and electricity tariffs.
The analysis also showed that electricity export compensation policies in Santa Fe and San Francisco limited the ability of PV systems to offset grid electricity costs. Nevertheless, solar generation remained more cost-effective than relying exclusively on grid electricity in those locations.
A sensitivity analysis identified basil market prices as the most influential factor affecting profitability, followed by the initial investment cost of the agrotunnel. The findings suggest that PV-powered agrotunnels could offer an economically viable approach to commercial indoor farming, particularly for high-value crops such as basil.
“Across all six locations, the basil production resulted in substantial profit margins of 517-829% and average payback periods around 2 years. Solar integration cut the levelized cost of energy and made the economics even tastier,” Pearce said. “Overall, solar-based mitigation of energy related risk substantially improves the indoor farming economics, making cleaner indoor basil highly profitable.”
The findings are presented in the study “
Technoeconomic Analysis of Indoor Basil Cultivation in Agrivoltaic Agrotunnels with Optimized Near-Zero Energy Systems
,” published in
Cleaner Energy Systems
Western University has previously investigated the effects of different PV technologies on agricultural productivity. In a
study on lettuce cultivation under extreme heat
, researchers tested 13 types of PV modules during an unusually hot Canadian summer and found that some agrivoltaic configurations increased lettuce yields by more than 400% compared with unshaded control plants. Another
study on agrivoltaic turnip cultivation
showed that semitransparent cadmium telluride modules and low-transparency crystalline silicon panels could improve crop growth by optimizing light distribution and reducing heat stress.
The university’s researchers have also examined the integration of PV systems into protected cultivation environments. In a
study on greenhouse electrification
, they found that semitransparent crystalline silicon modules could improve tomato yields while heat pumps eliminated the need for fossil fuel heating. A separate
investigation of agrivoltaic cold frames
showed that neutral semitransparent PV modules increased lettuce yields by 300% compared with open-air cultivation, highlighting the potential of combining solar generation with controlled-environment agriculture.

title: Paris leads EU capitals for rooftop solar generation potential - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Research from Greece on rooftop PV potential across the EU’s 27 capital cities identifies Paris, Budapest and Warsaw as having the highest annual generation potential, while highlighting cloud cover as the largest source of solar energy losses.
Patrick Jowett
11 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Paris is the EU capital with the largest area of PV-compatible roofs, the study found
Rooftop PV can make a substantial contribution to urban electricity supply across each of the EU’s 27 capital cities, according to new research.
A research team from Athens’ Institute for Environmental Research and Sustainable Development and National and Kapodistrian University developed a framework integrating urban datasets, a climatological record covering 2008 to 2023 and standardised PV simulations to quantify the potential of rooftop solar across the EU’s capital cities.
Their findings are presented in the research paper “
Unified framework for the assessment of rooftop solar PV electricity generation potential in EU-27
,” available in the December edition of the journal
Panagiotis Kosmopoulos, corresponding author of the study, told
pv magazine
the most important takeaway from the research is that rooftop solar has substantial potential in all European capital cities, but its contribution varies significantly depending on urban form, atmospheric conditions and local electricity demand.
Figures from the paper show Paris, France, has the largest exploitable and PV-compatible rooftop area, covering 72.2 km2, followed by Berlin, Germany, (52.4 km2) and Warsaw, Poland, (51.6 km2). On the other end of the scale, Nicosia, Cyprus, (6.2 km2) Ljubljana, Slovenia, (5.6 km2) and Valletta, Malta (2.6 km2) were found to have the smallest rooftop area that is realistically available for PV installations.
Analysis of annual electricity generation potential also saw Paris come out on top, at 3.810 TWh, followed by Budapest, Hungary (2.548 TWh), Warsaw (2.506 TWh), and Rome, Italy, (2.035 TWh), with Tallinn, Estonia, (0.305 TWh), Ljubljana (0.302 TWh), and Valletta (0.202 TWh) on the other end of the scale.
Kosmopoulos added that while rooftop availability stands as the primary determinant of total PV generation potential, shading, clouds and aerosols explain much of the different between cities with similar rooftop resources.
The framework used in the study also features three modification factors to account for the role of urban shading, cloud cover and aerosol shading. This analysis found cloud cover is generally the largest source of solar energy losses across Europe.
Kosmopoulos also told
pv magazine
that while the study found rooftop PV could cover up to around 35% of total electricity demand in the best-performing cities, rooftop PV alone is not sufficient as a standalone solution. “Achieving climate-neutral cities will still require storage, flexibility solutions, grid upgrades and complementary renewable technologies,” he said.
Kosmopoulos added the study also revealed that EU capitals face very different combinations of challenges for rooftop solar deployment. Northern and continental cities often have larger rooftop resources than Mediterranean cities, he said, but face greater losses from cloud cover and stronger seasonal variability. Meanwhile, dense urban environments face more shading and grid-congestion issues, while lower-density cities may benefit more from conventional rooftop deployment models.
“As a result, Europe can adopt common principles, such as simplified permitting, support for self-consumption, energy communities, and solar-ready buildings,” Kosmopoulos said. “However, the choice of incentives should reflect local circumstances.”
Kosmopoulos suggested denser cities may need stronger support for collective self-consumption and energy-sharing schemes, while cities with high solar potential may benefit from incentives for battery storage and flexibility services to address grid hosting-capacity constraints.
Northern cities may place greater emphasis on seasonal balancing and storage, he continued, while southern cities may focus on maximising local self-consumption and reducing summer peak demand.
“In other words, Europe should aim for a harmonised vision but not for identical policies. The study’s central message is that rooftop PV deployment should be guided by local urban realities rather than a one-size-fits-all approach,” Kosmopoulos concluded.
“The main barrier to rooftop solar in Europe is no longer the resource itself. The challenge now is enabling deployment through smarter policies, faster permitting, grid flexibility, storage and urban-specific implementation strategies.”
The research paper adds the framework for assessing rooftop PV potential is reproducible and transferable to other cities where equivalent datasets are available. Its conclusion says that future research will extend the framework to include major economic centers and port cities, such as Hamburg, Porto, Piraeus, Limassol, Rotterdam and Marseille.

title: Singulus signs SpaceX deal for heterojunction solar cell line - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
SpaceX is lining up heterojunction (HJT) solar cell manufacturing equipment from a German supplier to make cells for its satellites in Texas.
Brian Publicover
11 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Cell manufacturing
Heterojunction
Singulus Technologies has signed a contract with SpaceX for a turnkey HJT solar cell production line, with delivery scheduled for the first half of 2027. The Germany-based company said the contract is part of a strategic partnership under which it plans to deliver multiple additional lines.
Singulus said production will scale to support more than 100 GW of production equipment as SpaceX accelerates satellite manufacturing in Bastrop, Texas. It did not say whether the figure refers to annual or cumulative capacity, or how many lines that would involve.
Under the partnership, Singulus will develop both high-performance solar cells and the production equipment to make them, based on technologies already deployed at scale. Mike Nicolls, SpaceX’s senior vice president of Starlink, said the partnership gives SpaceX a high-performance manufacturing path for solar cells for its Starmind satellites at the Texas facility.
Lars Lieberwirth, a member of Singulus’ executive board, said the company’s platform combines wet chemistry, vacuum coating, and thermal processing, and that the partnership would allow it to industrialize those capabilities at scale and strengthen its position as a leading Western supplier of next-generation solar cell technology.
The two companies entered the partnership in March 2026. SpaceX provided significant funding to Singulus that month and again in October as part of a subordinated secured loan, Singulus said, without disclosing the amounts.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in January that SpaceX and Tesla were each working to build
100 GW a year of solar manufacturing capacity in the United States
, a target that would
far exceed current US production
, and has tied the push to
solar-powered computing in space
. Other manufacturers are also adding HJT cell capacity in Texas, including
Toyo’s planned 1.5 GW factory
SEG Solar’s planned 4 GW plant
near Houston.

title: New 300-mm silicon carbide wafers could boost production of EV chips
content: German chipmaker Infineon Technologies has announced that it has made working power chips on 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers at its plant in Villach, Austria. Announced on November 9, this is a first-of-its-kind attempt made in a full-scale fabrication facility, using equipment already in place for manufacturing silicon chips.The larger wafers could help Infineon increase its supply of power semiconductors for electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and AI data centers.The company said a 300-mm wafer can yield 2.3 times as many chips as a 200-mm wafer. It is showcasing a processed wafer at the electronica trade show in Munich, which runs from Nov. 10 to 13.Existing tools process larger wafersThe work in Villach established that Infineon could use existing silicon production equipment to turn the larger silicon carbide wafers into functional devices. The company plans to work with customers and partners on the technology and the timing of a production ramp-up. It will also continue developing its 200-mm silicon carbide manufacturing process.“This technological milestone further strengthens our leadership in power systems. Congratulations and thank you to our passionate team, making significant progress in bringing 300-millimeter SiC out of the lab into a manufacturing environment,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies.Silicon carbide is the second wide-bandgap material in Infineon’s 300-mm manufacturing plans, alongside gallium nitride. On October 27, the company announced an investment of about €1.1 billion in a high-volume facility in Villach to make gallium nitride power semiconductors on 300-mm wafers.A faster way to cut wafersInfineon also tested its Cold Split process on 300-mm silicon carbide at its Dresden, Germany, site. The technique separates a wafer from a boule, the block of silicon carbide crystal from which wafers are cut.According to the company, Cold Split takes less time and wastes less of the crystal than conventional wire sawing. That allows Infineon to obtain more wafers from the same boule. The company said the process also requires less capital spending than wire sawing.The two trials address different steps in manufacturing. The Dresden team showed that the company could separate wafers of that size using Cold Split. The Villach team showed that larger SiC wafers could be processed into working power devices using equipment already available at the fab.From EV chargers to AI data centersSilicon carbide helps power devices convert electricity with lower losses and handle high voltages and temperatures. It also allows power electronics to deliver more power in a given space. In electric vehicles, the material can be used in traction inverters that control power to the motor and in onboard chargers.It also has applications in external EV charging stations, large energy storage systems, and industrial motor drives. The material is also used in uninterruptible power supplies, which keep equipment running when its normal power source is interrupted or fails.Infineon says demand for the material is also rising in AI data centers, where it can be used in power supply units, solid-state transformers, and circuit breakers. The company already sells silicon carbide devices for power conversion under its CoolSiC brand.

title: US pitches 3,000 acres at Cold War-era nuclear site for energy hub
content: A vast nuclear reservation that once fueled America’s atomic arsenal is preparing for an unprecedented industrial makeover.Federal officials have launched a formal bidding process to lease thousands of acres at the Hanford site to private industry. The goal is to transform land originally cleared for wartime weapons production into a commercial center for clean power, high-performance computing, and advanced materials.The Department of Energy’s Office of Environmental Management (DOE-EM) confirmed it is offering up to 3,700 acres under its American Energy Hubs program. The move marks a pivot toward economic revival for an area long defined by complex environmental cleanup.Strategic advantage for power-intensive operationsThe solicitation begins with an initial 1,876-acre plot known as Tract 1. A neighboring 1,249-acre plot, designated Tract 2, could also open depending on demand. Both parcels sit along the Columbia River, a critical waterway in southeastern Washington state.The designated acreage borders another major low-carbon energy scheme. Just to the north, a consortium comprising Amazon, X-energy, and regional utility Energy Northwest is developing the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility. That project plans to deploy up to 12 Xe-100 high-temperature, gas-cooled small modular reactors (SMRs).Locating new commercial infrastructure alongside next-generation nuclear facilities provides a strategic advantage for power-hungry operations, particularly data centers and heavy industrial manufacturing.Modern data centers and advanced factories use electricity in immense quantities. For this reason, regulators have introduced safeguards. Bidders must follow a “build, bring, or buy” rule for their entire energy supply.Tenants cannot simply draw from the existing regional grid if doing so strains local supply. Instead, developers must build dedicated generation on- or off-site, import power from outside the region, or buy guaranteed commercial reserves. They must also independently fund all utility interconnections and absorb full lifecycle costs, from construction through to decommissioning.Resurrecting a dormant siteThis measure aligns with Washington’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, an effort to stop energy-intensive commercial developers from driving up power bills for nearby communities.Between 1943 and 1989, Hanford produced roughly two-thirds of all plutonium used in US nuclear warheads. Production ceased at the end of the Cold War, giving way to one of the world’s most demanding environmental remediation projects under state and federal oversight.Local officials say remediation has progressed enough to safely reintroduce commercial industry. The latest land offering follows an agreement reached in February with technology firm General Matter. Under that deal, the company leased Hanford’s 190,000-square-foot Fuels and Materials Examination Facility—empty since 1993—to develop advanced nuclear fuel processing technologies.Proposals for the newly offered parcels will be evaluated on technical viability, financial backing, environmental compliance, and formal collaboration with local municipalities and Native American tribes.“Exploring these opportunities is the next logical step for a site that is advancing cleanup and for a community that has always been all in on all-of-the-above American energy and innovation,” concluded Hanford Site Manager Ray Geimer.

title: XPeng's two-seat 'flying car' could challenge Tesla's future Roadster
content: Electric vehicle manufacturer XPeng reportedly revealed its two-seat flying car could begin limited commercial operations in China in the second half of 2027. The company plans to make the low-altitude aircraft available for recreational use in rural areas and emergency services. The vehicle, developed over a decade, has undergone extensive testing, including trials of flying motorbikes at XPeng’s Guangzhou facility.The company unveiled its flying car at CES 2025, featuring a modular architecture, which includes a detachable air module housed within the ground vehicle.Flying cars arriveXPeng plans to introduce its two-seat flying vehicle for limited commercial use in the second half of 2027. Priced at approximately $300,000 (£225,000), the aircraft has received approval from China’s civil aviation authorities for restricted operations following nearly a decade of development and testing.XPeng CEO Deli Zhao said the initial market would include recreational users interested in activities such as diving, surfing, and off-roading. However, the vehicle will initially be restricted to approved park areas in China and emergency services operating in locations that are difficult to access, as reported by The Guardian. The aircraft has a reported flight range of 18.6 miles (30 kilometers) and can cruise at altitudes of up to 0.6 miles (1 kilometer). XPeng plans to double its range by increasing battery energy density to 400 kilowatt-hours per kilogram, according to Zhao.The development is part of China’s broader push to establish a low-altitude economy covering drones, cargo aircraft and passenger-carrying vehicles. Zhao said XPeng was among about 20 Chinese companies developing flying vehicles and had signed agreements with the United Arab Emirates and Southeast Asian countries to explore potential applications.Last month, Elon Musk unveiled an experimental Tesla Roadster prototype featuring rocket-inspired thrusters and gravity-defying stunts. Demonstrated at a SpaceX facility in Texas, the vehicle used compressed-air nozzles to perform mid-air flips, jumps, and controlled landings. Modular flying vehicleIt is worth mentioning that Xpeng has also introduced its Land Aircraft Carrier, AEROHT, which is a modular transportation system combining a road-going EV with a detachable electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. It allows users to drive to a suitable location, deploy the aircraft, and take off without requiring a conventional airport. AEROHT, renamed ARIDGE in October 2025, is XPeng’s flying mobility subsidiary.The ground vehicle, known as the mothership, features a three-axle, six-wheel configuration with all-wheel drive and rear-wheel steering. Measuring approximately 5.5 meters (18 feet) long, 2 meters (6.6 feet) wide, and 2 meters (6.6 feet) high, it is designed to fit into standard parking spaces. Its rear compartment houses the aircraft and includes an automated deployment mechanism. The vehicle also functions as a mobile charging station. Its range-extender electric powertrain uses an 800-volt silicon-carbide platform and offers a claimed combined driving range exceeding 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) under China’s CLTC test cycle.The detachable aircraft is a two-seat electric vehicle featuring six rotors arranged in a dual-duct configuration. Its rotor arms and propeller blades fold inward, allowing it to fit inside the mothership. The aircraft uses carbon-fiber materials and features a 270-degree panoramic cockpit.It supports manual and autonomous flight modes, with a single-stick control system for manual operation. Autonomous functions include one-touch takeoff, route planning, flight control, and landing assistance. Redundant safety systems cover propulsion, flight controls, electrical power, and communications.An automated mechanism allows the aircraft to separate from the mothership and reconnect after landing in approximately five minutes. The ground vehicle can recharge it while driving or stationary.XPeng established a 1.29 million-square-foot (120,000-square-meter) manufacturing facility in Guangzhou, China. Trial production began in November 2025, and the factory is designed for an annual capacity of 10,000 aircraft modules, with an initial production target of 5,000 units. Customer deliveries were planned for 2026, which is now slated to begin next year.

title: Electric asphalt paver lays roads up to 21 feet wide with less noise
content: Ammann’s fully electric eABG 4820 asphalt paver has been used to build a cycle path in Groningen, Volvo Penta said. The machine uses a Volvo Penta electric driveline and is rated to lay up to 551 US tons (500 tonnes) of asphalt per hour without producing exhaust emissions at the work site.Ammann designed the paver for projects such as urban roadworks and cycle paths, where construction often takes place close to homes and businesses. The battery-powered machine reduces operating noise while aiming to match the surface quality of conventional asphalt pavers.Asphalt contractor Albert Santing, who has 28 years of experience in the industry, said the quieter operation improved working conditions on the Groningen project. “We work 10 hours a day, and with this machine, we don’t go home with a pounding headache from the noise. You can hear everything around you,” he said.Paving widths of up to 21 feetThe eABG 4820 can lay asphalt in strips up to 21 feet (6.5 meters wide). Ammann developed the machine in response to demand for quieter equipment that can work without direct exhaust emissions while maintaining the precision and steady movement needed for a consistent surface.The electric motors deliver torque as soon as the operator moves the control stick. That gives the machine an immediate response to operator inputs, since it can begin moving without waiting for a combustion engine to build up speed.“It doesn’t build up any RPMs, but when you move the stick, the machine obeys. It’s just like a giant sports car, only at a snail’s pace,” Santing said.Three battery units provide 270 kWhAmmann installed three battery units with a combined capacity of 270 kWh. The batteries use Volvo Group technology already employed in road vehicles. Volvo Penta’s integrated driveline also includes the electric motors, power electronics and control system.The control system coordinates power delivery with the paver’s hydraulics. Different machine functions require energy at different points in the paving process, so the system regulates how much power it supplies as demand changes.“It comes down to energy management and architecture. The electric driveline doesn’t just power the machine. It communicates seamlessly with the hydraulic,” said Philipp Bramer, who leads Ammann’s electric paver development team. “Simultaneously, the intelligent control system makes sure that the system supplies exactly the right amount of energy to the machine,” he added. Bramer also said that coordination is part of how the machine combines the immediate response of its electric motors with the controlled movement required to lay asphalt evenly.Electric driveline could reduce servicing tasksRemoving the combustion engine could eliminate some engine-related maintenance tasks. The electric driveline also has fewer moving parts, which could simplify parts of the servicing routine. Volvo Penta said the actual maintenance requirements and costs would depend on how the machine is used. The completed cycle path in Groningen is one example of the machine’s use on an urban project. Bicycles account for more than half of daily journeys in the city. Volvo Penta also identified roadworks near homes and businesses as a potential application for the quieter paver.

title: 3D-printed satellite hinges weigh 1.4 grams, cut weight by 93%
content: Researchers at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Polymer Research (IAP) have developed 3D-printed shape-memory polymer hinges that could help satellites deploy their solar panels while carrying significantly less mechanical hardware.Each hinge weighs approximately 1.4 grams, making it about 93 percent lighter than conventional hinges currently used in satellite systems, according to the researchers. The components use heat to trigger a programmed shape change, allowing folded solar panels to unfold after launch.The development is part of the Additive Manufacturing of Solar Panels for spACE applications (AM-SPACE) project, which brought together Fraunhofer IAP, German Orbital Systems (GOS), Orion Additive Manufacturing and the Fraunhofer Institute for Reliability and Microintegration IZM.Heat triggers shape recoveryThe technology uses shape-memory polymers (SMPs), materials that can be programmed into a temporary shape and recover their original form when heated.Researchers processed the polymers into filaments suitable for additive manufacturing and used them to produce hinges and hold-down and release mechanisms (HDRMs). The latter keep satellite components secured during launch before releasing them in a controlled manner once the spacecraft reaches orbit.After the release mechanism activates, the polymer hinges use heat to unfold the solar panels. A heating element raises the hinge’s temperature from 73.4°F to 284°F, triggering its programmed shape recovery. Under controlled laboratory conditions, the hinge completes deployment in about 60 seconds.The approach could reduce the need for conventional mechanical actuation systems, which add weight and complexity to satellite deployment structures.Printing speeds up productionThe researchers also used additive manufacturing to simplify the production of the components. Printing a hinge or an HDRM takes approximately 15 minutes, followed by another 30 minutes to program its temporary shape.A separate 4D-printing approach integrates the shape-changing response directly into the component during fabrication. Using this method, the team produced HDRMs in approximately five minutes.The researchers say the approach could help satellites launch in a compact configuration before deploying their solar panels or antennas in orbit. It may also enable other activatable components for small spacecraft.Unlike conventional 3D printing, 4D printing incorporates a programmed response that allows a printed object to change shape or function when exposed to an external stimulus, such as heat.The technology has undergone initial laboratory validation, including cleanroom tests, thermal cycling, and preliminary vacuum-chamber experiments. One of the polymers also passed outgassing tests conducted by Spain’s National Institute for Aerospace Technology (INTA).However, the components have not yet been tested in orbit, and their long-term reliability under actual space conditions remains to be established.German Orbital Systems has expressed interest in evaluating the components in space, while discussions are underway for a possible follow-up project aimed at an in-orbit demonstration.The AM-SPACE project ran from October 2023 to September 2026 and received funding through regional innovation programs, with support from the European Union.

title: FAA clears Dream Chaser spaceplane built to haul 12,000 pounds
content: Sierra Space has secured a key regulatory approval for Dream Chaser, bringing its long-delayed spaceplane closer to its first orbital flight. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has authorized the spacecraft to return from orbit and land at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.The authorization addresses a critical part of Dream Chaser’s flight operations. Its first mission will launch from Florida aboard United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan Centaur rocket. The spacecraft will then travel back through Earth’s atmosphere before touching down on a conventional runway.Vandenberg becomes primary landing siteThe FAA issued Dream Chaser’s vehicle operator license on November 9. Sierra Space confirmed the approval the following day. The five-year license permits up to four reentries annually under an unchanged vehicle configuration and mission profile.Vandenberg now serves as the designated landing location for the spacecraft. That represents a change from Sierra Space’s original plans. During an environmental review in 2024, the company identified Kennedy Space Center’s former Space Shuttle runway as its preferred landing site.Another milestone for #DreamChaser!The @FAANews has issued Sierra Space a license authorizing Dream Chaser to reenter and land at Vandenberg Space Force Base.Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation. pic.twitter.com/qIJgQL54CA— Sierra Space (@SierraSpaceCo) November 10, 2026Vandenberg initially appeared as a backup option. The newly issued license instead identifies the California installation as Dream Chaser’s landing destination.The arrangement also gives Sierra Space an approved runway for its first flight. However, the FAA authorization does not establish a launch date. Mission timing still depends on the availability of a Vulcan Centaur rocket.Tenacity brings cargo backDream Chaser’s first spacecraft, Tenacity, combines a lifting-body design with folding wings. The configuration allows it to fit inside Vulcan’s payload fairing during launch. Once in orbit, the spacecraft can carry approximately 12,100 pounds of cargo.Its return capacity reaches 4,080 pounds, according to the FAA’s environmental assessment. That capability addresses an important limitation of conventional cargo spacecraft.Capsules typically return through parachute-assisted landings, often involving ocean recovery. Dream Chaser instead offers a runway landing. Sierra Space says returning cargo experiences less than 1.5 times Earth’s gravity during the journey.The company also claims the spacecraft can use runways designed to accommodate Boeing 737 aircraft. That flexibility could benefit experiments and sensitive equipment requiring careful handling after landing.NASA mission takes new directionDream Chaser spaceplane originally entered NASA’s commercial resupply program in 2016. Sierra Space secured a contract to develop the spacecraft for International Space Station cargo deliveries.Repeated development delays and propulsion system problems pushed its debut further back. NASA and Sierra Space eventually revised their agreement in September 2025.The revised plan removed the space station docking requirement from Dream Chaser’s initial demonstration. Tenacity will instead conduct an independent free-flying mission in orbit.NASA can still purchase future resupply missions if the demonstration proves successful. Sierra Space has also lined up national security and commercial customers for the inaugural flight.In September, the company confirmed those customers would contribute payloads alongside NASA cargo. However, it has not disclosed their identities or the specific equipment planned for launch.Sierra Space previously targeted late 2026 for the debut mission. The company has tied that schedule to Vulcan Centaur availability. With the year nearing its end, the launch window remains uncertain.The FAA’s approval removes another regulatory hurdle. Tenacity still needs its launch vehicle and remaining mission preparations before its runway return becomes reality.

title: 5 mm radar wristband turns skin into a pressure-sensitive trackpad
content: Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable technology that turns the forearm into a trackpad, allowing smartwatch users to scroll, zoom and click without touching the device’s tiny screen.Called EpiPad, the system uses a compact millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensor to track finger movements and measure how firmly users press their skin. This enables multi-finger gestures and pressure-sensitive controls similar to those found on laptop trackpads.The researchers say the approach could give smartwatches a larger input surface without increasing their screen size. It could also provide a way to control screenless wearables, including smart glasses.EpiPad’s sensor array measures approximately 5 by 4 millimeters. It is mounted on a wristband and detects the subtle changes in the skin caused when fingertips press against the forearm.Radar tracks finger pressureUnlike conventional touchscreens, EpiPad does not require users to touch a display. Instead, its radar system detects movements and pressure through changes in the signals reflected from the skin.The researchers developed a signal-processing method based on millimeter-wave phase dynamics to estimate applied force. Lightweight machine-learning models then help recognise gestures and interpret the user’s input.Users must first complete a short calibration routine that adapts the system to their individual movements. The process takes 3 minutes and 54 seconds, according to the research paper.The current prototype resembles a wristband with an exposed circuit board. However, the researchers say its components could eventually be integrated into conventional smartwatch designs.Tested across 20 usersThe team evaluated EpiPad in experiments involving 20 participants. The system achieved 92.8 percent gesture-recognition accuracy and 90.2 percent force-detection accuracy, with a ranging precision of 10.2 millimeters on users who were not included in the training data.In a separate real-time evaluation, participants performed smartwatch input tasks using three methods: a conventional touchscreen, a tilt-based cursor, and EpiPad. The researchers reported that EpiPad outperformed the other two approaches in both error rate and efficiency.The results suggest that using the forearm as an input surface could make small wearable devices easier to control. However, the findings are based on a proof-of-concept prototype and a relatively small user study, rather than a commercially available product.The researchers estimate that the functional components, including the radar sensor array, could cost less than $10. That figure is an estimate from the research team, not the price of a finished device.The technology could eventually extend beyond smartwatches. The researchers suggest that screenless wearables, such as smart glasses, could use the skin as an interactive surface, allowing users to issue commands without relying on a display or physical buttons.The research was detailed in a paper titled “EpiPad: Enabling Multi-Finger and Force-Sensitive Skin Interface for Smartwatches,” published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies. The work was presented at the UbiComp/ISWC 2026 conference in Shanghai.

title: SpaceX orders 100 GW/year of solar gear for its 'sentient sun' plan
content: SpaceX has signed a supply deal worth more than $69 million with German equipment maker SINGULUS TECHNOLOGIES to build a production line for high-efficiency heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, securing a manufacturing route for its planned Starmind satellite network.The first turnkey production line is scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2027. It is part of a wider strategic partnership under which SINGULUS plans to supply multiple additional lines as SpaceX accelerates satellite manufacturing at its Bastrop, Texas, facility.SINGULUS disclosed the contract on November 10, saying the partnership will involve developing both high-performance solar cells and the equipment needed to manufacture them. The company said production would scale to support more than 100 gigawatts (GW) of production equipment, although it did not specify the output capacity of the first line.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk subsequently clarified the scale of the order in a post on X, saying the company had ordered 100 GW per year of HJT solar manufacturing equipment from SINGULUS in Germany. He linked the order to Starmind, describing its ambition as creating a “sentient sun.”SpaceX Senior Vice President of Starlink Mike Nicolls said the partnership provides a manufacturing path for solar cells intended for its Starmind satellites.Building cells in-houseHJT technology combines a crystalline silicon wafer with thin layers of amorphous silicon. These layers help reduce the loss of electrical charges at the wafer’s surfaces, improving the cell’s ability to convert sunlight into electricity.Manufacturing the cells requires several processes, including wafer cleaning, thin-film deposition, and thermal treatment. SINGULUS develops equipment for these stages, combining wet-chemical processing with vacuum coating technologies such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD).SpaceX has ordered 100 GW/year of HJT solar manufacturing equipment from Singulus in Germany. This is for Starmind to create a sentient sun. https://t.co/umtNyF9M7g— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 10, 2026Its production platforms are designed for high-throughput solar cell manufacturing. The company says its equipment supports HJT and other crystalline silicon cell technologies, including TOPCon and interdigitated back-contact designs.The agreement gives SpaceX access to SINGULUS’s manufacturing expertise while establishing a route to produce the cells at its own Texas facility. Neither company has disclosed the planned efficiency of the cells or the production capacity of the initial line.Powering orbital computingSpaceX’s Starmind program centers on satellites carrying computing payloads that use solar energy generated in orbit. The company’s published specifications for its AI1 satellite describe a deployed height of 30 meters, a wingspan of 75 meters, and a computing payload drawing up to 250 kilowatts at peak and 175 kilowatts on average.The satellites are designed to operate in sun-synchronous orbit and transmit data to the ground through laser links connected to the Starlink network, according to SpaceX.The scale of the planned network is substantial. In its 2026 securities filing, SpaceX outlined a long-term ambition to deploy up to 100 GW of power to orbit annually. The company said reaching that level would require thousands of launches each year, while noting that it could build a commercially viable business at considerably lower deployment rates.SINGULUS said its strategic partnership with SpaceX began in March 2026. SpaceX provided significant funding to the German company that month and again in October through a subordinated secured loan.The first production line is expected in the first half of 2027, as SpaceX prepares to expand satellite manufacturing in Texas.

title: OpenAI pulls the plug on two major voice modes as GPT-Live takes over
content: OpenAI will discontinue two legacy voice options in ChatGPT next month, leaving GPT-Live as the platform’s default voice experience. Advanced and Standard voice will disappear from the model picker on December 11, 2026.The change affects users who still prefer the older conversational modes. OpenAI says nearly all ChatGPT voice users have already switched to GPT-Live since its introduction in July. Voice usage has also nearly doubled during that period, signaling a significant shift toward the newer system.Users can continue accessing Advanced and Standard voice throughout the transition. However, those who rely on either option will need to adjust before the December deadline. The retirement also affects custom GPTs that currently use the older voice technology.GPT-Live takes center stageGPT-Live uses a different architecture from its predecessors. The model can listen and speak simultaneously, allowing conversations to flow without conventional turn-taking.That capability enables quicker exchanges and more natural interruptions. It can also acknowledge users with brief responses while they speak. The model can remain silent when someone needs time to think, making conversations feel less rigid.GPT-Live also connects with OpenAI’s text-based models for more demanding requests. It can delegate complicated questions and multi-step tasks without ending the ongoing voice conversation. This allows users to continue speaking while the system handles more complex work in the background.Advanced voice followed a more traditional approach. Its underlying model processed incoming and outgoing audio directly. However, it had to wait until users finished speaking before generating a response.Standard voice relied on three separate models. One converted speech into text, another generated the response, and a third converted that response into audio. The additional processing stages often introduced delays and lost information between audio and text.OpenAI now wants to consolidate these capabilities into one voice experience. The company also plans to improve response depth, conversational continuity, and personalization as GPT-Live develops.What users need to knowOpenAI began notifying users about the retirement on November 10. Existing Advanced and Standard voice users can keep their preferred settings until December 11.After that date, both options will disappear from Settings under the Voice section. ChatGPT will automatically switch affected users to GPT-Live. Users will not need to manually migrate their existing conversations or start new chats.Previous conversations will remain accessible through ChatGPT’s history. Users can continue those discussions through text or the new Live voice experience.Custom GPTs will also lose access to Advanced voice on December 11. Until the retirement date, conversations with custom GPTs will continue using the older model. Developers and users should account for that change when planning their existing voice workflows.Video and screen-sharing exceptionOne important capability will retain its existing voice infrastructure for now. Live video and screen-sharing will continue running through Advanced voice.GPT-Live does not yet support these features, according to OpenAI. The company will maintain the older system until its newer model gains equivalent capabilities.That leaves a temporary distinction between ChatGPT’s standard voice conversations and its interactive visual features. Users can still access live video and screen-sharing during the transition.OpenAI has not provided a specific timeline for bringing those capabilities to GPT-Live. For now, December 11 marks the end of the two selectable legacy voice modes, not every feature powered by Advanced voice.

title: US Navy's 200-mile LRASM missile gets advanced radio-frequency sensors
content: The U.S. Navy’s Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) program has reached another production milestone, with BAE Systems delivering all Lot 8 radio-frequency (RF) sensors to Lockheed Martin. These advanced sensors provide a critical part of the missile’s targeting system, helping it detect and engage maritime threats in heavily defended environments.BAE Systems supplies the RF technology that helps LRASM identify strategic naval targets. The sensor supports the missile’s ability to operate around sophisticated air defense networks, where electronic interference and other battlefield threats can complicate targeting.The company has also upgraded the sensor’s software without requiring hardware modifications. Extensive verification testing accompanied the improvements, allowing engineers to introduce additional capabilities through software updates.RF sensors improve targetingLRASM uses its onboard sensor technology to locate and engage enemy vessels across contested maritime environments. BAE Systems’ RF sensor plays an important role in this process by providing advanced radio-frequency detection capabilities.#NEWS: Ensuring U.S. military readiness.We have delivered all Lot 8 units of our advanced RF sensor for the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM).“We’re delivering essential weapon systems that provide operational asymmetry and a decisive advantage to our warfighters,” said… pic.twitter.com/kpWRkG8xfc— BAE Systems, Inc. (@BAESystemsInc) November 10, 2026The missile also incorporates an imaging infrared seeker for terminal targeting. Its onboard guidance architecture combines multiple technologies to help identify targets without depending entirely on external navigation or communication links.This becomes particularly important when adversaries deploy electronic warfare systems. Jamming and disrupted communications can complicate conventional targeting operations, making autonomous onboard capabilities increasingly valuable.BAE Systems continues to develop both the sensor’s hardware and software. Engineers are evaluating further improvements to keep the system aligned with evolving battlefield requirements.LRASM packs long-range firepowerLockheed Martin developed the AGM-158C LRASM from its AGM-158B Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile Extended Range (JASSM-ER). The weapon carries a 1,000-pound penetrator and blast-fragmentation warhead designed to destroy large surface vessels.Its reported range exceeds 200 nautical miles, allowing launch aircraft to engage enemy ships from considerable distances. The missile also incorporates reduced-observability features that help it penetrate sophisticated air defense networks.LRASM uses onboard navigation and targeting algorithms to operate in environments where GPS signals or communication links face disruption. Its guidance architecture helps the weapon refine its targeting information during flight.The U.S. Navy operates LRASM aboard F/A-18E/F Super Hornet fighters. The U.S. Air Force also employs the weapon aboard B-1B Lancer bombers.Production expands through 2028BAE Systems initially manufactured LRASM sensors at relatively low production volumes. Demand is now pushing the program toward significantly higher output.The contractor has invested in upgraded electronic warfare facilities to support increased manufacturing capacity. Its engineering and production operations span Austin, Texas; Greenlawn, New York; Nashua, New Hampshire; and Wayne, New Jersey.BAE Systems holds a contract to supply additional LRASM RF sensors through 2028. The company says it has demonstrated the manufacturing capacity needed to support accelerated deliveries.Vanessa Varrati, LRASM program director at BAE Systems, said the effort provides essential capabilities to American warfighters. She also highlighted the importance of manufacturing investments and partnerships with Lockheed Martin and the Department of War.The completed Lot 8 deliveries mark another step in expanding LRASM production. BAE Systems will continue refining its sensor technology as the missile program moves toward higher manufacturing volumes.

title: Google's Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96% after tackling 200 tasks
content: Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a new model designed to help robots learn physical tasks faster, handle delicate objects, and operate more reliably in real-world environments.The model achieved a 96 percent success rate in a factory proof-of-concept involving Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots on Mercedes-Benz production lines. The robots autonomously sorted automotive parts from bulk bins into organized trays, preparing components in the sequence required for vehicle assembly.The trial took place at production facilities in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Google said the work could help automate repetitive and physically demanding tasks while allowing factory technicians to focus on more complex assembly work.Gemini Robotics 2.5 is the company’s latest vision-language-action (VLA) model, which translates visual information and instructions into physical robot movements. It is currently rolling out to Google’s robotics partners.Model tackles 200 tasksGoogle evaluated Gemini Robotics 2.5 across more than 200 distinct tasks, including serving food with tongs, tying bows on gift boxes, and transferring liquids with pipettes.These activities test a range of capabilities, from handling delicate objects to manipulating flexible materials and using everyday tools.Compared with previous baselines, the model achieved success rates that were 30 percent to 100 percent higher, depending on the task. It also completed activities 20 percent to 30 percent faster, according to Google.The model works across different robotic platforms, including Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid and the Franka Duo system, which uses two-fingered parallel grippers.For the Mercedes-Benz demonstration, Google’s embodied reasoning model, Gemini Robotics ER, tracked the workflow, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled the robot’s arms and hands. Apollo 2 picked metal brackets from supply bins and placed them into sequencing containers, adjusting its movements when necessary.Safety and training advancesBeyond dexterity, Google has improved the model’s ability to navigate physical hazards. Its inference-time reasoning guidance helps robots avoid obstacles and operate around people.In company evaluations, the capability increased safe task completion by 33 percent around obstacles and 43 percent near people.Google also introduced ASIMOV-Jailbreak, an open-source benchmark designed to test whether robotic systems can resist disguised unsafe instructions. It contains hundreds of prompts spanning dozens of scenes.Google reported that Gemini 4 Argon achieved 99.5 percent resistance to these jailbreak attempts, compared with 82 percent for the previous Gemini Robotics ER 2 baseline.The company also credited Gemini 4 Argon with accelerating the development of its new robotics model. The system can generate thousands of simulated practice runs from real-world camera footage and create digital twins of physical environments.Researchers can combine these simulations with real training demonstrations to help robots generalize their skills to unfamiliar objects and settings. Argon can also analyze failed attempts and suggest improvements for subsequent training.The developments mark Google’s latest push to bring more adaptable robots into industrial and everyday environments. However, the 96 percent factory result remains a proof-of-concept, rather than evidence of widespread commercial deployment.Gemini Robotics 2.5 is currently being rolled out to Google’s robotics partners.

title: SpaceX launches Starlink Mini 2 with a swappable battery for $999
content: SpaceX has given its smallest satellite internet terminal a significant hardware overhaul. The new Starlink Mini 2 introduces a removable battery, faster wireless connectivity, and a more durable enclosure. These changes address some of the practical limitations that affected the original portable dish.The second-generation terminal retains its compact design but adds considerably more independence from external power sources. Its 71 Wh battery provides up to 4.5 hours of operation on a single charge. SpaceX has also introduced a quick-release mechanism that lets owners replace depleted batteries without tools.Preorders have opened for select US customers at $999, plus applicable taxes. The invitation-only offer includes the hardware and an entire year of Roam Unlimited service.Swappable battery changes everythingThe removable battery represents the biggest functional upgrade over the original Starlink Mini. Previously, users needed an external power source to operate the satellite terminal. That meant carrying additional equipment for camping trips, remote work, or extended journeys.Introducing Mini 2, the next-generation portable Starlink. Get up to 4.5 hours of connectivity on a single charge with the quick-swap battery, or plug in with USB-C.With built-in Wi-Fi, all you need is a clear view of the sky to get online in 60 seconds.Preorders are now open… pic.twitter.com/VRTuJZVBnH— Starlink (@Starlink) November 10, 2026Mini 2 addresses that limitation with a detachable 71 Wh battery pack. It weighs approximately 1.08 pounds (490 grams) and delivers up to 4.5 hours of connectivity. Owners can replace it with another charged battery when necessary.The battery also features LED indicators and its own USB-C charging port. SpaceX supports 60-watt USB-C Power Delivery charging for the pack. The retail kit includes a compatible 60-watt wall adapter and a three-meter USB-C cable.Users can also power the terminal through USB-C without relying on its battery. A physical power button replaces the original model’s simpler plug-and-play arrangement.Wi-Fi 6 joins the packageThe Mini 2 measures 12.36 × 10.35 × 0.91 inches (314 × 263 × 23.1 mm). Its enclosure is approximately half an inch thinner than the original Mini. However, the new model weighs 3.53 pounds (1.6 kilograms) with its battery and kickstand.The original terminal weighed approximately 2.43 pounds. Most of the additional weight comes from the removable battery, which users can detach when necessary.SpaceX has also upgraded the wireless hardware from Wi-Fi 5 to Wi-Fi 6. The integrated router supports coverage across approximately 1,800 square feet (167 square meters). An IP67 rating provides additional protection against dust and water.Other hardware details include a foldable kickstand and a standard 1/4-inch-20 tripod mounting thread. The terminal also offers a 55-degree field of view for satellite acquisition.Preorders include a yearSpaceX’s $999 preorder package includes the Starlink Mini 2 hardware and 12 months of Roam Unlimited service. The company values the included subscription at $2,100.The plan provides unlimited data for road travel, streaming, and video calls. It also supports connectivity while moving at speeds up to 100 mph. International travelers can use the service abroad for up to 30 days at a time.Customers can reserve their terminals with a refundable $100 deposit. SpaceX will charge the remaining $899, plus applicable taxes, when the device ships. Initial shipments should begin in mid-December.The introductory pricing and included subscription remain exclusive to customers receiving preorder invitations. SpaceX has not announced broader availability or international pricing.The Mini 2 makes portable satellite connectivity considerably more practical. Its removable battery eliminates a major dependency on external power. However, the $999 entry price makes the included subscription an important part of its value proposition.

title: 200,000 tons of waste could turn CO2 into carbon for batteries
content: A waste treatment plant which processes nearly 200,000 US tons (175,000 metric tons) of residual waste a year could become a source of carbon for batteries and construction materials. Located in the area of Eschbach, Germany, the site could capture CO2 from waste incineration and convert it into solid carbon for industrial use. The effort is part of a project called NECOC 2.0, which brings together researchers from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), EEW Energy from Waste, and other partners.The team will use liquid metal to extract carbon from CO2. They are believe that the technology could not only slash emissions and produce carbon powder, but also provide an alternative to fossil-derived carbon in industrial applications.The project secured over USD 5.8 million (EUR 5 million) from Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy. “With NECOC 2.0, we are bringing a solution developed at KIT a decisive step closer to practical implementation,” Thomas Hirth, PhD, a professor and VP for Transfer and International Affairs at KIT explained. From waste to carbonWaste incineration plants produce CO2 while burning residual waste in order to generate electricity. These emissions include carbon from fossil-based materials and biological sources. To address the issue, KIT’s NECOC process aims to capture the CO2 directly from the cleaned exhaust gases before it reaches the atmosphere. The captured CO2 first reacts with hydrogen to produce methane. This gas then passes through a reactor with liquid tin. There it breaks down into solid carbon and hydrogen.The hydrogen is recycled back into the first stage, while the carbon is collected as a fine powder. “We want to capture CO2 and convert it directly into a usable raw material,” Benjamin Dietrich, PhD, a researcher at the Institute of Thermal Process Engineering at KIT, who helped develop the technology, elaborated. According to the team, the recovered carbon could replace fossil-derived carbon in various industrial applications. The researchers will also investigate whether it is suitable for battery electrodes and building materials. “CO2 capture is an essential component of the future of thermal waste treatment for us,” Timo Poppe, CEO of EEW Energy from Waste, said. Testing the technologyThe technology has showed promise in earlier experiments. In 2020, KIT built an integrated experimental facility at its Karlsruhe Liquid Metal Laboratory (KALLA), where it combined methane production and decomposition into a single process.The system successfully converted CO2 into microgranular carbon, a fine-grained form of solid carbon. The results confirmed the process was feasible. However, as per the team, it has yet to be demonstrated as a whole system with CO2 captured from an actual industrial exhaust stream. EEW will evaluate and test CO2 capture at its Eschbach site. In turn, KIT will focus on methane production and decomposition. The Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems will also investigate ways to bind CO2 in calcium and magnesium carbonates.Poppe highlighted the importance of investigating in research and development. “As the consortium coordinator, we are contributing our industrial experience to the NECOC 2.0 project and working with our partners to investigate how CO2 can be captured from flue gases and used as a raw material,” he concluded in a press statement.

title: 184-foot converted fishing ship could hunt submarines for the UK Navy
content: Norwegian maritime technology company Kongsberg Maritime has unveiled an uncrewed surface vessel designed to help the Royal Navy detect submarines in the increasingly contested waters of the Arctic and North Atlantic. Called Arctic Hunter, the vessel adapts a commercial fishing ship design with autonomous navigation technology and submarine-hunting sensors, offering a potentially faster and less expensive way to expand Britain’s anti-submarine warfare capabilities.Unveiled on November 9, 2026, Arctic Hunter is being proposed for the Royal Navy’s Type 92 requirement, part of Britain’s planned hybrid fleet of crewed and uncrewed naval platforms. Kongsberg is working with Thales UK on sonar and military communications, while shipbuilding partner Balaena Maritime is expected to construct the vessels at its Birkenhead yard if the proposal is selected.The company plans to have ships ready for military integration and operational deployment by the end of the decade.A commercial fishing vessel becomes a submarine hunterRather than designing an entirely new military ship, Kongsberg has selected an existing Arctic commercial vessel design as the foundation for Arctic Hunter. The proposed platform is based on a 56-meter (184-foot) fishing vessel hull, originally developed for demanding North Atlantic and Arctic conditions.The conversion replaces the vessel’s fishing and processing equipment with remote-control systems, autonomous technologies and military mission equipment. Its substantial internal volume and deck space also allow additional sensors and payloads to be installed as operational requirements change.The vessel is designed to operate without a crew aboard, with Kongsberg proposing missions lasting up to 60 days at sea. It would operate from a forward support base inside the Arctic Circle, providing persistent submarine-detection coverage alongside crewed warships and other surveillance platforms.An important part of the design is reducing the vessel’s underwater acoustic signature. Machinery and propeller noise can interfere with sensitive sonar equipment, making a quiet operating platform essential for submarine detection. Kongsberg says it is optimizing the hull and propulsion system to reduce underwater noise.How Arctic Hunter could detect submarinesThe proposed vessel will carry Thales UK’s submarine-hunting sonar and secure military communications. Reporting by The War Zone identifies the planned sensor as the Sonar 2087, a towed-array sonar already used by Royal Navy Type 23 frigates and intended for the newer Type 26 fleet.A towed-array sonar consists of sensitive hydrophones housed in a long cable deployed behind a vessel. These sensors listen for underwater acoustic signals, including noise produced by submarine machinery and propulsion systems.Unlike active sonar, which sends out sound pulses and analyzes their echoes, passive sonar listens without transmitting signals. This can help naval forces detect and track submarines while limiting the risk of revealing their own position.By carrying this equipment on an uncrewed platform, the Royal Navy could distribute submarine-detection sensors across a wider area without assigning an additional crewed warship to every surveillance task. The resulting information could be transmitted to other naval assets for further assessment and coordinated operations.Part of Britain’s hybrid naval strategyArctic Hunter is being proposed for the Royal Navy’s Type 92 program, which forms part of its broader Hybrid Navy concept. The approach combines traditional crewed warships with uncrewed surface vessels, underwater systems and autonomous platforms.The initiative is closely connected to the UK’s Atlantic Bastion strategy, which aims to strengthen surveillance and protection of critical undersea infrastructure and monitor submarine activity across the North Atlantic and High North.The UK and Norway have also committed to expanding cooperation in autonomous maritime systems through the Lunna House Agreement, which identifies the High North as a priority for joint defense development.However, Arctic Hunter remains an industry proposal rather than an operational Royal Navy vessel. Its selection for Type 92, final configuration, and procurement quantities have not been announced.If adopted, the design could offer the Royal Navy a way to expand its underwater surveillance network using commercially built ships equipped with specialized military sensors. Rather than replacing frigates and other anti-submarine platforms, Arctic Hunter is intended to give them more persistent sensing coverage across some of NATO’s most strategically important waters.

title: 9-passenger hybrid-electric aircraft could fly near-silent US missions
content: The US Air Force will reportedly test a new nine-passenger hybrid-electric aircraft that could switch to battery power to fly quietly during special military operations.The fixed-winged transport aircraft, known as EL9 Ultra Short, is being developed by Virginia-based Electra Defense. It combines hybrid-electric propulsion with ultra-short takeoff and landing (Ultra-STOL) technology. It could operate from locations with limited runway access.On November 9, Electra Defense announced that it had secured a USD 4.7 million contract from the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL). The funding will support ground and flight tests to evaluate the aircraft’s performance, propulsion system, and potential military applications. The tests will also evaluate whether the aircraft can transport troops and urgent cargo to remote locations without relying on conventional airfields. “Power and propulsion are fundamental to unlocking new capabilities for military aviation,” Donn Yates, Electra Defense’s VP and General Manager, pointed out.A quieter way to flyThe program will primarily assess whether the EL9 can operate quietly using only its batteries. The plane is expected to undergo acoustic flight testing to measure its noise levels during battery-only operations. The goal is to find out whether it can fly into and out of mission areas without making much noise. Electra Defense explained that minimizing aircraft noise could reduce the risk of detection. However, the company has not specified the battery chemistry or how far the aircraft could travel on battery power alone.The company’s design for the EL9 Ultra Short Hybrid-Electric Aircraft.Credit: Electra DefenseEngineers will study the aircraft’s hybrid-electric propulsion system and verify key power technologies through extensive ground testing. Yates said the program will also use computer modeling and simulations to assess how the aircraft could handle different military tasks.“This award represents an important step in demonstrating how hybrid-electric aircraft technology can address some of the Air Force’s most pressing operational challenges,” he said. He added that the tests will generate real-world performance data to help the Air Force evaluate the technology’s potential.Missions without runwaysSince the EL9 can take off and land on very short runways, it could also be useful for military missions in remote areas with limited infrastructure. This means it will be able to operate from smaller spaces. It could help military staff and essential supplies reach difficult locations.The team will examine whether such aircraft could operate with fewer airport facilities and less ground support. “Future military operations will demand aircraft that can operate with greater flexibility, access more locations, and reduce the logistical burden on deployed forces,” Yates continued.The latest award builds on an existing partnership between Electra and AFRL. In 2023, Electra received a funding award valued at up to USD 85 million to support development of its full-scale preproduction aircraft. The firm also demonstrated its technology during AFRL’s Future Flag 25-3 exercise in 2025.Yates believes the plane’s hybrid-electric power and short takeoff capability could transform tactical mobility. “This contract will help us quantify those advantages and demonstrate their potential value to the Air Force,” he concluded in a press statement.

title: Ford EVs top 100,000 miles with over 90% battery capacity intact
content: Electric car batteries are holding up far better in daily driving than many motorists feared, according to extensive new road data from Ford. The carmaker says its battery packs keep more than 90% of their original capacity on average after 100,000 miles of travel.The figures offer rare, large-scale insight into how power packs age outside test laboratories. Battery degradation remains a key hesitation for drivers considering an electric model. Ford’s latest findings indicate that sudden, steep drops in storage capacity are largely absent across standard ownership cycles.Engineers based their conclusions on the 2021 Mustang Mach-E, the company’s first purpose-built electric crossover. Over five years, more than 36,000 of these vehicles have traveled across the United States and Canada. Together, they have covered roughly two billion miles on public roads.Across that entire group, average battery health stands at 92%. Crucially for researchers, the performance gap between individual cars is narrow. Ford found that 95% of the fleet falls within a tight health band between 87% and 97%. This consistency shows that extreme degradation remains rare, even in varying climates and driving conditions.Predictable aging curveThe trend continues among high-mileage motorists. More than 2,000 early owners have already crossed the 100,000-mile mark on their factory-installed batteries. That specific group still averages more than 91% usable capacity. A smaller set of roughly 30 drivers has driven past 200,000 miles, retaining an average of 88%.The fleet numbers explain unusual private milestones, including one driver who reached 400,000 miles in a 2022 model without replacing his pack. While that distance remains exceptional, Ford says it fits into a clear, predictable aging curve rather than acting as a statistical freak.Across its wider electric range in North America, Ford designs its power units to operate for at least a decade. The five-year data confirms that modern battery management software prevents early chemical exhaustion.How drivers maintain their cars depends on the underlying battery chemistry. The 2021 Mach-E models rely on nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) cells. For daily commuting, these units degrade more slowly when owners avoid charging them to 100%. Regular charging to 80% or 90% reduces chemical and voltage stress on the cell.Tailored charging adviceIn contrast, several newer Ford models carry lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) packs. These batteries handle frequent full top-ups without rapid wear. In fact, periodic charges to 100% help the onboard computers recalibrate and calculate accurate driving range figures.Ford now sends tailored charging advice directly through its smartphone app based on the specific pack installed in the car. For the automotive industry, real-world data at this scale confirms a shifting reality. Electric power packs are proving durable enough to outlast earlier expectations, easing long-term ownership concerns as the transition away from fossil fuels continues.“These rigorous quality tests are designed to help us understand how battery systems perform across a wide range of climates, charging behaviors, and driving conditions before customers get behind the wheel,” said Ford.

title: James Webb’s Mysteriously Bright Galaxies May Finally Have an Explanation
content:
Artist’s illustration of gas being cleared from the surroundings of a star-forming region in the early universe. Credit: Matt Twombly for Simons Foundation
Calculations suggest powerful ultraviolet light from young stars could sweep gas out of early galaxies while leaving dense star-forming regions intact, offering a clue to their mysterious brightness.
The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed something unexpected about the early universe:
bright galaxies were far more common
just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang than astronomers thought possible. A new analysis suggests these galaxies may not necessarily be producing more light than expected. Instead, powerful ultraviolet radiation from young stars could be clearing away gas and dust, allowing more of their light to reach us.
Researchers at the Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute in New York City and the University of Texas at Dallas investigated this possibility by examining how ultraviolet light called Lyman-alpha radiation interacts with material surrounding young stars. Their findings, published November 4 in
The Astrophysical Journal
, suggest that this radiation can drive gas and dust out of less dense regions of galaxies, potentially explaining why some of the earliest galaxies appear unusually bright.
“Our results show Lyman-alpha radiation can push low-density gas and dust away really, really fast,” says Shyam Menon, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Astrophysics and the study’s lead author. “It can sort of clear the ‘fog,’ allowing us to see stars in the early universe much more clearly than we would otherwise.”
Hydrogen makes ultraviolet light unusually powerful
Lyman-alpha radiation forms when an electron collides with a hydrogen atom or joins a hydrogen ion, and it can be especially abundant in regions where young stars are forming. When this light encounters gas or dust, it transfers momentum to the material, creating pressure that can push it outward.
What makes Lyman-alpha radiation particularly powerful is how hydrogen responds to it. While most absorbed light is released at a different wavelength, hydrogen atoms almost immediately re-emit Lyman-alpha radiation at the same wavelength, allowing nearby atoms to absorb and release it repeatedly. These repeated interactions increase the force exerted by the light, potentially pushing surrounding material away from regions where stars are forming.
An infographic explaining how radiation propelled light-blocking gas and gust. Credit: Lucy Reading-Ikkanda/Simons Foundation
Astronomers have long suspected that this pressure could reshape stellar nurseries by removing gas needed for star formation, possibly even stopping the process under extreme conditions. However, the repeated interactions between radiation and hydrogen are difficult to reproduce in computer simulations, making it challenging to determine how much influence the radiation actually has.
“We’ve known for a very long time that Lyman-alpha radiation could be important because it carries a lot of force,” Menon says. “But we’ve never actually been able to estimate how important it is in a realistic environment because of how challenging it is to model.”
Where ultraviolet light overcomes gravity
To address this problem, Menon and collaborator Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas analyzed snapshots from an existing simulation of a star-forming region in the early universe. Rather than tracking every interaction between light and matter, they calculated how much pressure Lyman-alpha radiation would exert on the surrounding gas and dust.
Their calculations revealed that the radiation behaves differently depending on the density of the surrounding material. In dense star-forming regions, gravity remained strong enough to hold gas and dust in place despite the outward pressure, suggesting that Lyman-alpha radiation had little effect on star formation there. In less crowded regions between stars, however, the radiation could overcome gravity and drive material outward at high speeds.
Multiple views of a 2.5-million-year simulation visualizing a gas cloud as it is cleared away and the formation of stars. From left to right, the views show the gas density, ionization, and temperature. Credit: Shyam Menon (Flatiron Institute) and Aaron Smith (UT Dallas)
“When the density is low enough, the Lyman-alpha radiation can push the gas to really high speeds, launching explosive winds that can shoot material clear out of the galaxy,” Menon says.
These winds could help explain the unexpectedly bright galaxies detected by the James Webb Space Telescope. By removing loosely distributed gas and dust from between stars, the radiation may create clearer paths for starlight to escape, making distant galaxies appear brighter without requiring them to produce unusually large amounts of light.
Three-dimensional simulations remain a challenge
Important questions remain, particularly about the properties of dust in the early universe and how radiation interacts with moving gas as stars form. Researchers will need more comprehensive simulations that account for these processes together to better understand their influence on early galaxies.
Recent work by Olof Nebrin of Stockholm University and study co-author Smith has demonstrated that these interactions can be modeled in two dimensions, although more realistic three-dimensional simulations remain a challenge.
“But the hope is that in the coming years, with improvements to computing power and the development of more effective algorithms, we can eventually do these simulations in three dimensions.”
Reference: “Lyα Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn” by Shyam H. Menon and Aaron Smith, 4 November 2026,
The Astrophysical Journal
