title: A Planet 11 Times Bigger Than Jupiter Is Challenging What We Thought About Planet Formation
content:
This artist’s impression shows how the planet inside the disc of Beta Pictoris may look. Credit: ESO/L. Calçada
New observations of the giant exoplanet Beta Pictoris b are challenging assumptions about how and where massive planets form.
New observations of Beta Pictoris b, a massive planet orbiting a young star, are challenging a method astronomers hoped could reveal where giant planets form. More precise measurements of the planet’s atmosphere have overturned an earlier result, raising doubts about whether a particular chemical signature can reliably trace a planet’s birthplace.
Located in a 23-million-year-old planetary system, Beta Pictoris b is approximately 11 times Jupiter’s mass. It orbits about 10 astronomical units (approximately 930 million miles) from its star, completing one revolution every 23 years. Earlier atmospheric measurements suggested the planet might have formed much farther away before migrating inward, but the latest evidence points to a different possibility.
A Chemical Fingerprint of Planet Formation
Astronomers have proposed using the relative abundance of two forms of carbon monoxide (CO) to determine where giant planets formed within their original disks of gas and dust. These molecules contain different carbon isotopes, 12C and 13C, which have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their slightly different masses can influence how they behave during chemical processes.
The method relies on the carbon monoxide snowline, the distance from a young star beyond which temperatures become cold enough for CO gas to freeze onto dust grains. Planets forming beyond this boundary may accumulate carbon monoxide ice, potentially leaving a different isotopic signature than planets that develop in warmer regions where CO remains gaseous.
Earlier observations of Beta Pictoris b using the original GRAVITY instrument produced a relatively low ratio of 12CO to 13CO. That result appeared consistent with formation beyond the snowline, followed by inward migration to the planet’s present orbit. However, the researchers cautioned that instrumental limitations could have affected the measurement.
The GRAVITY instrument of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) at the European Southern Observatory’s (ESO) Paranal Observatory. Credit: G. Rojas/ESO
Sharper Observations Change the Picture
A team led by Antonia von Stauffenberg, a doctoral student at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg, Germany, has now revisited the planet using GRAVITY+. The upgraded instrument operates at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), managed by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) in Chile.
The new observations reveal a substantially higher 12CO/13CO ratio than previously reported. While 12CO produces a readily detectable signal, its less abundant counterpart, 13CO, is considerably harder to measure accurately. GRAVITY+ provides improved adaptive optics and greater observational precision, allowing researchers to better distinguish the two molecules.
“The GRAVITY+ interferometric instrument is highly stable […], making it uniquely capable of high-fidelity characterization of directly imaged exoplanets,” says co-author and MPIA scientist Jonas Sauter.
The revised ratio agrees with independent measurements reported by González Picos et al. (2026) using a different instrument. This agreement supports the new result and indicates that systematic uncertainties affected the earlier GRAVITY measurements.
Possible Atmospheric Changes on Beta Pictoris b
The researchers also detected tentative variations in the planet’s observed brightness. These fluctuations appear to follow a period of approximately 8.7 hours, close to the planet’s rotation period.
If confirmed, the variations could arise from atmospheric clouds or chemical differences moving in and out of view as the planet rotates. However, the evidence remains statistically weak, and more sensitive observations will be necessary to establish whether the changes are real.
“The ability to accurately constrain both isotopologues and potential rotational variability using ground-based observations of a bona fide planet such as Beta Pictoris b demonstrates the exceptional data quality achieved with the updated GRAVITY+ instrument,” says von Stauffenberg.
Why the Planet’s Birthplace Remains a Mystery
Under the proposed formation model, the revised carbon monoxide ratio would favor an origin inside the snowline, consistent with Beta Pictoris b’s current orbital distance. Yet the measurement also closely resembles ratios observed throughout the Solar System and the interstellar medium, the gas and dust occupying the space between stars.
Similar values have been measured in most of the roughly dozen young giant planets studied using this technique. This widespread consistency suggests that differences in carbon isotope abundances across planet-forming environments may be too small to distinguish reliably, limiting the method’s usefulness for reconstructing individual planetary histories.
“It is still difficult to utilize 13CO as a formation tracer of giant planets, due to the uncertainties that still persist in the models and measurements,” explains von Stauffenberg.
Current models may be missing important details of carbon monoxide ice chemistry in planet-forming disks. Until those processes are better understood, atmospheric carbon isotope ratios alone cannot establish whether a giant planet formed in a warm, gas-rich region or farther out among frozen materials. More precise observations and additional chemical indicators will be needed to reconstruct these planets’ origins, with GRAVITY+ offering a powerful tool for investigating both their formation and atmospheric behavior.
Reference: “13CO and potential variability in β Pictoris b with GRAVITY+” by A. von Stauffenberg, J. Sauter, P. Mollière, M. Ravet, D. Trevascus, W. Brandner, A. Berdeu, M. Bonnefoy, G. Bourdarot, J.-B. Le Bouquin, G. Chauvin, F. Eisenhauer, M. Houllé, L. Kreidberg, E. Matthews, F. Millour, J. Scigliuto, J. Wang, J. W. Xuan and Y. Zhang, 9 July 2026,
Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: A Common Plastic Could Solve a Major Problem With Living on the Moon
content:
Scientists have developed a surprisingly durable insulating material from a familiar plastic that could help protect future lunar habitats from extreme temperatures. Credit: Shutterstock
The same plastic that keeps marathon runners warm could help future moon bases withstand extreme temperatures and years of rough treatment.
Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed an insulating material by stacking hundreds of thin sheets of Mylar. In laboratory tests, the stacks combined effective insulation in a vacuum with flexibility and resistance to repeated compression, qualities that could make them useful for long-term lunar construction.
Their study, published in
ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces
, calls the material hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). The approach addresses a persistent engineering problem: materials that resist heat flow often struggle to withstand physical damage.
“These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression, and maintain their insulating performance,” says senior author Igor Bargatin, an associate professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), “potentially allowing them to be packed, transported, and survive rough treatment over many years of use.”
Why Lunar Insulation Needs To Be Tough
On the moon, insulation must protect against temperatures ranging from hundreds of degrees below zero to the boiling point of water. But surviving those extremes is only part of the job. Materials must also endure transportation, installation, maintenance, and accidental impacts.
Some leading insulators are poorly suited to that treatment. Aerogels contain mostly empty space, making them lightweight and effective at slowing heat transfer in applications from
industrial pipelines
NASA’s Mars rovers
. Their porous structure, however, can also leave them susceptible to mechanical damage.
A sample of the stacked Mylar sheets the researchers created, which could one day provide insulation on the moon. Credit: Bargatin Lab, Penn Engineering
Multilayer insulation, widely used in space, takes another approach: reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers reduce heat transfer by radiation. These assemblies work well thermally, but they are not built to carry substantial loads and can tear during handling.
Making an insulator stronger can compromise its thermal performance. “For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both,” says Bargatin. “The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.”
A Familiar Plastic In A New Arrangement
Mylar offered the researchers an accessible starting material. Formally known as biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET, the plastic already appears in food packaging and aerospace equipment. Combined with aluminum, it reflects infrared radiation, which is how shiny emergency blankets help marathon runners retain body heat.
The team tested several film thicknesses and coated some sheets with an extremely thin layer of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to increase stiffness. Researchers then assembled the films individually into stacks.
The researchers discovered that the particles manufacturers use to separate layers of Mylar also play a role in heat transfer. Credit: Bargatin Lab
“At the moment, the process is very time-consuming,” says first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn chemistry doctoral graduate who also earned a master’s in MEAM. “We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.”
Once assembled, however, the films were far tougher than their delicate handling suggested. Under vacuum conditions and compression representative of a lunar habitat with indoor air at atmospheric pressure, the best stacks matched the thermal conductivity of other high-performance vacuum insulation technologies while remaining flexible.
Insulation That Survived Repeated Squeezing
In separate mechanical tests, the coated stacks retained their insulating performance at the highest compressive stresses the laboratory equipment could produce. Researchers repeatedly squeezed samples to approximately 20 megapascals (about 2,900 pounds per square inch), roughly equivalent to concentrating 200 pounds onto an area the size of a fingertip.
“We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress,” recalls Levin. “But the stacks didn’t survive just one high-stress cycle—they survived 10 in a row.”
A sample of the stacked Mylar sheets the researchers created, which could one day provide insulation on the moon. Credit: Bargatin Lab, Penn Engineering
That durability could make the material easier to transport and reuse, as well as more forgiving once installed. “You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them,” says Bargatin. “When we’re talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it’s really important to have tough materials that can last long enough.”
“The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the moon,” says Levin. “This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable, and reusable lunar insulation.”
Tiny Particles Shape How Heat Moves
The study also identified an overlooked feature of commercial Mylar that could help explain its performance: microscopic particles added to keep the plastic from sticking to itself. These “antiblocking” particles protrude slightly from the surface, separating neighboring sheets and making thin films easier to manufacture and handle.
Their industrial purpose was already understood, but their influence on heat flow through stacked films had received little attention, according to the researchers. Because conventional multilayer insulation primarily targets radiation, there had been less reason to investigate how these particles affect heat conducted directly between sheets.
The researchers subjected the stacked layers to mechanical stresses to see how well they might hold up to the rigors of building habitats on the moon. Credit: Bargatin Lab, Penn Engineering
The researchers built models of heat transfer across the interfaces between layers and compared their predictions with experimental measurements. The results suggest that, in a vacuum, heat passes between sheets mainly at the tiny contact points where antiblocking particles touch neighboring films.
Those contacts could become a design tool. Instead of working around whatever particles commercial Mylar happens to contain, future insulation could use carefully selected particle sizes, numbers, and distributions to regulate heat transfer.
Why Thinner Films Were Not Better
The particles also helped explain a result that contradicted the team’s initial expectations. Thinner sheets should allow more layers to fit into a given space, creating more interfaces that impede heat transfer. The researchers therefore expected their thinnest films to provide the strongest insulation.
Instead, the thinnest films they successfully characterized performed similarly to medium-thickness films when both received an alumina coating. The team suspects that particles in the thinner films create additional contact between neighboring layers, opening more pathways for heat to flow.
“As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes,” says Levin. “It’s not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.”
Improving the material will therefore require balancing film thickness, stiffness, and particle distribution. Simply making each sheet thinner may provide little benefit if the resulting contacts allow more heat through.
The current samples cover only about one square centimeter (0.16 square inches), and manually cutting and stacking them takes hours. Producing practical insulation at the scale of a meter (about 3.3 feet) will require a much faster assembly method.
The researchers see potential in manufacturing techniques such as continuously coating large rolls of Mylar. Eventually, film thickness, coatings, and particle distribution might be adjusted before the material is wound into large stacks.
Larger versions still need testing, including whether they can withstand repeated bending, bumps, and scuffs. If the laboratory results carry over to practical production, HyLIFS could provide flexible insulation for lunar habitats, spacesuits, rovers, electronics, and other equipment that must operate for years in space.
For Levin, the findings show how much remains to be discovered in familiar materials. “The simplest configuration ended up being the best one,” she says.
Reference: “Robust Layered Thermal Insulator Film Stacks for Vacuum Applications” by D. R. Levin, M. F. Campbell, G. Aldan, O. H. Omodior and I. Bargatin, 1 September 2026,
ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces
DOI: 10.1021/acsami.6c09126
This work was supported by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

title: Brick Kilns Became Cleaner and More Profitable, but Workers Saw No Benefits
content:
Bangladesh’s brick kilns are large, often open-air facilities where clay bricks are shaped, dried, and fired at high temperatures, typically using coal as fuel. These traditional kilns produce billions of bricks each year to support the country’s booming construction industry. Credit: Shutterstock
Bangladesh’s brick kilns found a way to pollute less and earn more, but workers saw no measurable improvement in their pay or working conditions.
Simple adjustments to how coal is fed and bricks are stacked helped traditional kilns burn less fuel, release less pollution, and produce better bricks. Yet a companion study found no measurable improvement in wages, health, child labor, or coercive working conditions during the study period.
The findings expose a gap between improving an industry’s performance and improving life for its workforce. They also suggest that protecting workers requires measures aimed directly at their needs.
The multiyear research effort involved Nina Brooks, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and a faculty affiliate of its Center for South Asian Studies.
A Cleaner Way To Make Bricks
Bangladesh’s rapid urban growth depends on an industry with a substantial environmental footprint. The country is the world’s fourth-largest brick producer, and roughly 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of its domestic brick consumption. Alongside carbon emissions, the kilns release fine particles known as PM2.5. Ambient air pollution causes 4.9 million premature deaths globally, with South Asia accounting for 32% of them.
Brooks began investigating brickmaking about eight years ago during her doctoral studies. She and her collaborators mapped kilns with satellite imagery and machine learning, studied regulation, and examined health effects in communities downwind. Their work revealed why restricting kiln locations alone could not solve the pollution problem.
“Bangladesh is one of the world’s most densely populated countries,” Brooks said. “It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities, and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution.”
Instead, researchers worked with owners, managers, and workers to improve existing operations. They introduced more continuous coal feeding, brick-stacking arrangements that improved airflow, and measures to reduce heat loss. None required replacing kilns or purchasing major new equipment.
Less Fuel, Better Bricks
After a small pilot, the team expanded the approach to hundreds of kilns. Results published in
showed that training and technical support reduced energy use by about 10.5% across kilns assigned to the program. Estimated emissions fell by 171 metric tons (about 188.5 US tons) of carbon dioxide and 0.45 metric tons (about 990 pounds) of PM2.5 per kiln over a firing season.
Among kilns that adopted the practices because of the program, energy use dropped about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2.5 emissions each fell roughly 20%. Owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater proportion of higher-quality bricks.
Adoption had increased when researchers returned the next firing season, suggesting the changes had staying power. “Because the changes are economically beneficial for owners, they had a strong incentive to continue following them,” Brooks said.
For businesses facing expensive equipment upgrades and authorities struggling to enforce environmental rules, the findings offered a practical route to cleaner production.
Workers Saw No Measurable Gains
The researchers then examined whether those business benefits reached workers. Bangladesh’s brick industry relies on a large, mostly informal workforce whose employment can involve debt, advance payments, long hours, hazardous conditions, and restrictions on leaving. A companion study in the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
examined 246 kilns in the Khulna Division and included private interviews with 1,442 workers.
Seventy percent of workers reported having no personal protective equipment, and 71% lacked a formal labor contract. Forty-two percent described restrictions on movement or communication. Across the sample, roughly 20% met the U.S. Department of State’s definitions of labor trafficking. At nearly half the kilns, at least 1 in 6 workers met those definitions.
Adult workers also reported child labor at more than 70% of the kilns, with most reported cases involving children ages 14 to 17.
The intervention lowered fuel costs by 9.6% and improved brick quality by 8.1%, but researchers detected no corresponding improvement in trafficking, child labor, wages, health, or working conditions. Although changes were possible within the study period, the economic gains did not produce measurable benefits for workers.
Why Productivity Was Not Enough
Higher productivity is often expected to help employees through better pay or conditions. The kiln studies show why that outcome cannot be assumed when coercion and limited bargaining power shape the labor market.
“In many countries, not just Bangladesh, labor laws are hard to enforce, particularly in informal sectors. So, it’s critical to find other ways to protect workers from exploitation,” said Grant Miller, a professor of medicine at Stanford University. “Our study shows that we cannot rely on productivity gains alone to do that, at least not in the short run. Finding approaches that work beyond regulation is a central goal of our ongoing research.”
Why Some Kiln Owners Hesitated
Expanding the cleaner production program revealed that kiln owners in other regions were more reluctant to adopt the changes. In districts around Dhaka, owners were considerably less likely to adopt the practices than those in Khulna. Yet participating kilns achieved comparable reductions in fuel use and emissions, Brooks said. “So, we’re seeing greater hesitation,” she said. “But once they adopt, we see the same benefits.”
Sameer Maithel, the research team’s lead technical expert, said the reasons are still being investigated. Owners operating on narrow margins may hesitate to change familiar methods while facing unpredictable coal prices, brick demand, and regulation. Differences in kiln size, land, and production practices can also make adoption easier in one location than another.
“Informal brick production in South Asia faces a lot of uncertainty: weather, energy prices, market demand, and regulation all shift unpredictably. Many kiln owners also have limited technical and managerial support, and conditions vary from region to region,” Maithel said. “All of this makes scaling up slow and complex, and it takes sustained, dedicated effort.”
Putting Worker Protection First
The lack of improvement for workers has prompted the team to test more direct measures. During the most recent brickmaking season, researchers returned to Khulna with recommendations developed through pilot work and conversations with workers.
They recommended masks for people crushing coal, goggles and protective footwear for fire workers, and head protection for brick carriers. Other measures included sanitation and cooking facilities, shaded rest areas, clean water, heat-stress awareness, and information about child labor.
“None of the owners I interviewed objected to improving conditions for workers, though some disagreed with specific components. They saw the cost as negligible compared to what they spend running a kiln. As they put it, if workers do better work because of it, it’s worth doing,” said Mohammad Saeed Munim, a research officer in the Health Systems and Population Studies Division of the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh.
Researchers had expected more resistance. Owners’ willingness to consider these changes now gives the team an opportunity to test whether targeting workers’ daily needs can deliver improvements that greater productivity alone did not.

title: Antarctica’s Melting Ice Has Triggered a Sudden Shift Deep in the Ocean
content:
Sea ice off Victoria Land, Antarctica, with Mount Melbourne in the background. Credit: Alberto C Naveira Grabato
Ocean measurements show a vast Southern Hemisphere water layer growing saltier and denser, a shift that could send more heat into deep waters than climate models predict.
Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean. That seasonal supply helps sustain Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a layer of relatively fresh seawater that spreads across much of the Southern Hemisphere’s ocean. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen, and drive global currents, redistributing heat, fresh water, and carbon around the planet.
The findings, published in
Nature Climate Change
, provide the first direct observational evidence of this change in the AAIW’s properties. The international research team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, alongside satellite and atmospheric datasets.
Sea ice floes from marine voyage. Credit: Alberto C Naveira Grabato
Less sea ice, less fresh water
The study was led by Associate Professor Bishakhdatta Gayen, of the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and Kaushik Mishra, a PhD student at IISc. Gayen said:
“The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River’s entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km.
“From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge, and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon’s annual flow.”
Antarctic Intermediate Water shifted from freshening before 2016 to becoming saltier, denser and deeper afterward. Credit: Kaushik Mishra
Co-author Professor Alberto Naveira Garabato, of the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom, described the changes as an urgent reminder that climate change is affecting almost every part of Earth’s surface.
“As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean’s global ‘overturning circulation’, a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation – the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic.
“It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather, and storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally.”
The globe shows sea ice around Antarctica month by month. The first time-series graph shows whether sea-ice area was above or below normal (the 1993-2024 mean), based on satellite observations. The bottom graph tracks the saltiness of Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer that sinks from the surface into the ocean’s interior, using Argo float data from 2004. From 1993 to 2015, Antarctic sea ice slowly expanded (blue trend line), releasing more freshwater, making the waters beneath it fresher. After 2016, sea ice dropped sharply (red trend line), and the layer turned saltier. Less melting ice means less freshwater reaching the ocean interior. Credit: Kaushik Mishra
More heat could reach deeper waters
Changes in how water moves between the surface and deeper layers could also affect the oceans’ role as a “climate buffer,” as Gayen described it. Oceans absorb and redistribute most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries. This slows and moderates atmospheric warming and its immediate effects.
Mishra said the abrupt reversal revealed a critical missing feedback loop.
“The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”
“If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away – although the magnitude and timing are uncertain,” Gayen said.
“This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere.”
The changes of the sea-surface salinity after sea ice decline in 2016. Credit: Kaushik Mishra
According to Gayen, the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica.
“That transition took thousands of years, not two decades,” he said.
Reference: “Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline” by Kaushik Mishra, Bishakhdatta Gayen and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, 28 October 2026,
Nature Climate Change

MOES/11/2024) and the Australian Research Council Discovery Grant (grant no. DP240102823). title: NASA Warns a Monster El Niño Could Surpass the Historic 1997 Event
content:
The 2015-16 El Niño was also very strong, as elevated sea levels in October 2015 (middle) show. But its pattern differed from those in October 1997 (top) and October 2026 (bottom): less of the elevated water reached the coast of South America, which contributed to different weather patterns that year. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory maps by Lauren Dauphin, using NASA-SSH altimetry data provided by Josh Willis, Severine Fournier, and Kevin Marlis, NASA/JPL-Caltech
An El Niño that could beat 1997’s record is taking shape in the Pacific, leaving scientists watching for its next move.
El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that returns roughly every two to seven years. Its most recent
very strong
events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, disrupted weather worldwide. Consequences included
fires in Indonesia
and the Amazon, crop failures caused by
drought in southern Africa
heavy rain
and coastal flooding in Southern California.
Satellite measurements show that the
current El Niño
resembles the 1997–98 event, with warm water stretching across the equatorial Pacific to South America. But that oceanic resemblance does not guarantee the same weather during winter 2026–27, as the outcome also depends on how the atmosphere responds.
How El Niño Builds Momentum
Every El Niño starts with a change in the tropical Pacific’s winds. Trade winds normally push warm surface water westward, leaving sea levels higher in the western Pacific than in the east. When those winds weaken, warm water begins moving back toward the central and eastern Pacific.
As warmth spreads eastward, the trade winds weaken further and sometimes reverse, allowing still more warm water to follow. This feedback loop helps El Niño intensify.
But strength alone does not determine its effects. The location of the warmest water and the atmosphere’s response also shape the outcome. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.”
Satellites Reveal the Ocean’s Heat
Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface. Across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, unusually high water therefore provides a signal of El Niño’s heat buildup.
The maps compare
sea surface height
anomalies on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). JPL scientists processed measurements from
TOPEX/Poseidon
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich
, respectively. Red shows higher-than-average sea levels, white indicates normal conditions, and blue marks lower levels. Seasonal effects and long-term trends have been removed to highlight El Niño and other short-term natural changes.
“What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.”
Why The 1997 Comparison Matters
Although the 2026 El Niño developed much more abruptly, by October it shared two defining features with 1997: lower sea levels in the west and higher levels in the east, with warm, elevated water reaching South America. Willis thinks that resemblance could translate into similar impacts, including the abundant rainfall seen across California and the southern United States in 1997–98.
The powerful 2015–16 event shows why the arrangement of that heat matters. A map based on
measurements from October 12, 2015, appears alongside the 1997 and 2026 comparisons. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator did not reach as far against South America. That winter, rainfall effects were concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States, with significant flooding in Mexico.
NOAA’s October 8, 2026,
El Niño outlook
assigned an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong event through the first three months of 2027. Still, its effects during winter 2026–27 and beyond remain uncertain. El Niño’s influence passes through a chaotic atmosphere, and its signal becomes harder to distinguish beyond the tropics.
“There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”

title: Researchers Discover New Lace Bug Species on Japan’s Remote Ogasawara Islands
content:
Omoplax desecta (adult). Credit: Jun Souma
DNA uncovered a hidden species among Japan’s lace bugs and hints that a tree introduced by humans could help give rise to another.
Lace bugs living on two groups of Japan’s remote Ogasawara Islands had been classified as a single species, despite differences in their diets and coloring. Comparisons of their DNA have now revealed that they belong to two species, a distinction supported by subtle physical differences.
The archipelago lies roughly 900 to 1,000 kilometers (560 to 620 miles) south of Tokyo and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site. Its land snails and plants are celebrated for including species found nowhere else. About 440 insect species are also known to be unique to the islands, but their evolution has received far less attention.
Omoplax desecta (nymph). Credit: Jun Souma
DNA distinguishes two lace bug species
Among those insects is
, a genus of lace bugs thought to have diversified rapidly across the islands. Jun Souma, of Hirosaki University’s Shirakami Research Center for Environmental Sciences, investigated these insects with Naoyuki Nakahama, of the Graduate School of Agriculture at Osaka Metropolitan University.
“The reason I took a particular interest in
Omoplax desecta
is that it feeds on both the native plant
Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi
and the introduced plant
Calophyllum inophyllum
in the Chichijima island group,” Souma said. “This is quite unusual for lace bugs, which typically exhibit high host specificity. I was also intrigued by the fact that it is distributed across multiple island groups, which is different from other
species.”
To investigate relationships among the insects, the researchers analyzed 52 specimens using MIG-seq, a method that provides DNA data from across the genome. Populations classified as
Omoplax desecta
on the Chichijima and Hahajima island groups were genetically distinct. The study is published in the open-access journal
Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi. Credit: Jun Souma
The genetic evidence helped explain differences Souma had noticed in the Hahajima insects.
“I had wondered why it fed exclusively on
Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi
and why there were no individuals with dark brown to black pronotum, which are sometimes seen in the Chichijima island group,” Souma explained. The pronotum is the plate just behind an insect’s head. “After conducting population genetic and phylogenetic analyses, I began to suspect that this population might be a distinct species. Upon closely observing their morphological characteristics, I was certain of this.”
Subtle differences in male genitalia confirmed the distinction. The Hahajima population is now described as
Omoplax sandoru
, named after the local name of its host plant.
A new diet could divide a species
Omoplax desecta
in the Chichijima group, the introduced tree offered another clue to how these insects might diversify. The DNA data indicate that its shift to feeding on
Calophyllum inophyllum
happened once, and recently. Whether that change will eventually produce another species remains a possibility rather than an established outcome.
“I also find it interesting that the introduction of
Calophyllum inophyllum
Omoplax desecta
,” Souma added.
Calophyllum inophyllum. Credit: Jun Souma
Lookalikes aren’t always the closest relatives
The researchers also reconstructed an evolutionary tree to trace relationships among the insects. That allowed them to test whether species with similar appearances and food preferences were one another’s closest relatives.
“The most surprising finding of my research was that species feeding on the same plant and appearing very similar are not necessarily sister groups,” said Souma, referring to groups that are each other’s closest evolutionary relatives. “Adaptive radiation among insects on oceanic islands may be more complex than comparisons of morphological characteristics and life histories would suggest at first glance.”
Jun Souma, conducting observation on Calophyllum inophyllum where Omoplax desecta feeds. Credit: Jun Souma
Adaptive radiation is the diversification of related organisms into species adapted to different ecological roles. Here, the findings point to both geographic isolation and shifts between host plants as drivers of species formation.
The researchers could not obtain DNA from two rare species, leaving gaps in the evolutionary picture. Further sampling will be needed to trace how these insects reached the islands and diversified.
Reference: “Genome-wide SNP data reveal phylogenetic relationships and further new species of lace bugs (Hemiptera, Heteroptera, Tingidae) endemic to the Japanese oceanic islands (the Ogasawara Islands), providing insight into their speciation” by Jun Souma and Naoyuki Nakahama, 8 October 2026,
DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1294.205145

title: How a Single Missing Atom Can Leave a Secret Fingerprint in Laser Light
content:
An illustration of atomic defects within hexagonal boron nitride altering light, creating an optical fingerprint. A University at Buffalo-led study predicted the optical fingerprints for 10 known defects within this material, which could have applications for quantum technologies. Credit: Vasili Perebeinos/University at Buffalo
Researchers have uncovered subtle optical signatures that could help distinguish atomic defects in a promising quantum material.
An atomic defect too small to see could leave a recognizable signature in laser light, giving scientists a new way to identify structures that may be useful for quantum technology. Researchers at the University at Buffalo have predicted how different atomic imperfections alter the optical behavior of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), a material made of boron and nitrogen atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern.
Using computer simulations, the team examined 10 types of defects, including missing boron or nitrogen atoms and sites where carbon atoms had taken their place. Some defects were predicted to dramatically increase the light produced at twice or even three times the frequency of an incoming laser. The strength of these signals depended on the light’s polarization, which describes the orientation of its electric field.
How Light Reveals Hidden Atomic Structures
Even defects containing identical atoms can produce different optical responses if those atoms are arranged differently. When the researchers compared two configurations of four carbon atoms, they found that one was predicted to generate strong signals in two polarization directions, while the other produced a strong response in only one.
“These distinctive light responses could eventually allow us to experimentally identify not only which atoms are involved in a defect, but also precisely how they’re arranged,” says co-corresponding author Paras N. Prasad, SUNY Distinguished Professor, Samuel P. Capen Chair in the Department of Chemistry, and executive director of UB’s
Institute for Lasers, Photonics, and Biophotonics
The findings, published October 19 in the American Chemical Society’s
Nano Letters
, could provide a reference for experimentally identifying atomic defects. By comparing measured light responses with the predicted optical fingerprints, researchers may eventually be able to determine which defects are present in a sample.
Identifying Defects for Quantum Technology
Some atomic defects in h-BN can emit single photons, individual particles of light released one at a time. These photons could transmit quantum information in future communication systems and support advanced sensing technologies. However, different defects have different properties, making accurate identification essential for finding useful sources of quantum light.
“Not all atomic defects are created equal. Making it easier to identify defects brings us another step closer to determining which ones have the properties we’re looking for,” says co-corresponding author Vasili Perebeinos, PhD, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in the UB School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.
The simulations could help guide efforts to determine which defects generate quantum light and how to create them at specific locations within a material. Rather than relying on isolated photon emitters, the researchers ultimately hope to build organized arrays of precisely positioned defects.
“The ultimate goal is to create a material where we can precisely control the placement of defects that produce quantum light,” Perebeinos says. “Instead of relying on individual sources of quantum light, we want to create entire arrays of them that could be used in future quantum technologies. That’s the main motivation for studying defects in these materials.”
Reference: “Nonlinear Optical Fingerprints of Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride” by Olga Savkina, Davoud Adinehloo, Ivan Zhigulin, Pranati R. Kuntla, Viktor Labuntsov, Cecilia L. A. V. Campos, Alexander Baev, Andrey Kuzmin, Huamin Li, Igor Aharonovich, Paras N. Prasad and Vasili Perebeinos, 19 October 2026,
Nano Letters
DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03684
The work was supported by the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research as part of the Multidisciplinary University Research Initiative (MURI). Support also came from the U.S. National Science Foundation, Australian Research Council, and the University at Buffalo Quantum Institute.

title: “This Should Not Happen”: Scientists Discover a Strange New Way To Control Atoms
content:
Impression of the experiment where the spins of the electron (blue) and the nucleus (orange) within a single atom are independently controlled by wave signals from the probe tip of a tunneling microscope. Credit: Studio Scixel
A new technique allows researchers to manipulate magnetism deep within a single atom.
Scientists have used radio waves to control the magnetic spin of a single atomic nucleus, achieving a result that challenges their understanding of how atomic magnetism works. The experiment, conducted at
Delft University of Technology
and published in
Nature Communications
, demonstrates that nuclear spin can be manipulated under conditions where researchers did not expect it to respond.
Unlike the relatively strong magnetism associated with electrons, nuclear magnetism is extremely weak and more isolated from its surroundings. “By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons,” says lead researcher Sander Otte. “But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.”
An Unexpected Response From the Atomic Nucleus
To investigate magnetism at the atomic scale, Otte’s team uses a modified scanning tunneling microscope capable of directing electrical signals at individual atoms. Previous experiments primarily examined electron spin, which is easier to detect and manipulate. Nuclear spin could be observed indirectly through the hyperfine interaction, a quantum coupling between the magnetic properties of an electron and the nucleus.
In the latest experiment, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues applied two signals simultaneously, one targeting the electron and another targeting the nucleus. By examining their effects separately, the researchers discovered that they could flip the nuclear spin even when it was largely disentangled from the electron spin. This contradicted their expectation that the nucleus would not respond independently to the microscope’s electrical signals.
“According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen,” says Otte. “The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.”
Controlling Atomic Magnetism With Precise Frequencies
The researchers achieved this control by adapting double magnetic resonance, an established technique, to work with a single atom. The method allowed them to address the nucleus and electron independently using signals tuned to their respective magnetic resonances. In quantum mechanics, spin can change between specific allowed states, and each transition requires a signal with the appropriate frequency.
“You can compare it to the strings of a guitar,” Vennema explains. “Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The ‘notes’ of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.”
Implications for Quantum Information Storage
Nuclear spins are promising candidates for storing quantum information because they are relatively well protected from external disturbances that can disrupt delicate quantum states. The ability to control an individual nuclear spin could eventually support new methods for storing and reading quantum information, although practical applications remain a future possibility.
For now, the experiment leaves a fundamental question unanswered: What physical mechanism allows the nuclear spin to respond when its coupling to the electron spin is insufficient to explain the observed behavior? Understanding that process will require further investigation.
“Back to the drawing board, then,” says Otte. “That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out.”
Reference: “Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe” by Hester G. Vennema, Cristina Mier, Evert W. Stolte, Leonard Edens, Jinwon Lee and Sander Otte, 24 October 2026,

title: A Hidden Cancer-Killing Mechanism Could Change the Future of Immunotherapy
content:
Perforin increases endosomal-mitochondrial contact sites in tumor cells. The left has no perforin; the right has perforin. Credit: University of Michigan Rogel Cancer Center
An immune protein called perforin can turn iron against cancer cells in laboratory experiments, suggesting a possible route to more effective immunotherapy.
The immune system can attack cancer cells by punching holes in their outer membranes and sending in enzymes that kill them. Research led by the
University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center
shows that the protein making those openings can also kill tumor cells on its own.
That protein, perforin, is made by T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. For decades, scientists have known that it allows protein-cutting enzymes called granzymes to enter target cells and trigger their death. But the new study, published in
, found that tumor cells could be killed even when major granzymes were missing. Losing perforin, however, caused a catastrophic failure of the immune response against tumors in the study.
“If T cells and NK cells are the soldiers of the immune system, perforin is the weapon, and granzymes are the ammunition,” said co-senior study author Weiping Zou, MD, PhD, Charles B. de Nancrede Professor of Pathology, Immunology, Biology, and Surgery at the University of Michigan (U-M). “At least, that’s what the classic understanding was.”
Perforin can kill on its own
To investigate perforin’s role, the researchers combined three approaches: genetic and biochemical experiments in cells grown in the laboratory, studies in mice, and data from people with cancer.
“We wanted to know if perforin, by itself, can do the job,” Zou said. “The answer is yes.”
The laboratory experiments traced that killing to ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Beyond making holes in a cancer cell’s membrane, perforin interfered with its iron uptake, causing iron to accumulate inside the cell, including in its mitochondria, structures that help supply energy. The excess iron rapidly oxidized lipids, the fatty molecules that help make up membranes.
Ferroptosis occurs when lipid peroxides, or oxidized fats, build up in the membranes surrounding cells and their internal structures. It differs from apoptosis, the form of cell death triggered by granzymes, and from pyroptosis, which is often caused by bacterial infection.
“Our findings show, for the first time, that perforin can independently induce ferroptosis in tumor cells,” said co-senior author Ilona Kryczek, PhD, a researcher at U-M. “This work changes our understanding of one of the longest-held mechanisms of T cell and NK cell-mediated tumor clearance.”
Zou and Kryczek worked closely with co-senior author Judy Lieberman, PhD, of Harvard Medical School, one of the international pioneers of cytotoxic lymphocyte research, the study of immune cells that kill other cells.
Iron-rich diets may fuel some tumors
In the mouse studies, animals fed an iron-rich diet had slower tumor progression, a result related to their perforin expression. That observation comes with an important caution for anyone considering what it might mean for cancer treatment.
“We need to be very cautious here,” Zou said. “That’s because some cancer types enjoy an iron-rich diet. For those tumors, and we don’t totally know which ones yet, an iron-rich diet may accelerate progression.”
Can perforin make immunotherapy more effective?
The human data offered another connection between perforin and cancer outcomes. Patients with higher perforin expression had better survival and better responses to immune checkpoint blockade, treatments that release molecular brakes on immune cells. These findings were associations in patient data.
“It is a new way of thinking about how immune cells kill tumors,” said Hannah Bell, PhD, the study’s first author, until recently a postdoctoral researcher in Zou’s lab and now an assistant professor in Molecular and Integrative Physiology at U-M.
Ferroptosis was
formally introduced
over a decade ago, so scientists still know less about it than more established forms of cell death.
“It’s a very hot area that needs a lot of research,” Zou said.
In 2019, his group was the
first to report the immune system’s role in ferroptosis in tumors
, highlighting the pathway as a potential target for immune checkpoint therapy. Previous work has also shown that immune checkpoint blockade can enhance T cell-mediated ferroptosis, making that connection a likely direction for further research.
It is still too soon to say how the new findings might translate into clinical applications.
“If we can understand what makes a tumor cell susceptible to perforin, we may be able to increase the effectiveness of immunotherapy,” Zou said.
The team plans to examine the cell death mechanism more closely, test whether multiple routes to cell death could be working together, and explore potential clinical applications.
“At the end of the day, the whole goal of different forms of cancer therapies — immunotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy — is to kill tumor cells,” Zou said. “Improving our understanding of cell death, like we do in this study, is so fundamental and so important. That’s why we’re going to continue to push on this.”

title: Massive Study of 2.8 Million People Reveals New Secrets of Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
The largest genetic study of Alzheimer’s disease to date has uncovered dozens of previously unknown genetic associations, offering new insights into the disease’s complex biology. Credit: Stock
A genetic analysis of 2.8 million people points to specific brain cells that may influence Alzheimer’s, offering researchers new leads to investigate in the search for treatments.
Alzheimer’s disease is the leading cause of dementia, which is projected to affect more than 150 million people worldwide by 2050. Genes play a substantial role in Alzheimer’s risk, but scientists still do not fully understand which genes matter or how they influence the disease. Connecting those genetic clues to what happens inside the brain could help researchers identify possible targets for treatment.
An international team has now identified 127 regions of human DNA associated with Alzheimer’s risk, including 48 that had not previously been mapped in this context. The findings offer a more detailed view of the biological processes involved, pointing to roles for both the brain’s immune cells and several specific types of nerve cells.
Led by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and published in
, the research is the largest genetic association study of Alzheimer’s to date. Researchers analyzed genetic data from approximately 2.8 million people with diverse genetic backgrounds, including 183,620 people with Alzheimer’s.
Alzheimer’s clues point beyond immune cells
“We already knew that immune processes play an important role in Alzheimer’s disease. What makes this study particularly valuable is that we can now connect new genetic risk factors to more specific biological processes, while also uncovering evidence pointing to the involvement of other brain cell types. This gives us a more detailed picture of the biology underlying Alzheimer’s and provides new directions for investigating potential treatments,” said research lead Danielle Posthuma of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
The analysis strengthened the evidence for the involvement of microglia, immune cells in the brain that help clear away harmful substances and damaged cellular material. Linking genetic risk factors to the processes these cells carry out gives researchers more specific biological connections to investigate.
For the first time, the researchers also identified several specific types of neurons, the cells that receive and transmit information, that were enriched for genetic signals associated with Alzheimer’s. In other words, the genetic evidence pointed toward these particular cell types more often than expected. The findings suggest that they may play a key role in the disease’s development, opening research directions beyond the immune system.
Shared data expands Alzheimer’s genetic map
Pooling data from 30 research groups allowed the team to detect genetic associations that might have gone unnoticed in smaller studies. The collaboration brought together academic researchers, biobanks, and industry under the International Psychiatric Genomics Consortium. Its Alzheimer’s disease working group is co-led by Posthuma and Ole Andreassen of the University of Oslo.
Among the contributors was the University of Exeter-led
study. Professor Anne Corbett of the University of Exeter, who leads PROTECT, said, “This exciting new genetic analysis has uncovered new information on how our genes influence our risk of Alzheimer’s disease. We’re delighted that the PROTECT-UK study contributed to these important new findings. PROTECT collects genetic samples from all participants through a simple at-home saliva sample. This data can then be combined with cohorts from around the world to help us to better understand dementia risk and how it can be treated.”
The genetic associations provide starting points for further investigation, rather than proof that targeting a particular gene will produce an effective treatment. Follow-up research must establish which associations reflect a causal role in Alzheimer’s and whether intervening in the processes involved would be safe and meaningfully beneficial.

title: An Ancient Virus May Hold the Secret to What Makes the Human Brain Different
content:
An ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have contributed to a surprising difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Credit: Shutterstock
Could a virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago help explain how the human brain became different?
Researchers at
Lund University
have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome silences a gene involved in early human brain development. Their study, published in
Science Advances
, found that the gene, LINC00662, remains active in human brain organoids, where it helps support the development of nerve cells and the connections between them.
The finding offers a way to explore how humans and chimpanzees developed different biological traits despite sharing much of their genetic makeup. Evolution can change how existing genes are used, as well as which genes a species carries.
“The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development,” says Johan Jakobsson, professor of molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.
How Viral DNA Silences A Gene
The genetic remnant belongs to PTERV1, an endogenous retrovirus. Its DNA became embedded in the chimpanzee genome during an ancient infection and has been inherited ever since. The researchers found copies of the viral sequence at numerous locations throughout chimpanzee DNA.
Those sequences are systematically shut down through methylation, a chemical process that helps regulate gene activity. At the LINC00662 location, the inherited viral insertion also keeps the neighboring gene silent.
Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University. Credit: Tove Smeds
To examine this difference during brain development, the team grew brain organoids from human and chimpanzee stem cells. These miniature, three-dimensional structures resemble brain tissue and reproduce some features of its early development.
“The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids,” says Patricia Gerdes, a postdoctoral researcher in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.
Removing the Virus Restores Gene Activity
The researchers then tested whether the viral sequence caused the shutdown. Using the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, they removed it from chimpanzee cells. LINC00662 became active again.
“This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees,” says Patricia Gerdes.
A separate experiment explored the gene’s role in humans. When the team used CRISPR to silence LINC00662 in human brain organoids, genes involved in nerve cell development and the formation of connections between those cells became less active.
For Jakobsson, the results show how an infection can leave a lasting genetic change across a population, while helping explain how gene regulation can protect the brain or contribute to damage. The team will next investigate whether other viral remnants influenced brain evolution and whether such sequences are linked to brain diseases.

title: James Webb Discovers a Nearly Pristine Galaxy From the Dawn of the Universe
content:
JWST image of the massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416 (background) and a three-color composite of the extremely faint galaxy LAP1-B (inset). Invisible in the NIRCam image, LAP1-B was detected through sensitive NIRSpec observations of hydrogen and oxygen emissions. The inset shows gas velocity and spatial distribution (blue: hydrogen Lyα; green: oxygen [OIII]; red: hydrogen Hα), with Lyα shifted by 200 km/s for clarity. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA & K. Nakajima et al., Nature.
Some of the faintest galaxies near the Milky Way may be survivors from the earliest chapters of cosmic history. Their ancient stars preserve clues about how galaxies formed, but astronomers have struggled to connect these nearby relics to the small, primitive galaxies that existed billions of years ago.
An international research team led by Associate Professor Kimihiko Nakajima of Kanazawa University has now identified a possible link. A tiny galaxy called LAP1-B, seen as it existed 13 billion years ago, contains remarkably little oxygen and has several characteristics that resemble some of the oldest galaxies still found near the Milky Way.
The chemical evidence reaches back to a time when the universe was only beginning to acquire the elements familiar to us today. Shortly after the Big Bang, the universe consisted primarily of hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements, including the carbon and oxygen essential for life, were produced later inside the first generations of stars and eventually released into space.
A galaxy with almost no oxygen
Astronomers have long wanted to study galaxies from this early period to understand how those elements first accumulated. The challenge is that such galaxies are extraordinarily small and faint, making their chemical composition difficult to measure even with powerful telescopes.
LAP1-B became accessible thanks to gravitational lensing, a phenomenon in which the gravity of a massive object bends and magnifies light from something farther away. In this case, a massive galaxy cluster amplified the distant galaxy’s light approximately 100 times, allowing researchers to examine an object that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study.
Building on earlier detections, the team observed LAP1-B for more than 30 hours using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They used spectroscopy, a technique that analyzes light to identify the chemical elements present in a distant object.
The observations revealed an oxygen abundance just 1/240th that of the Sun, a record low that places LAP1-B among the most chemically primitive galaxies ever characterized.
“I was instantly thrilled by the extreme lack of oxygen revealed in the data,” says Associate Professor Nakajima, the research team leader. “Finding a galaxy in such a primitive state is astonishing. It’s a chemical signature that clearly indicates a primordial galaxy caught in the moments shortly after its formation.”
This diagram compares galaxy stellar mass and oxygen abundance. LAP1-B (red circle) has an exceptionally low stellar mass and just 1/240th the Sun’s oxygen abundance, a record low for a star-forming galaxy, revealing its chemically primitive state. Brown symbols represent distant galaxies, while the dashed line shows the trend in nearby galaxies. Credit: Nakajima K. et al., Nature (2026), Springer Nature.
The researchers also found an unusually high ratio of carbon to oxygen. That distinction matters because the relative amounts of different elements can reveal how a galaxy acquired its chemical ingredients. In LAP1-B, the elevated carbon-to-oxygen ratio closely matches theoretical predictions for material scattered into space by the explosions of the universe’s first-generation stars.
Together, these measurements suggest that LAP1-B was observed during an exceptionally early stage of chemical enrichment, when the products of the first stars were beginning to accumulate in its gas.
“Usually, we act like ‘cosmic archaeologists,’ trying to guess the past by looking at old stars in our own neighborhood. But now, we can analyze the gas directly from the original scene 13 billion years ago,” emphasizes Nakajima. “We are witnessing the moment when a galaxy first inherited the chemical building blocks created by the universe’s earliest stars.”
A possible ancestor of cosmic fossils
The galaxy’s extremely small size provides another clue about its origins. The team estimates that LAP1-B contains less than 3,300 times the Sun’s mass in stars and is associated with a halo dominated by dark matter, the invisible material thought to account for much of the mass in galaxies.
Those characteristics resemble a class of nearby objects called ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs). These exceptionally dim galaxies contain ancient stars and relatively few heavy elements, leading astronomers to suspect that they preserve conditions from the universe’s earliest periods of galaxy formation.
This diagram compares oxygen abundance and carbon-to-oxygen ratios. LAP1-B (red circle) closely matches predictions for material produced by the universe’s first stars (purple region) and the chemical composition of present-day ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (blue outline). Its unusual chemistry suggests enrichment by the earliest stars 13 billion years ago. Grey symbols represent ancient Milky Way stars and distant gas clouds, while orange indicates later stellar enrichment. Credit: Nakajima K. et al., Nature (2026), Springer Nature.
“UFDs are not only the faintest galaxies; they are composed of ancient stars over 12 billion years old and are often described as ‘fossils of the universe,'” explains Professor Masami Ouchi (NAOJ/University of Tokyo), a member of the research team. “Astronomers suspected they might be the remains of the universe’s earliest galaxies because they lack heavy elements, but astronomers never had a direct link—until we found LAP1-B.”
LAP1-B offers a rare opportunity to examine what a possible predecessor of these nearby galaxies actually looked like billions of years ago. Its low oxygen abundance, unusual carbon-to-oxygen ratio, and dark matter-dominated structure are consistent with the idea that today’s ultra-faint dwarf galaxies descended from small systems that formed very early in cosmic history.
“It is a profound surprise to find that LAP1-B looks exactly like the ‘ancestor’ we had only imagined in theories. This helps us solve the mystery of why these cosmic fossils have survived in their current form to the present day.”
The search for even earlier galaxies
Although the findings provide a compelling connection between early galaxies and nearby cosmic fossils, LAP1-B represents one example. Examining more objects with similarly primitive chemical compositions could help researchers determine how common these early systems were and how they developed into the galaxies observed today.
The team plans to continue using JWST to search for even more chemically primitive galaxies, with the ultimate goal of identifying some of the first galaxies ever formed. Such observations could help establish when the earliest stars began producing heavier elements and how those materials spread through the young universe.
Associate Professor Nakajima concludes, “We hope this discovery marks a historic step in understanding how the elements that make up our own bodies were first born and accumulated across the Universe.”
Reference: “An ultra-faint, chemically primitive galaxy forming in the reionization era” by Kimihiko Nakajima, Masami Ouchi, Yuichi Harikane, Eros Vanzella, Yoshiaki Ono, Yuki Isobe, Moka Nishigaki, Takuji Tsujimoto, Fumitaka Nakamura, Yi Xu, Hiroya Umeda and Yechi Zhang, 13 May 2026,

title: Caelux and Heliene start US production of perovskite-tandem modules rated above 27%
content:
Caelux and Heliene start US production of perovskite-tandem modules rated above 27%
and solar module manufacturer
have brought their Hybrid-Tandem module into commercial-scale production for the US market, with module conversion efficiency of up to 27%+. The two companies have signed a multi-year, multi-gigawatt agreement to commercialize the module, an initial industrial-scale commercial order is underway, and deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2027.
Image credit: Heliene
The module combines Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass, which builds a perovskite layer into the module’s top glass, with Heliene’s N-type silicon cells. Both layers generate power, which the companies say yields up to 20% more energy than a conventional N-type silicon module and allows the same output from less roof or land area. They are targeting module efficiency above 29% by 2028.
Heliene is producing the modules at its plant in Mountain Iron, Minnesota. The company operates two US module factories with a combined annual output of 1.3 GW and employs more than 500 people across those sites and its corporate office in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. Heliene CEO and founder Martin Pochtaruk said a key advantage of the Caelux technology is that the glass drops into existing manufacturing lines without requiring a separate production setup. Caelux CEO Scott Graybeal said the partnership brings together two domestic supply chains and is intended to set a new benchmark for American-made solar.
The announcement marks the first of Caelux’s commercial agreements to reach production. The company
began commercial shipments of its Active Glass product
earlier this year and has since signed a run of gigawatt-scale supply deals, including
5 GW with Rayzon Solar in July
4 GW with GREW Solar in September
3 GW with INA Solar in October
, alongside an earlier partnership with
The Mountain Iron facility, which has a nameplate capacity of 800 MW per year, cut 93 jobs in August in what Heliene described as a permanent adjustment to current customer demand, leaving 182 employees at the site.

title: HKUST-led team builds chiral multiple quantum wells from 2D to 3D perovskite phases
content:
HKUST-led team builds chiral multiple quantum wells from 2D to 3D perovskite phases
Researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Chongqing Normal University and Sivananthan Laboratories have built oriented chiral perovskite multiple quantum wells with a two-step seed-assisted crystallization method. The wells have varying widths and span the 2D, quasi-2D and 3D perovskite phases, with continuous intrinsic chirality across all of them.
The graded energy landscape between the coupled wells lets spin transfer from well to well with less loss, which the team calls a “spin cascade”. The researchers say this extends the spin coherence lifetime to about 5 ns at room temperature, a regime where long-lived spin polarization has typically required ultralow temperatures.
The material showed circularly polarized luminescence with a dissymmetry factor (|glum|) of 1.4 × 10⁻² and spin-dependent charge transport with a polarization degree of over 80%. The team demonstrated circularly polarized light photodetectors and X-ray-triggered dissymmetric photopolymerization as proof-of-concept applications. The work was led by Prof. Haipeng Lu of HKUST, who says it provides a platform for chiroptical and spintronic devices.

title: 聚焦ICCAD 2026：威宏科技将携核心方案重磅亮相！-索比光伏网
content:
核心摘要：威宏科技将亮相 ICCAD 2026，展示在 ASIC／SoC 设计、先进封装、Chiplet 集成及系统级解决方案等领域的技术实力、
威宏科技将亮相 ICCAD 2026，展示在 ASIC／SoC 设计、先进封装、Chiplet 集成及系统级解决方案等领域的技术实力，并重点呈现 3D Vision 智能视觉 Demo Kit，以及与 Skymizer 联合展示的高性能 PCIe AI 加速平台，展现从智能感知、边缘计算到大型 AI 模型推理的创新应用。
威宏科技是一家专业的系统级半导体芯片设计服务提供商（System-Level IC Design Service Provider），提供从系统架构规划、芯片设计、验证、物理实现到量产导入的一站式 ASIC／SoC 设计服务。核心技术涵盖 SoC 实现、高速接口集成、2.5D與3D先进封装、矽光子整合方案、超大型與Chiplet架構CPU設計服務、EVB／DVB 开发及系统级验证，并具备 CPU、Networking、Edge AI 与智能视觉等领域的开发及量产经验，协助客户加速创新产品的商业化。
展示亮点一：3D Vision 智能视觉解决方案
本次展出的 3D Vision Demo Kit 采用双目立体视觉（Stereo Vision）技术，可实时生成深度图（Depth Map）与三维点云（Point Cloud），实现空间感知、距离测量、目标检测及环境分析等功能。现场参观者可直观体验从双目影像采集、深度计算到三维空间重建的完整流程，并了解如何结合 Edge AI 技术，实现智能机器人、工业自动化、智慧物流、无人系统及智能安防等应用。通过软硬件协同设计与 ASIC／SoC 集成能力，威宏科技协助客户将智能视觉算法转化为具备量产潜力的芯片与系统解决方案。
展示亮点二：携手 Skymizer 展示高性能 AI 加速平台
威宏科技亦将携手 Skymizer 展示高性能 PCIe AI Accelerator 解决方案，呈现大型语言模型（LLM）推理与多卡扩展应用能力。本次展示分为录像与现场两部分。录像部分播放异构 PD 分离推理：平台由一台 GPU 服务器搭配 8 张 HTX301 LPU 卡组成，GPU 负责 Prefill，HTX301 LPU 负责 Decode，运行超大模型 Kimi K3 的文本生成。现场部分则在一台搭载 NVIDIA GPU 卡与一张 HTX301 LPU 卡的主机上，以 Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B 实机演示会议记录整理、日历图片识别等应用，并展示同一模型的异构 PD 分离推理，以及单卡 4 路并发解码（每路 40–43 tok/s）。参观者可借此了解从中型到超大模型，GPU 与 LPU 如何分工、各展所长。
威宏科技致力于成为客户值得信赖的 ASIC／SoC 设计合作伙伴，结合专业设计团队与产业技术联盟，提供从系统规划、IP 集成、FPGA 原型验证、先进封装到量产导入的完整服务，协助客户降低开发风险、缩短上市时间并提升产品竞争力。
诚挚邀请业界伙伴莅临 ICCAD 2026 威宏科技展位(D085 / D086)，现场体验 3D Vision 与 AI 加速创新应用，共同探索 ASIC／SoC 设计及系统级技术合作的新机会！

title: 新能源产品出海与国际采购大会在沪开幕 GNEEC全球新能源供应链平台及欧洲站同步启动-索比光伏网
content:
2026年11月10日，新能源产品出海与国际采购大会在上海虹桥国际中央商务区的全球新能源赋能中心(GNEEC)开幕。政府领导、行业领军人士、企业嘉宾及媒体代表，共同出席本次开幕活动。坐落于GNEEC的全球新能源供应链平台及欧洲站同步启动，标志着中国新能源产业深度链接全球公共采购体系迈出关键一步。
上海虹桥国际中央商务区管委会副主任杨旭波、上海市青浦区人民政府副区长陈锡琦，全球绿色能源理事会(GGEIC)主席、亚洲光伏产业协会(APVIA)主席、协鑫(集团)控股有限公司董事长朱共山，全球储能与电池理事会(GESBC)主席、亚太新能源行业协会(NIEAAP)主席、天能控股集团董事长张天任，以及欧洲储能行业协会代表Johnny Browaeys出席活动并致辞。
(上海虹桥国际中央商务区管委会副主任杨旭波)
杨旭波在致辞中指出，全球能源转型加速推进，中国新能源产业正从单一产品出口迈向“产业链出海”与“体系化赋能”并重的新阶段。虹桥国际中央商务区作为国家战略的重要承载地，致力于打造企业“走出去”的服务高地与海外企业“走进来”的首站门户。他强调，全球新能源供应链平台及欧洲站启动，既是全球新能源赋能中心功能升级的关键一步，更是虹桥服务新能源企业出海的务实举措：一是以平台为支点，打通国际采购“最后一公里”;二是以欧洲站为窗口，深耕高标准区域市场;三是以虹桥为底座，构建“出海一站式”服务闭环。
(上海市青浦区人民政府副区长陈锡琦)
陈锡琦在致辞中指出，绿色低碳已成全球共识，中国新能源产业经过多年积淀，已形成覆盖光伏、风电、储能、新能源汽车的完整产业链，产品竞争力与出口规模均居世界前列。中国绿能走向世界，既有坚实产业根基，更有广阔市场空间，长三角与上海的集群效应尤为明显。青浦是上海唯一同时与浙江、江苏接壤的行政区，既是进博会永久举办地、虹桥国际开放枢纽核心承载区，更是长三角生态绿色一体化发展示范区的主阵地。期待与各方一道扬帆远航，共同驶向全球绿色发展的广阔蓝海。
(全球绿色能源理事会(GGEIC)主席、亚洲光伏产业协会(APVIA)主席、协鑫(集团)控股有限公司董事长朱共山)
朱共山在致辞中指出，全球新能源供应链平台是中国新能源产业面向全球的出海母港，数据、认证、碳核算、海外仓、金融等关键服务可在此一站备齐;欧洲站则是前置到全球高端市场的登陆阵地，当地政策、项目信息和行业规则可第一时间传回虹桥、送达企业。两大平台高效联动，形成境内外双中心，通过甄选会员标识、买家目录、项目采购匹配、本地服务网络等特色服务，助力我国新能源企业编队出海，全面提升中国品牌的国际关注度、认可度与信赖度。
他表示，活动现场首批纳入GNEEC全球新能源供应链平台的核心供应商已集结到位，协鑫、天能、国电南自、中建材海外、TCL中环、麦田能源、长风绿能、冠隆电力、首航新能源等中坚力量协同发力，德国莱茵TÜV提供权威认证护航，十家标杆企业覆盖材料、制造、集成、认证与出海全链条。在全球新能源赋能中心的聚合下，一支结构完整、能打胜仗的中国新能源联合舰队正式成型、即将启航。
(全球储能与电池理事会(GESBC)主席、亚太新能源行业协会(NIEAAP)主席、天能控股集团董事长张天任)
张天任在致辞中指出，全球新能源赋能中心旗下“全球新能源供应链平台及欧洲站”启航，是中国新能源融入全球、服务双循环的具体行动。当前绿色低碳正从倡议变为规则和订单，联合国采购的合格评定、碳足迹、ESG等要求已成为国际市场硬门槛，中国新能源产业需推动产品优势升级为标准、认证、方案优势，深度进入国际规则体系。
平台的核心价值在于将短期展会对接延伸为常态化合作，打通从认证到市场准入的全链条。国际采购考验体系化能力，关键在于“接口”适配与集群协同，要把分散的企业能力转化为联合交付能力，打造中国新能源供应矩阵和集群品牌。真正的全球化考验“融入”深度、赢得“信任”认可，企业要做“生态共建者”，从产品输出走向本地共生。他呼吁联合国机构与国际采购伙伴多到中国工厂和海外项目走访，深化全球合作，以产业之力推动全球能源转型。
(欧洲储能行业协会专委会委员Johnny Browaeys)
Johnny Browaeyss在致辞中指出，全球新能源赋能中心欧洲站正式启动，欧洲业务由设于荷兰的团队负责。欧洲能源转型在可再生能源、储能、充电基础设施及清洁能源供应链领域创造了可观市场，但市场增长并不会自动降低进入门槛。企业进入欧洲不仅需要优质产品，更需了解当地要求、对接合适伙伴并建立信任。欧洲站旨在帮助双方务实对接：既助力欧洲开发商和买家更便捷地获取适配技术与供应商，也助力中国及其他国际企业获得更清晰的欧洲市场路径与本地合作渠道。平台以信任为核心，强调信息可核查、责任清晰、持续跟进，推动临时会面转化为全年常态化合作。诚邀制造商、开发商、投资者及服务伙伴共同参与平台建设。
(GNEEC全球新能源供应链平台及欧洲站启动剪彩现场)
在大会核心环节，天能控股集团董事长张天任先生，华电集团国电南自股份有限公司副总裁杨乘胜先生，合肥协鑫集成新能源科技有限公司总经理孙国亮先生，德国莱茵TÜV大中华区太阳能与商业产品服务高级副总裁兼全球电力电子产品服务高级副总裁李卫春先生，南京冠隆电力科技有限公司董事长张海波，麦田能源股份有限公司董事长、总经理朱京成先生，TCL中环新能源科技股份有限公司海外业务副总裁韩启明先生，长风绿能(苏州)科技有限公司副总经理张书昊先生，深圳市首航新能源有限公司市场部总监汪力先生，欧洲储能行业协会专委会委员Johnny Browaeys先生，以及全球新能源赋能中心COO童真女士等共同为GNEEC全球新能源供应链平台及欧洲站启动剪彩。这标志着GNEEC在搭建全球新能源协同发展网络上迈出了实质性一步，也意味着其在全球服务体系构建与中欧市场协同对接方面取得了关键进展。
后续GNEEC将持续围绕新能源企业出海全链条需求，整合行业展会、跨境对接、合规咨询、本地化服务等核心资源，重点为光伏、储能等领域国内企业提供欧洲市场准入辅导、精准采购商匹配、海外项目对接等务实服务;同时面向欧洲及全球采购商开放平台资源，建立优质供应商分级筛选体系，降低采购端选型与合作风险，打造连接中国新能源产业供给端与全球市场需求端的专业化枢纽平台。
(GNEEC欧洲站介绍、分享与对话现场)
随后举行了GNEEC全球新能源供应链平台欧洲站的介绍、分享与对话活动。该活动由上海新能源行业协会专家竺新原主持，欧洲储能行业协会专委会委员Johnny Browaeys详细介绍了GNEEC欧洲站的方案与服务，随后南京国电南自自动化有限公司党委委员、副总经理余亮，天能控股集团副总裁徐海，TCL中环新能源科技股份有限公司海外业务副总裁韩启明，长风绿能(苏州)科技有限公司副总经理张书昊，南京冠隆电力科技有限公司运营副总裁章梦然参与对话。
Johnny Browaeys在介绍欧洲站时表示，欧洲站将面向现有GNEEC会员及已在欧企业延伸网络、对接项目渠道，欢迎有明确欧洲目标且能持续跟进的企业加入，无需万事俱备，平台将协助补齐短板，企业可说明自身优势、目标市场及首要难题，会后可向GNEEC咨询会员方案及申请流程。
最后，嘉宾们围绕中国新能源企业开拓欧洲市场过程中面临的合规准制、本地供应链搭建、项目对接、市场准备度建设、品牌信任构建等核心问题展开深度对话。
大会首日同步开放新能源展区，为参会企业、国际采购方与资本服务机构搭建展示交流平台，展示活动将持续至2027年6月4日。

title: 97.3亿千瓦时！意向交易电量创历史新高——河北省绿电交易洽谈会在张家口召开-索比光伏网

电力交易知识宣讲。

河北南网区域绿电集中签约仪式。
据介绍，本次会议打造集政策解读、市场服务、供需洽谈于一体的对接平台，核心是促进绿色电力资源与重点产业用能需求精准匹配、高效对接。河北省将统筹推进全省绿电市场建设，依托张家口等资源富集区域的实践基础，持续畅通绿电供需对接渠道，推动绿电资源加快转化为产业发展优势。
参会企业代表深入交流。

title: Hornsea 3 turbine components reach ABLE Seaton Port
content:
Ørsted has announced that components for the 2.9 GW Hornsea
3 offshore wind farm
are currently at ABLE Seaton Port in north east England, where they will
be loaded out for offshore installation operations.
The wind turbine components include blades, nacelles and tower sections.
According to the company, the turbine towers will be delivered in four
sections and assembled on site.
Once installed, each turbine tower will stand 130 metres tall, while the
turbine blades will measure 115 metres in length.
The project is expected to be completed by the end of 2027 and generate
enough renewable electricity to power 3.3 million UK homes, supporting
the UK's net zero goals.
Ørsted said that, through its agreement with ABLE Seaton Port and its contractors,
around 70 new workers have been employed to support the project. The company
have said Hornsea 3 is expected to support up to 5,000 jobs during the
construction phase.

European Commission approves support scheme for First Princess Elisabeth Zone project
The European Commission has officially approved the state aid mechanism
for the first plot in Belgium's Princess Elisabeth Zone (PEZ 1).
The approval removes the final barrier to relaunching the tender process.
The previous tender was paused in 2025 due to a range of legal, financial
and technical concerns.
Following the suspension, the federal government revised the tender framework
in an effort to provide greater certainty for developers and investors
while maintaining competition. The updated structure includes a two-sided
Contract for Difference (CfD) support mechanism.
The updated framework also extends the project's construction period from
four years to five years. Belgian Energy Minister Mathieu Bihet said the
Commission's decision was the final element needed to relaunch the tender.
“This is an important step which demonstrates the quality of the work
delivered by the teams and the robustness of the framework we have built,”
said the Federal Minister of Energy, Mathieu Bihet.
The Princess Elisabeth Zone forms part of Belgium's offshore wind expansion
plans and is intended to support the country's energy security and economic
competitiveness.
