title: Berwick Bank B offshore wind project expected to support 2,600 UK jobs
content:
Berwick Bank B offshore wind project expected to support 2,600 UK jobs TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Berwick Bank B offshore wind project expected to support 2,600 UK jobs
SSE has announced that the 1.4 GW Berwick
offshore wind project is expected to create more than 2,600 jobs in the
UK. The large-scale offshore wind farm will not only support renewable
energy ambitions but also boost industrial growth while supporting skilled
regional jobs.
The announcement follows news that Siemens Energy has been selected as
the preferred supplier of wind turbines and substations for the project.
However, the agreement remains subject to a final investment decision.
Darren Davidson, Managing Director of Siemens Energy UK & Ireland,
said: “While the project remains subject to final approvals and contract
award, we are proud to be working alongside SSE as it progresses this nationally
significant development.”
According to the announcement, the jobs will span manufacturing, engineering,
project delivery and service roles, totalling 2,677 skilled positions.
Siemens Energy will also utilise its established operations across the
UK, which currently support 2,222 jobs, including roles in wind and grid
technologies and at its wind turbine blade factory in Hull.
SSE and Siemens Energy will support an additional 455 engineering, project
delivery and service jobs, bringing the total to more than 3,000.
UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: “This is another vote of confidence
in British homegrown clean energy."
“Investment in offshore wind and clean power is creating quality jobs
and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower
bills and reach net zero.”
Scottish Energy Minister Stephen Gethins said: “I warmly welcome the news
that SSE’s Berwick Bank project will now support almost 1,000 jobs in
Scotland, including the 130 new roles based in Glasgow and Montrose that
have been announced today.”

title: Cadeler sign exclusivity agreement for UK offshore wind farm
content:
Cadeler has announced that it has signed an exclusivity agreement for turbine
and foundation installation work at a large-scale UK offshore wind farm.
The client has yet to be disclosed, however, the announcement states that
the agreement demonstrates the importance of securing installation capacity
early, especially for larger-scale developments.
The company has confirmed that it will use A-Class and O-Class vessels
to carry out foundation installation work, while the turbine installation
campaign will be undertaken using one of its P-Class vessels.
Mikkel Gleerup, CEO of Cadeler, commented: “We are very pleased to announce
this significant project, which is another important endorsement of the
capabilities of our fleet, the experience of our people and Cadeler’s
ability to deliver increasingly large and complex offshore wind projects.”
Cadeler currently operates one of the largest offshore wind installation
fleets globally, consisting of eleven installation vessels, with an additional
three newbuilds scheduled for delivery. This enables the company to support
larger-scale and more complex projects.
According to the announcement, its work on the project is expected to begin
around 2030.

title: RWE and KKR finalise financing for 2.8GW Vanguard offshore wind projects
content:
RWE and KKR have announced that they will jointly deliver the Vanguard
and Vanguard
offshore wind projects, located 50 and 80 kilometres off the Norfolk coast.
The Vanguard offshore wind farms are expected to have a combined capacity
of 2.8 GW, enough to power 3 million U.K. homes. The projects have the
potential to support the local economy by creating long-term jobs and reinforcing
East Anglia's position as an offshore wind hub.
The announcement follows the companies' joint venture transaction announced
in January 2026, under which KKR acquired a 50% equity stake in each project.
The agreement combines RWE's offshore wind development and operational
expertise with KKR's capital resources and global infrastructure investment
experience.
According to the announcement, the wind farms require around £12 billion
to support construction and associated infrastructure. Funding has been
backed by equity commitments from RWE and KKR, while additional financing
has been secured from a consortium of international lenders.
Both projects have now reached financial close, securing £11.1 billion
in non-recourse project financing facilities and a further £1.7 billion
in ancillary facilities from a group of 35 international banks. The financing
marks a milestone as the largest project financing package ever secured
for U.K. offshore wind.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "This major investment in U.K.
renewables is a vote of confidence in building in Britain. And it is great
news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British
control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world."
TGS | 4C Senior Analyst Jordan May commented: "RWE and KKR's financial
close is a great step for the UK, marking the first Allocation Round 7
project to make FID, and a large amount of capacity getting ready to come
online before 2030."
"The UK has 10.5 GW under construction some of which is expected to
complete construction soon. Adding on another 2.76 GW will allow UK waters
to stay busy, keeping the industry well stocked with active UK projects.
It also goes to show industry resilience to global geopolitical events
which challenge the global investment environment."

title: Anthropic, Others Warn of AI Acceleration
content: In recent weeks, my colleagues and I have been trying our hand at being venture capitalists: today, the end result of that process is our annual list of the 50 most promising startups of this year , published today. We’ve had a pretty good track record in past years: AI startups we’ve previously highlighted include OpenRouter , when the model-routing startup was valued at $500 million; Cursor , when the coding agent was valued at $400 million; and Perplexity , when the AI-powered search engine was valued at $150 million. OpenRouter was recently acquired by Stripe for more than $7 billion, Cursor in August was acquired by SpaceX for $60 billion, and Perplexity was most recently raising at a more than $30 billion valuation. Each year, however, it gets more difficult to pick promising AI startups that fall within our requirements of having raised less than $100 million and being valued less than $1 billion. These days, it feels like the moment any young AI company has a hint of revenue traction, investors are all over them. Still, we’ve managed to uncover a number of under-the-radar gems in this year’s list. In fact, we had trouble whittling down the entrants for our AI infrastructure and security categories, which included everything from companies that help developers train their models using multiple cloud providers to those that use AI to protect employees’ devices. Such companies have become even more important as the rate of AI-powered cyberattacks have increased .— Stephanie Palazzolo Now, onto today’s column… AI researchers that focus on ensuring AI doesn’t harm humans have reason to be a little rattled. Two recent reports suggest AI is advancing even more quickly than previously thought, and that’s increased these safety researchers’ worries that AI will escape human control to wreak havoc. The first report , from AI research nonprofit METR , found Anthropic’s internal AI use is helping it improve the capabilities of its models at around twice its previous speed. Anthropic gave METR access to internal information for the report, published last Thursday. The second report was from the AI Futures Project , a nonprofit whose “AI 2027” forecast, published a year and a half ago, gained attention among safety researchers for predicting superhuman AI would likely arrive by the end of next year. In its new report, out Tuesday, AI Futures Project predicted the advent of superhuman AI researchers—models so good at doing AI research that Anthropic might prefer to fire all their human researchers—by late 2027, compared to 2029 or later in their original forecast. Driving these forecasts, researchers increasingly believe that recursive self-improvement, a continuous loop where one generation of AI models helps build the next generation, may be becoming a reality at AI companies far faster than previously expected. “We're at the beginning of the takeoff period,” Daniel Kokotajlo , the ex- OpenAI researcher who heads the AI Futures Project, told The Information. “All those things that people have been warning about for years and for decades: superintelligence, recursive self-improvement, catastrophic loss of control, it seems like those things are a real possibility in 2027.” Along with these forecasts, Anthropic also updated its IPO filing on Tuesday morning to say it now expected its models to be able to double its non-AI-assisted rate of capabilities progress. Because it had met that threshold, Anthropic’s safety commitments say it should now undertake stronger safety and monitoring measures such as systematically testing that Claude’s behavior and propensities are aligned with human values. Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic employee whose public resignation in September over Anthropic’s efforts towards superintelligent AI made him a minor celebrity, told me he was “glad Anthropic put out some information about this.” “But I don’t think they shared nearly enough,” he said in a statement. “Given the stakes, I think they have a responsibility to provide experts with enough information to assess how fast things are going.” The new reports don’t beat around the bush. In its report, METR wrote that AI R&D acceleration could lead to “extreme and risky capabilities.” “If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict,” METR researcher Ajeya Cotra wrote of last week’s research acceleration finding. These warnings may sound alarmist to a lot of readers. But what spooks some researchers is that AI 2027 has an uncannily good track record with its predictions. The original forecast was initially dismissed as “a work of fiction” by critics including New York University neuroscience professor Gary Marcus . But the report correctly predicted the rise of AI agents and assistants and models speeding up AI research. Some of AI 2027’s predictions were misses. It predicted mass protests against AI, a single leading AI lab in the U.S., and a centralized, government-controlled lab in China, which haven’t come to pass yet. Critics such as Princeton professor Arvind Narayan have argued that even fast progress in AI capabilities takes time to impact society. Google DeepMind research scientist Sebastian Krier over the weekend criticized METR’s report as relying on flawed measures, and argued that one factor that might slow down Anthropic’s progress is the fact that developing and running these uber-advanced models has gotten so expensive. But for some AI researchers I spoke to this week, such criticisms haven’t diminished their sense that AI is moving incredibly fast—faster than most people thought—and so are the risks. Their expected probabilities of doom, or P(doom) , have just shot up. Here’s what else is going on… Earnings Report CoreWeave reported third quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, more than double the year earlier number of $1.365 billion, but its losses also ballooned. SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion spent on non-refundable advance payments to secure data center equipment, reflecting a review of its data center plans, the company said in reporting its September quarter results. The writedown includes $0.9 billion written off related “to contract modifications and settlements.” Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Anthropic in the past month inked new commitments with Microsoft and Google to spend roughly $10 billion more to rent cloud servers between now and 2033 than it previously disclosed. Anthropic also launched new workplace software applications for spreadsheets, presentations, and note-taking on Tuesday, sending Microsoft shares tanking. Mercor , which organizes human experts to train and evaluate frontier AI models and enterprise agents, raised $750 million in Series D funding at a $20 billion valuation with participation from Benchmark , Felicis , and Fundomo. Fractile , a chip developer, raised $720 million in Series C funding at a $7 billion post-money valuation led by Thrive Capital , Founders Fund , Lightspeed and Redpoint . Oura, which makes smart rings, agreed to acquire Counsel Health , the AI-powered primary-care platform it has partnered with since May, for $625 million in cash, with the deal expected to close near the end of 2026. Path Robotics , which builds physical AI for industrial welding and manufacturing, raised $300 million in Series E financing at a $2.45 billion post-money valuation, led by Georgian. Rox , an AI sales startup, raised $100 million in Series B funding at a $1.3 billion valuation led by General Catalyst and March Capital . Daylight , which combines AI agents with human security experts to detect and respond to cyber threats, raised $80 million in a Series B funding round led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Charta Health , an AI medical chart review platform built for billing accuracy, raised $55 million in a Series B funding round led by Insight Partners. Bay , a Tel Aviv-based startup that vets AI agents’ actions before they execute and sets enterprise guardrails, emerged from stealth with $50 million in total funding: a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures and a previously undisclosed $13 million seed round co-led by YL Ventures and Striker. Mosaic Intelligence Labs , which is building AI-native, sensing-enabled surgical robots that let physicians navigate the body's blood vessels, emerged from stealth with $47 million in seed funding, backed by investors including 8VC , Fundomo , and Lingotto Innovation. Garage , an AI-powered marketplace for used fire trucks and other essential municipal equipment, raised $41 million in a Series B funding round led by Invus Opportunities. Graphon Labs , an applied AI lab building a persistent-memory infrastructure layer for AI agents, raised $35 million in a Series A funding round led by RRE Ventures. Dreeze , which combines AI agents with cloud-native engineers to restore entire cloud applications (not just their data) after an outage or cyberattack, emerged from stealth with $33 million in seed funding led by Norwest and Bessemer Venture Partners. Nidus , which builds embodied-intelligence AI that lets industrial robots perform precision assembly tasks inside America's defense factories, raised $30 million, backed by Kleiner Perkins and Costanoa. Tendrils , a Cambridge, U.K.-based developer of chips, raised $30 million in funding led by Benchmark . PsiThera , which combines protein physics and physical artificial intelligence to design oral small-molecule drugs for immune and inflammatory diseases, closed $25 million in financing led by Samsara BioCapital and Lightstone Ventures. Sumary , which builds an AI operating system that automates accounting-firm workflows like month-end close and VAT returns, raised a $25 million seed round led by Singular. SPARETECH , a Munich-based provider of enterprise AI for industrial spare-parts management, raised $20 million in a Series B funding round co-led by Blume Equity and Insight Partners. WhiteMatter , formerly known as QuilrAI, which monitors and controls AI agents running inside an enterprise, raised $20 million in a Series A funding round led by Blumberg Capital. PORT , a London-based urban logistics startup building an AI-powered autonomous delivery system, raised €14.5 million (about $15.8 million) in a funding round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Balnord. Alterra Labs , a New York startup building simulated medical environments to stress-test and train AI models on clinical tasks before deployment, raised a $12.5 million seed round led by Oak HC/FT and Flare Capital Partners . PromptPath , an AI-enabled conversation assist platform that coaches automotive-dealership sales and service reps in real time, raised $12 million in a Series A funding round led by FM Capital and Armory Square Ventures. The Nvidia board on Tuesday announced that it had hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct its independent investigation into the conduct of CEO Jensen Huang . OpenAI has acquired the AI travel planning platform Odessia , Odessia’s founder Francis Davidson announced on Tuesday. Davidson will be joining OpenAI to focus on “the future of travel,” he said in an X post. OpenAI also rolled out a “Business Hub,” a new beta feature that allows companies to claim their business in ChatGPT , provide business details and product information, and understand how people engage with it. Rain , a stablecoin card and payment infrastructure startup, said it is launching vaults for AI agents, which are spending accounts with budget limits for agents. Rain’s vault product will compete with Stripe , a major provider of payment infrastructure for agents. title: Introducing The Information’s 50 Most Promising Startups of 2026
content: As artificial intelligence changes how companies get hacked, investors are paying up for startups that promise to keep defenders ahead. That dynamic shaped this year’s The Information 50 , our annual list of the most promising startups. For the first time, our list includes a category devoted solely to security, and it holds some of the list’s biggest bets. Two of the four most highly valued companies in this seventh edition of the list are security startups valued at more than $1 billion apiece, and six of the security firms are run by Israelis, which have a long history of breakout hits in this field. At a time when many people use AI to research new companies, our reporters didn’t use AI to find candidates. They just had good ol’ fashioned conversations with dozens of founders and investors—including many that pointed us to startups they missed out on—and collected hard data on revenue and growth rates at the companies. You can view the list here , and join our conference call for The Information subscribers at 12pm PT / 3pm ET to discuss the list with several of the founders whose companies are on it. To qualify for the list, startups must have raised $100 million or less in equity funding while being valued at less than $1 billion, or be less than two years old and valued at $1.5 billion or less. The cap in prior lists was $1 billion, but valuation inflation prompted us to relax it. Security is one of seven categories this year, alongside enterprise apps, AI infrastructure (mainly software), deep tech (bio, energy, defense), robotics, crypto and fintech, and Asia. The seven startups in our security category are products of the AI era. All were founded in 2024 or later, and most use AI agents to do work that has long fallen to human security staff, such as triaging alerts, hunting threats and probing for weaknesses. The pressure on defenders is coming from several directions. AI-driven attacks are generating more security alerts, and companies are producing more code thanks in part to AI, which has increased potential weak spots. Hackers also keep getting in through the devices employees use at work, as in the recent $6 billion crypto heist of Binance, which began with hackers tricking an employee into downloading malware. Startups are positioning themselves as cheaper alternatives to cybersecurity-focused models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, which can scan customers’ code for vulnerabilities. Those models are expensive and often turn up dozens or hundreds of potential holes, leaving companies unsure what to patch first. Tenzai’s AI, for instance, tries to hack customers the way sophisticated attackers would, aiming to find the vulnerabilities that pose the biggest immediate risk, and it is cheaper to run than Mythos or Astra. Another security startup focuses on protecting more than business’ code: securing networks, cloud infrastructure and employee devices, too. Others on the list want to replace tools security teams already use, including so-called endpoint software that protects employee devices; or do the grunt work of a corporate security operations center, deciding whether alerts are malicious, responding to threats and hunting for new ones. Two of the security startups on the list that got started this year don’t want their data in the public cloud. One of them, Cylake , founded this year by Palo Alto Networks co-founder Nir Zuk, sells hardware and software to companies and governments that run computing in their own data centers or private clouds. Zuk says the majority of cyberattacks will continue to be related to tricking employees (including phishing), hiring people who become insider threats or inserting malicious code in other software and hardware (so-called supply chain attacks), rather than to AI that exploits application vulnerabilities. As Rene Bonvanie, Cylake’s chief marketing officer, put it, “Attackers will successfully get in; the focus in cyber has to shift on deploying techniques to catch them as fast as possible based on their behavior.” The Rest AI agents run through much of the rest of the list . In the enterprise apps category, one startup’s product fields calls and books appointments for HVAC and plumbing businesses, and another startup’s AI agents scour invoices and supplier contracts, then try to negotiate better terms. These startups are battling for customers against a slew of other startups as well as SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, which are pushing their own workplace agents. Some of the list’s most capital-efficient companies are involved with software “infrastructure” for AI. One of them makes models run faster and more cheaply on Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices chips, generating more than $40 million in annualized revenue with 16 employees. Another startup in that category provides performance and cost benchmarks for AI models, is on pace to generate more than $100 million annually yet has a valuation of less than $100 million. It also hasn’t raised much capital. Startups in the deep tech category are working on compact gas turbines, truck-borne batteries and aluminum-fueled backup generators, among other things. The category also includes AI drug discovery startups. Four of the seven robotics startups collect, sell, manage or evaluate the physical-world data robot developers need. Another firm that generates data for humanoid developers, Noitom Robotics (“motion” spelled backwards), which is listed in the Asia category, says it counts all the major American frontier AI developers as customers. Other highlights from the list: We broke our unwritten rule of not naming the same company in multiple The Information 50 lists. In this year’s list, AI agent startup Town was included despite being named to last year’s list because it has pivoted its business model since then and is widely viewed as an attractive acquisition target. Most companies on the list generate revenue, but some are just getting started. Eight generate no revenue, up from six last year. Two others didn’t disclose revenue, and two describe theirs as nominal. The startups on our list, mirroring other AI firms, are hitting sales milestones earlier than ever. Twenty-three companies generate more than $10 million in annualized revenue, up from 20 last year and 13 in 2024. Four generate more than $70 million, the same as last year. Twenty-four companies were founded in 2025 or 2026, including seven founded this year. The oldest, a longevity drug developer, was founded nearly a decade ago but has gained renewed traction this year. The vast majority of companies are small. Just nine have more than 100 employees, the same as in each of the past two years. At least five have fewer than 20. Many founders, including Zuk, previously started or worked at successful technology firms. Greylock showed up most often among investors that led funding rounds in companies on our list. The 60-year-old firm backed five companies on the list, including three of the seven security startups. Sequoia Capital and Battery Ventures each led rounds in five; Andreessen Horowitz , Benchmark , and Y Combinator each led or co-led rounds in four startups on our list, and CRV and Lux Capital led or co-led three. Outside Asia, corporate investors were scarce again. Nvidia , Qualcomm and Samsung all backed robot-data startups on our list, and the OpenAI Startup Fund backed one of the AI agents on our list. That’s a far cry from our 2024 list, when OpenAI invested in eight of the companies. In Asia, tech giants showed up as key investors once again; they included Ant Group , Meituan and Tencent . Other Chinese entries count regional and university-affiliated funds such as Henan Investment Group, Kunshan High-tech Venture Capital and Tsinghua Holdings Capital among their leading backers.

title: Amazon and Google Win Big From Anthropic IPO
content: If you’re looking for a cheaper way of getting exposure to Anthropic than buying the stock directly, consider Amazon or Google. Anthropic’s updated IPO filing on Tuesday shows just how many shares each of those two tech giants will own in Anthropic, along with how much money they’re making on their early investments in the AI firm. Neither tech giant will own voting shares in Anthropic, so antitrust cops won’t have to worry about their influence over its management. But their stakes are significant. In theory, Amazon could own around 20% of Anthropic’s outstanding shares. But because of a self-imposed ownership cap, Amazon won’t hold more than 12% of Anthropic. The rest of its holdings are convertible notes that can convert to equity over time. Regardless, Amazon’s economic return is pretty damn good. Forgetting about the ownership cap for a minute, Amazon’s entire 20%-or-so stake would be worth about $258 billion at the midpoint of Anthropic’s proposed IPO pricing range. That’s from an investment totaling around $18.6 billion. (Anthropic’s final IPO price may well end up higher than the preliminary range, a Financial Times report tonight suggests). Google hasn’t done quite as well. It will end up with a roughly 10% stake worth $132 billion, on an investment of about $33 billion. Still, that’s not bad! Both Amazon and Google have committed to put more money into Anthropic through 2030, under certain conditions, so their investments could grow. (Google’s ownership is also capped, at 14.99%, which will limit how quickly it can convert any convertible notes it gets for future investments). And these numbers represent just the equity investments. Both Amazon and Google are also destined to get a lot of cloud business from Anthropic. Anthropic’s latest filing says it has committed to spend at least $121 billion with Google Cloud through July 2033, “regardless of actual usage.” Additionally, it is committed to spend up to another $150 billion on computing capacity using Google’s TPU AI chips. Anthropic has also committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s cloud unit through 2036—again “regardless of actual usage.” Anthropic has made similar commitments with Microsoft (totaling $49 billion through 2033) and SpaceX (up to $120.5 billion through 2029). Anthropic is a competitor to big tech firms in AI and, increasingly, in software. On Tuesday, for instance, shares of Microsoft and Google fell after Anthropic launched new workplace software apps that compete with productivity applications sold by Microsoft and Google. But it’s swings and roundabouts in this industry. Anthropic owes its existence to advances from big tech firms that were looking to generate some cloud business. Those bets have worked out spectacularly for Big Tech. CoreWeave’s New Financing Tactic For neoclouds looking for ways to finance their data center expansion, getting customers to “prepay” has become a popular tactic, particularly now that interest costs have skyrocketed. CoreWeave is the latest neocloud to call out the benefits of prepayment. “This year we have collected prepayments on 70% of our deals, with customers funding up to 100% of the contract value upfront,” said CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator on Tuesday’s call. But anyone prepaying for computing capacity is likely to ask for some concessions. If interest rates are low, it can be cheaper to borrow money than to take the hit on rates that come from getting customers to prepay. Indeed, CoreWeave hasn’t always been a fan of prepayments. In February, Intrator bragged that it was “very exciting for us” that CoreWeave could reduce its dependency on prepayments thanks to the falling cost of capital. At current interest rates, Intrator said on Tuesday, prepayments are more attractive. “Looking ahead, we will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields,” he said. In Other News • OpenAI has acquired the AI travel planning platform Odessia, Odessia’s founder Francis Davidson announced on Tuesday. Davidson will be joining OpenAI to focus on “the future of travel,” he said in an X post. • SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion spent on non-refundable advance payments to secure data center equipment, reflecting a review of its data center plans, the company said in reporting its September quarter results. The writedown includes $0.9 billion written off related “to contract modifications and settlements.” More here. • The Nvidia board on Tuesday announced that it had hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct its independent investigation into the conduct of CEO Jensen Huang. • Rain, a stablecoin card and payment infrastructure startup, said it is launching vaults for AI agents, which are spending accounts with budget limits for agents. title: The Anthropic-OpenAI Valuation Gap
content: If you want proof of the widening gap in sentiment between public and private investors, take a look at the valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI. On Tuesday, Anthropic disclosed it was targeting a valuation of between $1.26 trillion and $1.4 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. The prospectus update comes on the heels of OpenAI’s most recent fundraising, which valued the company at $1.25 trillion . That means Anthropic expects public investors to value it at only 12% more than OpenAI, assuming it achieves the valuation at the high end of its range. That is in spite of the fact that Anthropic generated 70% revenue than OpenAI in the third quarter and has been growing far faster for much of this year. Still, Anthropic’s advisers may be guiding the valuation downward now to make sure there’s plenty of demand for the stock on the first day of trading. There’s a good chance Anthropic can increase the IPO price or sell even more shares if investors’ demand is strong, as some Anthropic investors are expecting. As I reported today , OpenAI told investors it had generated $10 billion in third quarter revenue, up nearly 50% from the second. Increased use of Codex and demand for image models helped growth rebound from a sluggish second quarter. Still, OpenAI trails Anthropic, whose third quarter revenue neared $17 billion in the third quarter, up 47% from the second. Of course there are important differences in how each company reports revenue generated from sales of their AI through cloud partners—but not enough to make up for the sales gap. And Anthropic looks like it’s held onto its lead in the current quarter. Anthropic’s annualized revenue pace—roughly its last 28 days time 13—hit $81 billion in October, up nearly six times the comparable figure in February . OpenAI’s annualized revenue was nearing $50 billion in September, double its February pace . (Its October pace couldn’t be learned.) Anthropic is also a more efficient business compared to OpenAI. As revenue picked up steam in the third quarter, OpenAI operating losses rose to $10.9 billion, slightly up from $10.1 billion in the second quarter, said a person familiar with the matter. Anthropic also reported an operating loss, but a far smaller one. It swung to a $567 million loss in the third quarter, mostly due to costs to secure short-term computing capacity and $2 billion to match donations made by employees. Public investors have been notably skittish about tech stocks, sending the Nasdaq Composite last month to its worst month since March 2025 on concerns about the returns on AI investments. Those jitters grew after the Democratic sweep in Congress made it likely that more AI data centers will face delays. That cautiousness doesn’t seem to have spilled over in a big way to private markets yet, as Morgan Stanley tech banker Diana Doyle reminded me last month. The real referendum on whether public and private markets are converging will happen in the next few months, after Anthropic lists its shares and while OpenAI fills out the second, $9 billion installment of its fundraise. Just on fundamentals, the fastest growing company should sport the highest revenue multiple. But private investors have been known to inject a bit more hope into their valuations than public shareholders—suggesting this gap could hold. title: Booz Allen Switches to Nvidia’s Nemotron
content: Nvidia is managing the worst hit to its reputation in its three-decade history from the revelations that its CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly working for China’s spy agencies (read our latest on that here ). But in one bright spot for the AI chip giant, there are early signs of headway in its efforts to build the world’s best open-source models . Booz Allen Hamilton—the $10 billion-market capitalization government contractor—several months ago switched from primarily using Anthropic’s models to run its software for cybersecurity and defense to using Nvidia’s Nemotron models, CTO Bill Vass told me. That move has resulted in significant cost savings, he said, though the company declined to share specifics. (Booz Allen spends tens of millions of dollars annually on AI, according to a person familiar with the company.) “What we've been doing is the opposite of tokenmaxxing,” the term for using as much AI as possible, Vass said in an August interview. When it comes to actually building, rather than running, its software, Booz Allen developers still mostly use Anthropic’s Claude Code unless its customers ask them to use other coding tools, Vass said. That’s likely because Claude Code is still lauded as the best tool for software engineering. However, Vass said he is interested in having the firm’s developers use Nemotron models for coding as their capabilities improve. Nemotron has been making inroads with contractors and government agencies in part thanks to its relationship with Palantir. The software firm and Nvidia have partnered more closely lately, as both companies have positioned themselves as suppliers of AI that can help enterprises avoid relying on frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Nvidia recently signed a big deal to use Palantir’s software internally to manage its supply chain. And Palantir in late June launched a product aimed at helping U.S. government agencies and enterprises use Nvidia open source models through its software. Some government customers have already switched from closed-source frontier AI models to Nemotron, Palantir CEO Alex Karp told me this summer. It’s not just big customers trying Nemotron. Open-source coding software platform Kilo Code says Nvidia’s Nemotron models accounted for nearly 17% of the roughly 50 trillion tokens processed through its software in October, up from 8% the previous month. Individual developers as well as those from small and large enterprises primarily use Kilo Code to access open source models for coding work. Despite that progress, Nvidia’s models are still eclipsed by frontier models. Nemotron models accounted for just about 4% of tokens processed through OpenRouter over the past month, down slightly from a peak of 7% one week in August. OpenRouter, the Stripe-owned software that lets businesses autonomously switch between different models from one place, processes a lot more tokens than KiloCode (about 700 trillion monthly) and for a broader set of tasks than coding. So far in November, Anthropic accounted for a higher share (31%) of OpenRouter customers’ spending than any other AI provider, while Nvidia accounted for less than 1% of spending. Tokens as Benefits Those OpenRouter statistics show that most companies are still spending the lion’s share of their AI budgets on Anthropic’s models. As those firms look to moderate spending, they’re diverging on whether to dictate firm token caps to their software engineers, as I laid out in this story today with Phoebe and Catherine. That’s becoming a sticking point for engineers. Maria Colacurcio, the CEO of human resources software startup Syndio, said talent acquisition leaders at Syndio’s large enterprise clients have begun receiving requests from new job candidates to get higher token budgets as part of their employment packages. The requests come after the candidates are offered the job for higher or unlimited token budgets and access to the latest OpenAI and Anthropic models. “So there's all of these sort of side addendums being created where candidates are getting basically agreements to these carve outs,” she explained. Right now, these aren’t formal benefits. “Nobody‘s writing it down. It’s not really part of policy,” she said. If AI prices stay high and enterprises further restrict spending—as companies such as Apple, Microsoft, and Disney have—tokens could potentially become a formalized, coveted employee benefit. title: OpenAI Revenue Jumps to $10 Billion in Third Quarter Amid Growing Losses
content: OpenAI has told investors that revenue jumped nearly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, rebounding from a period of slower growth as demand for its more recent models and enterprise products picked up, according to a person familiar with the matter. However, the company’s operating losses also grew during the third quarter from $10.1 billion to $10.9 billion, the person said, demonstrating how it is still struggling to make its sprawling business model profitable. There are signs of progress: Its adjusted operating margin improved from -150% to -109%. The company shared some financial metrics with investors during a call on Tuesday as it seeks to close a new fundraising round at a $1.25 trillion valuation. OpenAI’s revenue growth is higher than the 17% gain in the second quarter from the first. The third-quarter revenue figure was 2.6 times the year-ago quarter. Demand for the company’s recent model releases, including GPT 5.6 and Astra, as well as image models drove sales of its models through its application programming interface. The company’s topline also benefited from growing ad sales, which reached a $1 billion annualized pace in August. OpenAI’s loss was far larger than that of rival Anthropic, who reported an operating deficit of $567 million in the third quarter. At the same time, OpenAI’s revenue is still trailing Anthropic’s, which hit nearly $17 billion in the third quarter, up 47% from the second quarter. Anthropic’s revenue overtook OpenAI’s in the second quarter of this year as the company’s focus on building tools for enterprises, including its popular Claude Code coding tool and Claude Cowork agent, paid off. OpenAI, which started as a consumer app, scrambled to get a bigger piece of these developers’ dollars. It started to throw more resources toward its own coding tool, Codex, abandoned some projects like a video app , and pursued more contracts with large companies. OpenAI President Greg Brockman said last week that OpenAI’s enterprise business doubled during the third quarter and now makes up a majority of OpenAI’s revenue. Unlike Anthropic, OpenAI still has a large consumer business. The company said last month it has 1.2 billion weekly active users, the vast majority of which are using the platform for free. In the third quarter, the company reached nearly 100 million paying users, the person with knowledge said. It added about 200 million non-paying users and 22 million paying users, the person said. OpenAI has been trying to make money from its consumer business through advertising, which has emerged as a bright spot for the business after reaching a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate in August.

title: Why HubSpot, Snowflake and Others Are Avoiding AI Spending Caps
content: While some companies are curbing employees’ AI use to contain soaring costs, many others in the tech industry are pushing ahead with full-throttle spending. As the chart below shows, large cloud providers including Amazon Web Services and software firms such as Palantir, Snowflake and HubSpot haven’t put firm caps on engineers’ spending as employees use AI coding tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex to build apps and features. Neither have the frontier labs themselves. And venture capitalists say many of their portfolio companies are still urging employees to use as much AI as possible. Meanwhile, Salesforce in recent months has moved to implement team-level spending caps for its forward deployed engineers, who are focused on building AI agents for customers, according to a person familiar with the company. Not all those employees are aware of the caps, though: one Salesforce forward deployed engineer told The Information they believed their budget was unlimited. The different practices show how industry leaders are taking sharply divergent views on how to manage AI use more than half a year after concerns erupted about soaring spending. In April, The Information reported Uber had already blown through its full-year AI budget and that Meta Platforms employees had been competing to consume as many AI tokens—the units of information processed by AI models—as possible in a phenomenon known as tokenmaxxing. Around that time, many companies began voicing concerns about the high cost of AI tools. Meta has told staff that it plans to implement caps on engineers’ AI spending, and Uber developed its own software for coding called a harness that can swap between different AI models to cut costs. At enterprise software company Workday, the per-engineer budget starts very low, typically ranging between $100 and $300 monthly, according to an engineer at the company. (A Workday spokesperson said that budget is a “starting point,” not a firm “ceiling,” and Chief Technology Officer Gabe Monroy said in an interview that additional budgets are granted for special projects.) For startups invested by Salt Lake City-based Oquirrh Ventures, the budgets are bigger, even though the companies are all far smaller than Workday, with $15 million to $80 in annual sales. Eight tech companies backed by the venture firm have around $500 per engineer spend budgets, said Oquirrh founder Ron Heinz. Some companies are still trying to encourage engineers to use coding tools. Duncan Lennox, chief product and technology officer at HubSpot, said the software company has been pushing engineers to use its in-house coding tool that can swap between Anthropic, OpenAI and open-source models. Of the company’s more than 2,000 engineers, about 15% regularly used the coding tool for their jobs at the start of the year. By late September, that figure had surged to more than 90%. Cost is “not a significant issue,” Lennox said, because the coding tool has improved engineers’ productivity so much. That’s also true for most of the roughly 50 portfolio companies of venture capital firm S3 Ventures and the more than two dozen early stage portfolio firms of Bain Capital Ventures, none of which have firm token caps. “As an early stage, venture-backed company, your imperative is to be at the frontier of technology, both in the product you deliver but also the tools you give your employees,” said Bain Capital Ventures partner Alysaa Co. “So I think we’re seeing very little control on spending,  and I think that’s the right approach.” S3 Ventures partner Eric Engineer said part of what’s making its portfolio companies less nervous about cost is that they’re reducing their workforces or slowing hiring. Compared to the cost of hiring another engineer, he said, spending large sums on AI coding tools is “not a big deal, and they’re not feeling like they need to put a cap on it if they’re getting the value.” Tech companies such as Rippling and Uber have token budgets, but they are relatively high and engineers can request higher spending levels, which are typically granted. Similarly, software firm Autodesk gives teams a budget equal to $2,500 per engineer for each month, but team leaders decide how that budget is allocated to their teams. Of course, some companies are pulling back. Walmart recently lowered the token budgets for engineers, according to an employee. Apple also cut its engineers’ daily budgets to $200 from $300, according to Bloomberg. Microsoft recently slashed monthly budgets for engineers by a tenth, The Information reported last month. And one Disney software engineer said the company has paused employee requests to tap its tiered AI coding tool budgets, which range from $50 per month to $25,000. Other companies that don’t have caps are moving toward them. Blackstone is set to introduce caps on engineers’ spending with new settings from its main cloud platform, AWS, that can limit AI spending per employee, according to a person familiar with the company. In the coming quarters, the private equity firm will likely set its budget around $5,000 per month for power users of coding tools and AI models, while employees who use less AI users may have a lower limit of $250 per month, though they’ll be able to request higher amounts. Matt Garman, chief executive of AWS, said during Blackstone’s technology conference in San Jose last week that the hyperscaler has let employees “go crazy” experimenting with AI tools for productive purposes but advises them not to waste company money. He pointed to the example of one employee he said used company AI tools to create a TV sitcom. “ And I was like, ‘Great. Is that the best use of company money?’ Like, probably not,” he said. While Amazon doesn’t have spend limits now, it’s moderating costs by using tools that autonomously route engineers’ requests between different frontier and open-source models, which has in some cases reduced costs by 40% for engineering work, Garman said. Amazon and other AI providers also are planning or providing features to make it easier for customers to track spending. Customers of Anthropic’s Claude Enterprise can set spending limits for their company or individual employees and can view a dashboard launched this summer showing AI usage. OpenAI has similar capabilities. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the companies most central to the AI boom are letting their own employees use as many tokens as they need. An OpenAI spokesperson said its lack of a cap is because the company thinks arbitrary limits would constrain experimentation—though OpenAI does have internal dashboards that show per-employee usage and doesn’t encourage tokenmaxxing, according to the spokesperson. At Nvidia, one employee said AI budgets are as high as $50,000 monthly per engineer and up to $10,000 for non-engineers. Another employee said they know of only one person in the company to ever hit the cap, and that person was using open source AI to generate data for model training.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.
To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud.
Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be.
—Antonio Regalado
This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.
The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

How refrigeration ruined fresh food
Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus.

MARLIN: Innovative Marinekommunikation im Härtetest
Die MARLIN Challenge der Agentur für Innovation in der Cybersicherheit GmbH (Cyberagentur) und des Marinekommandos erreicht den nächsten Meilenstein. Sechs Teams entwickeln neuartige Lösungsansätze für maritime Kommunikation, die auch bei Ausfall konventioneller Systeme funktionieren sollen. Vom 7. bis 11. Dezember 2026 erproben die Cyberagentur und das Marinekommando die Technologien für störungsresistente Kommunikation auf See erstmals unter realitätsnahen Bedingungen in Eckernförde.
Sechs Teams entwickeln neue Kommunikationslösungen
Wie können Marineeinheiten miteinander kommunizieren, wenn konventionelle Funk- und Satellitenverbindungen gestört werden oder vollständig ausfallen? Dieser Herausforderung stellen sich die sechs Finalistenteams der MARLIN Challenge. Seit August 2026 arbeiten Astrolight UAB, VisionSpace Technologies GmbH, SAILWINT GmbH, Sirius Computer Germany UG, Rueb Holding UG und Lemvos GmbH an ihren technologischen Ansätzen. Mit ihren Konzepten hatten sie zuvor die Fachjury überzeugt und sich für die Erprobung der Ideen qualifiziert.
Ziel der Challenge ist es, neuartige Kommunikationsverfahren zu identifizieren, die auch unter extremen maritimen Einsatzbedingungen eine zuverlässige Datenübertragung ermöglichen. Im Mittelpunkt stehen disruptive Technologien, die über bestehende technische Standards hinausgehen und neue Möglichkeiten für die maritime Handlungsfähigkeit eröffnen.
Erste Bewährungsprobe auf der winterlichen Ostsee
Vom 7. bis 11. Dezember 2026 stehen die ersten Zwischenexperimente am Marinestützpunkt Eckernförde an. Die technische Herausforderung besteht darin, Informationen über sogenannte Beyond-Line-of-Sight-Distanzen (BLOS) zu übertragen. Gemeint sind Kommunikationsverbindungen über die direkte Sichtlinie hinaus. Gleichzeitig müssen die Lösungsansätze simulierten gegnerischen Störmaßnahmen standhalten. Wechselnde Wetterbedingungen und Seegang auf der winterlichen Ostsee erhöhen die Anforderungen an die Belastbarkeit der Systeme.
Die Zwischenexperimente dienen der technischen Standortbestimmung. Sie ermöglichen den Teams, die Leistungsfähigkeit ihrer theoretischen Ansätze zu überprüfen, Schwachstellen zu identifizieren und ihre Ideen gezielt zu optimieren. Die gewonnenen Erkenntnisse fließen unmittelbar in die abschließende Entwicklungsphase ein.
Finale Entscheidung im Februar 2027
Die Fähigkeit zur sicheren Kommunikation ist eine wesentliche Voraussetzung für die Führungs- und Handlungsfähigkeit maritimer Einheiten. Dies gilt insbesondere bei gestörten Kommunikationsverbindungen und für das Zusammenwirken bemannter und unbemannter Systeme. MARLIN verbindet deshalb die Erforschung technologisch risikoreicher Ansätze mit konkreten operativen Anforderungen der Marine.
Im Februar 2027 erreicht die Challenge mit der abschließenden Demo-Week ihren Höhepunkt. Dann werden die weiterentwickelten Lösungsansätze erneut unter realitätsnahen Bedingungen getestet. Ein hochrangig besetztes Preisgericht bewertet die Demonstratoren insbesondere nach ihrem disruptiven Innovationspotenzial, ihrer technischen Belastbarkeit und ihrer praktischen Eignung.
Auf Grundlage der Ergebnisse wird die Gewinnerlösung der MARLIN Challenge ermittelt. Die Erprobungen sollen zugleich Erkenntnisse über das Potenzial neuartiger Kommunikationstechnologien für zukünftige maritime Anwendungen liefern.

Im neuen Verbundprojekt LaHDo entwickelt das Laser Zentrum Hannover e.V. gemeinsam mit Industriepartnern ein neues Schweißverfahren und die zugehörige Systemtechnik, welches dickwandige Stahlbauteile bis 30 Millimeter besonders energie- und ressourcenschonend fügen soll.
Beim Schweißen dickwandiger Stahlbauteile werden bislang große Mengen an Energie und Zusatzmaterial benötigt. Im Projekt „Laserstrahl-Hybridschweißen mit Doppeldraht für prozess- und energieeffizientes Fügen von dickwandigen Bauteilen“ (LaHDo) arbeiten die Verbundpartner an einem neuen Hybridverfahren, das diesen Verbrauch senkt. Dabei füllt ein Lichtbogen mit zwei abschmelzenden Drahtelektroden die Schweißnaht mit hoher Füllrate auf. Ein zusätzlich gependelter Laserstrahl aktiviert gezielt die Fugenflanken und sorgt für eine bessere Anbindung des Materials. Im Gegensatz zu konventionellen Verfahren, bei dem die Fuge durch mehrere Lagen aufgefüllt wird, soll im neuen Verfahren eine Lage ausreichen. Dadurch lässt sich dann Energieeinsatz und Materialverbrauch deutlich reduzieren.
Die Projektpartner nutzen im Projekt dickwandige Bauteile aus unlegierten Stählen mit Materialstärken bis 30 Millimeter. Solche Bauteile kommen unter anderem im Maschinenbau, in Pipelines, in Turbinenschaufeln und im Schiffbau zum Einsatz.
LZH entwickelt Bearbeitungskopf und Schweißprozess
Im Projekt bauen die Partner die gesamte Prozesskette auf. Die Gruppe „Maschinen und Steuerungen“ des LZH entwickelt einen leistungsfähigen Hybridbearbeitungskopf und die Gruppe „Fügen und Trennen von Metallen“ die dazugehörigen Schweißprozesse. Die MERKLE Schweißanlagen-Technik GmbH steuert eine angepasste Schweißstromquelle bei, die 4D Photonics GmbH eine prozessintegrierte Inline-Prozesskontrolle und die HAANE welding systems GmbH & Co. KG die Demonstratoranlage. Ergänzend entwickelt die DURUM Verschleißschutz GmbH neuartige Fülldrähte mit Durchmessern bis 2,4 Millimeter und passenden Eigenschaften.
Unterstützt werden die Entwicklungsarbeiten durch assoziierte Partner aus der Industrie unter anderem: B.I.G. Technology Services GmbH, CIVAN Lasers Europe GmbH, Laser on demand GmbH, Precitec GmbH & Co. KG und Westfälische Drahtindustrie GmbH.
Über LaHDo
Das Verbundvorhaben „Laserstrahl-Hybridschweißen mit Doppeldraht für prozess- und energieeffizientes Fügen von dickwandigen Bauteilen (LaHDo)“ wird im Rahmen der Förderung angewandter Energieforschung im Rahmen des 8. Energieforschungsprogramms aus Mitteln des Bundesministeriums für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördert (FKZ: 03EN4132A).

title: 60 Jahre ELIZA, 50 Jahre Computerkritik – Was Joseph Weizenbaum uns heute noch zu sagen hat
content:
60 Jahre ELIZA, 50 Jahre Computerkritik – Was Joseph Weizenbaum uns heute noch zu sagen hat
Was passiert, wenn Menschen mit Maschinen reden? Diese Frage stellte der Informatiker Joseph Weizenbaum bereits vor 60 Jahren als er sein inzwischen berühmtes Computerprogramm ELIZA veröffentlichte.
Der erste Chatbot der Geschichte simulierte ein psychotherapeutisches Gespräch und zeigte, wie schnell Menschen Maschinen Empathie und andere menschliche Eigenschaften zuschreiben. Zehn Jahre später, im Jahr 1976, veröffentlichte Weizenbaum sein Buch „Computer Power and Human Reason“ (deutsche Übersetzung: „Die Macht der Computer und die Ohnmacht der Vernunft“), in dem er vor einer Gesellschaft warnte, die Entscheidungen und Verantwortung zunehmend Computern überlässt. 60 Jahre nach ELIZA und 50 Jahre nach Erscheinen seines Buches sind diese Fragen aktueller denn je.
Das Weizenbaum-Institut hat dieses Jubiläum mit einem Themenjahr gewürdigt. In zehn Veranstaltungen stellten Forschende unter anderem aus Kanada, den USA und Großbritannien gemeinsam mit den Wissenschaftler:innen des Weizenbaum-Instituts ihre Arbeiten zur Interaktion von Mensch und Maschine vor.
„Weizenbaums Kritik ist kein Blick zurück, sondern ein Kompass für die Gegenwart“, sagt Christoph Neuberger, Wissenschaftlicher Geschäftsführer des Weizenbaum-Instituts. „Seine zentrale Frage, was wir Maschinen überlassen wollen und was nicht, stellt sich angesichts der rasanten Entwicklung Künstlicher Intelligenz mit neuer Dringlichkeit. Sie berührt grundlegende Fragen unserer individuellen und demokratischen Selbstbestimmung.“
Internationale Resonanz
Internationale Wissenschaftler:innen, deren Perspektiven das Themenfeld nachhaltig prägen, haben das Jubiläumsjahr gemeinsam mit den Weizenbaum-Forschenden gestaltet: Zu den Gästen 2026 zählen mit Kate Crawford, Adrian Daub, Anna-Verena Nosthoff, Zizi Papacharissi, Sarah Ciston, David M. Berry, W. Patrick McCray, Sarah Sharma und Simon Strick. Ihre Perspektiven reichen von den ersten ELIZA-Versionen aus den 1960er Jahren, deren Programmcode von einem achtköpfigen Team um Ciston und Berry im MIT-Archiv entdeckt und detailliert analysiert wurde, über Sarah Sharmas Blick auf die großen Technologiekonzerne aus feministischer Perspektive, Papacharissis Forschung zu affektiver KI und dem demokratischen Miteinander bis hin zu Crawfords historischer Einordnung von KI als Machtfrage.
„ELIZA hat damals schon Fragen aufgeworfen, die uns bis heute noch begleiten, auch wenn die Technologie heutiger Chatbots eine gänzlich andere ist“, sagt Christian Strippel, Forschungsgruppenleiter am Weizenbaum-Institut und Verantwortlicher für das Jubiläum. „Von Fragen der Vermenschlichung von Computern, über die Rolle von Geschlecht im Kontext von Technik bis hin zur mythologischen Aufladung der Potenziale von KI: das Themenjahr hat gezeigt, dass all diese Themen seit ELIZA nicht an Relevanz und Aktualität verloren haben.“
Mit zwei weiteren Veranstaltungen im November klingt das ELIZA-Jubiläumsjahr aus:
- Am 17. November spricht Sarah Sharma über feministische Kritik an der Macht großer Technologiekonzerne: Insufferable Tools. Feminism Against Big Tech
- Am 19. November widmet sich Simon Strick in seinem Vortrag den politischen Dynamiken der Digitalisierung: Faschisierung. Fluchtlinie des Digitalen
Alle Veranstaltungen greifen zentrale Fragen des Jubiläumsjahres auf und führen die Auseinandersetzung mit den gesellschaftlichen Folgen digitaler Technologien weiter.
Auch über das Jubiläumsjahr hinaus wird die Auseinandersetzung mit Weizenbaums Erbe fortgeführt: Unter dem Titel „60 Years of ELIZA“ widmet etwa das Weizenbaum Journal of the Digital Society ELIZA ein umfangreiches Sonderheft. Mit rund 20 wissenschaftlichen Beiträgen internationaler Autor:innen beleuchtet es die Bedeutung des ersten Chatbots und die bis heute aktuellen Fragen der Mensch-Maschine-Interaktion. Das Sonderheft soll Mitte Dezember 2026 erscheinen.

Auf ihrer diesjährigen Mitgliederversammlung hat die renommierte acatech – Deutsche Akademie der Technikwissenschaften CISPA-Faculty Prof. Dr. Andreas Zeller in den Kreis ihrer wissenschaftlichen Mitglieder gewählt. Die acatech widmet sich der Förderung von Wissenschaft und Forschung und zählt derzeit über 700 Mitglieder, die den Ingenieur- und den Naturwissenschaften, der Medizin sowie den Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaften angehören. Entscheidend für die Aufnahme neuer Mitglieder sind deren wissenschaftliche Leistungen und Reputation. Die 2026 hinzugewählten Wissenschaftler:innen werden ihre Forschung auf der Mitgliederversammlung im kommenden Jahr vorstellen.
Andreas Zeller hat seine wissenschaftliche Karriere der Softwaresicherheit gewidmet. In seiner Forschung erarbeitet er Methoden und Tools, mit denen Softwareprodukte zuverlässiger und weniger fehleranfällig gestaltet werden können. So haben er und seine Forschungsgruppe etwa ein Open-Source-Tool für das automatisierte Testen von Software entwickelt. Basierend auf einem evolutionären Algorithmus generiert es unzählige hochwertige Testeingaben, die exakt den Anforderungen der Software-Entwickler:innen entsprechen. Über seine Aufnahme in die acatech sagt Andreas Zeller: „Ich freue mich sehr darauf, meine wissenschaftliche Expertise künftig in die gemeinwohlorientierte Politik- und Gesellschaftsberatung von acatech einzubringen. Der Dialog zwischen Wissenschaft und Gesellschaft und die transparente Kommunikation wissenschaftlich fundierter Erkenntnisse sind wichtige Pfeiler einer demokratischen Gesellschaft.“
Prof. Dr. Andreas Zeller ist Faculty am CISPA Helmholtz-Zentrum für Informationssicherheit und Professor für Software Engineering an der Universität des Saarlandes. Er forscht vorranging zu automatisiertem Debugging, Mining von Softwarearchiven, Spezifikationsfindung und Sicherheitstests. Den langfristigen internationalen Einfluss seiner Forschung belegen insgesamt 11 Test of Time Awards. Diese Auszeichnungen bemessen die überdauernde Wirkung einzelner Forschungsbeiträge. Zeller ist einer der wenigen Forschenden, die der European Research Council mit zwei ERC Advanced Grants ausgezeichnet hat. Andreas Zeller ist ACM Fellow, IEEE Fellow, Mitglied der Academia Europaea, und Träger eines ACM SIGSOFT Outstanding Research Award sowie eines ACM SIGSOFT Influential Educator Award.

acatech – Deutsche Akademie der Technikwissenschaften ist die von Bund und Sitzland Bayern geförderte nationale Akademie und Stimme der Technikwissenschaften im In- und Ausland. Sie berät Politik und Gesellschaft in technikwissenschaftlichen und technologiepolitischen Zukunftsfragen. Unter der Schirmherrschaft des Bundespräsidenten erfüllt acatech ihren Beratungsauftrag unabhängig, faktenbasiert und gemeinwohlorientiert. Die derzeit über 700 Mitglieder der Akademie sind herausragende Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler aus den Ingenieur- und den Naturwissenschaften, der Medizin sowie aus den Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaften.

title: KI für die Zellforschung: TH-Köln-Student erreicht zweiten Platz bei Kaggle-Wettbewerb
content:
KI für die Zellforschung: TH-Köln-Student erreicht zweiten Platz bei Kaggle-Wettbewerb
Soheil Ayati, Student im Masterstudiengang Automation & IT am Campus Gummersbach der TH Köln, hat beim internationalen Wettbewerb „Biohub Cell Tracking During Development“ den zweiten Platz unter 3.947 Teams erreicht. Für seine selbstständig entwickelte Lösung zur automatischen Zellverfolgung erhielt er eine Kaggle-Goldmedaille und ein Preisgeld von 12.000 US-Dollar.
Wie bewegen und teilen sich Zellen während der Entwicklung eines Embryos? Diese Frage stand im Mittelpunkt des Wettbewerbs, den die US-amerikanische Forschungsorganisation Biohub auf der Plattform Kaggle ausgelobt hatte. Anhand dreidimensionaler Mikroskopieaufnahmen von Zebrafisch-Embryonen sollten die Teilnehmenden Algorithmen entwickeln, die einzelne Zellen erkennen und ihre Entwicklung über mehrere Zeitpunkte hinweg verfolgen.
Die Lösungen mussten dabei nicht nur bestimmen, wo sich eine Zelle befindet und wie sie sich bewegt. Sie sollten auch Zellteilungen erkennen und rekonstruieren, welche Tochterzellen aus welcher Mutterzelle entstanden sind.
Zellen über viele Aufnahmen hinweg verfolgen
Biohub beschäftigt sich unter anderem mit der Verbindung von künstlicher Intelligenz und biologischer Forschung. Die Aufgabe stellt hohe Anforderungen an die automatische Bildauswertung: In einem sich entwickelnden Embryo bewegen sich zahlreiche Zellen gleichzeitig. Sie ähneln einander, liegen dicht beieinander und verändern ihre Position. Bildrauschen erschwert die Erkennung zusätzlich. Zudem war nur ein kleiner Teil der Zellen in den Trainingsdaten manuell gekennzeichnet.
Eine Zelle auf einer einzelnen Aufnahme zu erkennen, genügte deshalb nicht. Die Algorithmen müssen ihre Identität über viele aufeinanderfolgende Bilder hinweg korrekt zuordnen und zwischen einer Bewegung und einer Zellteilung unterscheiden. Eine weitere Herausforderung war, dass nur ein kleiner Teil der vorhandenen Zellen in den Trainingsdaten manuell gekennzeichnet war. Der Wettbewerb verband damit künstliche Intelligenz, maschinelles Lernen, dreidimensionale Bildverarbeitung, mathematische Optimierung und biologische Forschung.
Soheil Ayati musste funktionierende Algorithmen entwickeln, die auf unbekannte Mikroskopiedaten angewendet wurden. Ihre Ergebnisse wurden anhand eines einheitlichen mathematischen Bewertungssystems beurteilt. Dabei wurde unter anderem berücksichtigt, wie zuverlässig Zellen über verschiedene Zeitpunkte hinweg miteinander verknüpft und wie korrekt Zellteilungen erkannt wurden.
Nutzen für die Forschung: KI als Werkzeug für die Entwicklungsbiologie
Die automatische Zellverfolgung ermöglicht es Wissenschaftler*innen, die Entstehung und Entwicklung biologischer Strukturen besser zu untersuchen. Solche Analysen sind bisher teilweise sehr zeitaufwendig und erfordern umfangreiche manuelle Arbeit. Zuverlässige KI-Algorithmen können diesen Prozess erheblich beschleunigen und neue Möglichkeiten für die Entwicklungsbiologie sowie für die Untersuchung von Krankheiten und biologischen Prozessen eröffnen.
Ayati entwickelte und testete seine Lösung selbstständig und optimierte sie in zahlreichen Experimenten – in unzähligen Stunden und häufigen Nachtschichten. Für den Masterstudenten war es bereits die zweite Teilnahme an einem Kaggle-Wettbewerb. „Mein Ziel war es, zu gewinnen und dadurch andere Studierende zu inspirieren,“ sagt der 25-Jährige, der bereits das Studium der Elektrotechnik am Campus Gummersbach absolviert hat. Für sein Studium verließ er den Iran und zog in seine neue Heimat Gummersbach. Ayati beschäftigt sich außerdem im VDI-Team mit der Entwicklung autonom fahrender Roboter beschäftige. Das Preisgeld beim Kaggle-Wettbewerb in Höhe von 12.000 Euro will Ayati teilweise spenden.
Goldmedaille im internationalen Teilnehmerfeld
Für den Wettbewerb stellte die Organisation insgesamt 60.000 US-Dollar Preisgeld bereit. Insgesamt traten rund 4.500 Personen aus 120 Ländern an, organisiert in knapp 4.000 Teams, darunter etablierte Softwareentwickler*innen, Ingenieur*innen und Wissenschaftler*innen aus den Bereichen KI und Bildverarbeitung. Im Verlauf des Wettbewerbs wurden 95.438 Lösungen eingereicht. Mit dem zweiten Platz gehörte Soheil Ayati zu den besten rund 0,05 Prozent der teilnehmenden Teams. Insgesamt erhielten 17 Teams eine Goldmedaille.
Kaggle ist im Besitzt von Google LLC. und ist eine der weltweit größten Plattformen für künstliche Intelligenz (KI), maschinelles Lernen (Machine Learning) und Data Science. Unternehmen, Forschungseinrichtungen und weitere Organisationen richten dort Wettbewerbe zu technischen und wissenschaftlichen Fragestellungen aus.
Die TH Köln zählt zu den innovativsten Hochschulen für Angewandte Wissenschaften. Sie bietet Studierenden sowie Wissenschaftler*innen aus dem In- und Ausland ein inspirierendes Lern-, Arbeits- und Forschungsumfeld in den Sozial-, Kultur-, Gesellschafts-, Ingenieur- und Naturwissenschaften. Zurzeit sind über 21.000 Studierende in mehr als 90 Bachelor- und Masterstudiengängen eingeschrieben. Die TH Köln gestaltet Soziale Innovation – mit diesem Anspruch begegnen wir den Herausforderungen der Gesellschaft. Unser interdisziplinäres Denken und Handeln, unsere regionalen, nationalen und internationalen Aktivitäten machen uns in vielen Bereichen zur geschätzten Kooperationspartnerin und Wegbereiterin.

Diepholz, 9. November 2026. Ein Parkplatz, der mehr kann, als Autos einen Stellplatz zu bieten: Die Private Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Technik (PHWT) hat am Campus Diepholz eine außergewöhnliche Solar-Carportanlage errichten lassen, die künftig einen wichtigen Beitrag zur nachhaltigen Energieversorgung des Hochschulstandortes leisten wird. Am 9. November wurde die Anlage offiziell eingeweiht.
Das Besondere an der Anlage ist bereits auf den ersten Blick erkennbar: Der bestehende Parkplatz ist mit zwei Stellplatzreihen halbkreisförmig angelegt. Diese besondere Geometrie sollte bei der Überdachung aufgegriffen werden. Der Firma PfefferKnecht aus Süddeutschland gelang es als erster eine spezielle Metallkonstruktion für den Halbkreis zu entwickeln. Diese überspannt die Parkflächen und trägt die darauf installierten Photovoltaikmodule. Die Konstruktion wurde von der lokalen Firma Böckmann, einem langjährigen Partnerunternehmen der PHWT, errichtet. Insgesamt sind so 90 überdachte Pkw-Stellplätze entstanden.
Auf rund 1.150 Quadratmetern Dachfläche erzeugen die integrierten Glas-Glas-Photovoltaikmodule Solarstrom. Mit einer installierten Leistung von rund 230 kWp auf den Carports und weiteren 7,3 kWp auf einem zusätzlichen Fahrradunterstand erreicht das gesamte Projekt eine Photovoltaikleistung von rund 237 kWp. Der Bikeport bietet Platz für 20 Fahrräder. Eine patentrechtlich geschützte Besonderheit der Konstruktion: Die einzelnen Photovoltaikmodule übernehmen gleichzeitig die Funktion einer nahtlos wasserdichten Dacheindeckung. Eine darunter liegende Dachhaut ist somit nicht erforderlich. Integrierte LED-Lichtbänder sorgen zudem für eine Beleuchtung der überdachten Stellplätze.
Innovative Speichertechnologie ergänzt die Photovoltaikanlage
Ein wesentlicher Bestandteil des Projekts ist die Verbindung der Photovoltaikanlage mit einem modernen Batteriespeicher. Hier setzt die PHWT bewusst auf die neueste Batterietechnologie statt den bisher üblichen Lithium-Ionen-Speichern. Damit steht der erste Natrium-Ionen-Speicher in Niedersachsen (dritte in Deutschland) am PHWT-Campus in Diepholz. Er besteht aus zwei Natrium-Ionen-Speichercabinets der Firma PHENOGY mit einer gemeinsamen Speicherkapazität von 200 kWh und einer Lade- und Entladeleistung von 100 kW. Damit kann die PHWT einen größeren Anteil des selbst erzeugten Stroms zeitversetzt am Campus nutzen, beispielsweise für Lastspitzen, die nicht mehr teuer über das Netz, sondern über den gespeicherten Strom gedeckt werden können.
Die Natrium-Ionen-Technologie basiert auf gängigem Salz, dass auch in Deutschland vorkommt, sie kommt ohne Lithium, Graphit oder Kobalt aus. Dadurch ist die Speicherbatterie kaum brennbar und hat den weiteren Vorteil, ohne Leistungsabfall kälte- und hitzeresistent zu sein.
Ein anspruchsvolles Bauprojekt mit regionalen Partnern
Den Anstoß für das besondere Bauprojekt, das Architektur, erneuerbare Energieerzeugung und innovative Speichertechnologie vereint, gaben Prof. Dr. Dennis De, Präsident der PHWT, und Andreas Knecht, Geschäftsführer der PfefferKnecht GmbH. Die Planung und Umsetzung der Solarbauwerke übernahm die PfefferKnecht GmbH unter ihrer Marke LICHTKRAFT.
Die Umsetzung des Projekts erforderte eine intensive Planung, Abstimmung und Genehmigungen. Von der ersten Projektentwicklung bis zur Fertigstellung vergingen nur knapp 18 Monate. Ohne die entgegenkommende Unterstützung der Stadt Diepholz (Bauamt) hätte es deutlich länger gedauert – ihr gilt ein großer Dank. Die eigentliche Bauphase musste innerhalb eines engen Zeitfensters von nur zehn Wochen während der Semesterferien erfolgen. In dieser Zeit wurden unter anderem Erd- und Fundamentarbeiten durchgeführt, die Stahlkonstruktionen errichtet, die Photovoltaikdächer montiert und die technische Infrastruktur installiert. So konnten die Parkflächen rechtzeitig zum Beginn des neuen Semesters wieder zur Verfügung gestellt werden.
Die neue Solar-Carportanlage ergänzt ein bereits bestehendes nachhaltiges Energiekonzept am Campus Diepholz. Der Campus wird bereits über eine Eisspeicheranlage beheizt und gekühlt. Mit der Kombination aus Eisspeicher, Photovoltaik und innovativer Batteriespeichertechnologie baut die Hochschule ihre nachhaltige Energieinfrastruktur konsequent weiter aus und ist inzwischen Vorreiter weit über Niedersachsen hinaus.
Für die PHWT ist die Anlage damit nicht nur eine Investition in die eigene Energieversorgung, sondern auch ein sichtbares Beispiel für die Verbindung von technischer Innovation, Nachhaltigkeit und unternehmerischer Zusammenarbeit.

title: Neuer berufsbegleitender Master Car IT und Elektronik
content:
Neuer berufsbegleitender Master Car IT und Elektronik
Softwareentwicklung, Cybersecurity und Künstliche Intelligenz: OTH Regensburg und TH Deggendorf starten im April 2027 einen neu ausgerichteten Weiterbildungsmaster
Am 10. April 2027 startet der berufsbegleitende Masterstudiengang Car IT und Elektronik, den die OTH Regensburg gemeinsam mit der Technischen Hochschule Deggendorf anbietet. Hervorgegangen ist er aus dem 2007 eingeführten Master Automotive Electronics. Auf Basis einer Bedarfserhebung wurde der Studienplan gezielt weiterentwickelt: Fahrzeugtechnik und Elektronik bleiben, dazu kommen eigene Blockwochen für Automotive Cybersecurity sowie für KI und Data Science. „Die Bedarfserhebung hat ziemlich klar gezeigt, wohin es geht: neben der Hardwareentwicklung auch zunehmend in Richtung Datensicherheit und KI“, sagt Studiengangleiter Prof. Dr. Christian Schimpfle von der Fakultät Elektro- und Informationstechnik der OTH Regensburg. „Deshalb haben wir den Studiengang umgebaut und nicht einfach umbenannt.“
Der Master richtet sich weiterhin an Berufstätige aus Elektrotechnik und Maschinenbau, jetzt aber verstärkt auch an Beschäftigte der Automobilbranche, die aus der Informatik kommen. „Im Fahrzeug lassen sich Hardware und Software längst nicht mehr getrennt entwickeln. Deshalb sitzen in diesem Master Leute aus der Elektrotechnik, dem Maschinenbau und der Informatik in derselben Blockwoche“, sagt Prof. Dr. Rainer Holmer, Dekan der Fakultät.
Bedrohungsanalyse für die Ferndiagnose
Seit Juli 2024 muss jeder Hersteller, der in der EU neue Pkw, Busse oder Lkw zulassen will, nachweisen, dass er seine Fahrzeuge systematisch gegen Cyberangriffe absichert. So verlangt es die UN-Regelung R155. In der Blockwoche Automotive Cybersecurity führen die Teilnehmerinnen und Teilnehmer selbst eine vereinfachte Bedrohungs- und Risikoanalyse durch, etwa für den Fall, dass eine Werkstatt per Fernzugriff Fehler aus dem Fahrzeug ausliest. „Das betrifft alle, die eine Fahrzeugfunktion oder ein Steuergerät entwickeln, nicht bloß die Security-Abteilung“, sagt Prof. Dr. Schimpfle.
In der Woche KI und Data Science geht es um maschinelles Lernen in der Programmiersprache Python, samt einem selbst gewählten Datenanalyseprojekt. Die übrigen Wochen reichen vom Fahrzeug als Gesamtsystem über Software, die in Sekundenbruchteilen reagieren muss, bis zur Vernetzung: im Auto selbst und zwischen Fahrzeugen und Verkehrsinfrastruktur. Wie schon beim Vorgänger unterrichten Lehrende beider Hochschulen und Fachleute aus der Automobilbranche; den Abschluss verleihen OTH Regensburg und TH Deggendorf gemeinsam. Organisiert wird das Studium vom Zentrum für Weiterbildung und Wissensmanagement der OTH Regensburg (ZWW).
Sechs Blockwochen in Regensburg
Das Studium dauert vier Semester und endet mit dem Master of Engineering (M.Eng.). In den ersten drei Semestern reisen die Teilnehmerinnen und Teilnehmer je zweimal für eine Woche nach Regensburg. Hinzu kommen rund 250 Stunden Eigenstudium pro Modul. Das vierte Semester gehört der Masterarbeit. Voraussetzung sind ein abgeschlossenes Studium in Elektrotechnik, Maschinenbau, Mechatronik, Technischer Informatik oder einem verwandten Fach sowie mindestens ein Jahr Berufspraxis. Bewerbungsschluss ist der 17. Januar 2027.
Interessierte können sich für eine unverbindliche Online-Beratung zum Studienkonzept, den Inhalten und der Organisation jederzeit an die Studiengangkoordinatorin Bianca Hirthammer des ZWW wenden. Kontakt und Bewerbung: www.oth-regensburg.de/weiterbilden
